title: Dynamic Governance of Multi-LLM Agent Systems for Collaborative Conversational Outcomes
comment: 13 pages, 3 figures, 3 tables. Submitted to AI Engineer World's Fair 2026
summary: When two LLM agents with structurally opposed objectives interact across multiple turns, the absence of a shared goal function produces not competition but collapse: the visitor capitulates, the site agent stops varying its approach, and the conversation terminates without achieving either agent's stated objective. This paper asks whether a control-theoretic governance layer can substitute for that missing goal function. The Experience Orchestrator (EO) addresses this in a simulated financial services environment where a site agent guides a visitor toward advisor contact while the visitor maintains psychologically realistic resistance. EO governs the joint trajectory through three mechanisms: a Contextual Bandit (CB) that selects content arms calibrated from real-world web analytics, a PID controller that enforces behavioral consistency via dynamic schema constraints, and a POMDP belief tracker that maintains a probabilistic model of visitor intent. Across 60,000 simulations, EO achieves a +32 percentage point lift in high-intent advisor contact rate (78.1% vs. 46.1% over a naive LLM control), with CB variant selection accounting for 97% of between-factor outcome variance -- confirming that the governance policy, not environmental initial conditions, determines where trajectories end up. Persona-level analysis reveals two distinct regimes: for visitors with no natural inclination toward conversion, the governance layer is the difference between a functional system and a non-functional one; for visitors already near alignment, a naive LLM's empathetic defaults are largely sufficient. All findings are conditional on LLM-to-LLM simulation. The PID controller has not been calibrated against real human unpredictability, and validating EO on live traffic is the critical next step.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces a control-theoretic governance layer, the Experience Orchestrator (EO), that coordinates multi-turn interactions between opposed LLM agents in a financial-services-like setting, substantially improving conversion outcomes over naive LLM control.
AI.motivation: Multi-agent LLM interactions with structurally opposed objectives tend to collapse: one side quickly capitulates, the other stops exploring strategies, and neither stated goal is achieved. The authors want to know whether adding an external governance layer, grounded in control theory, can replace the missing shared goal function and stabilize/improve outcomes, specifically in a web-style financial services context where a site agent aims to drive advisor contact while a visitor resists.
AI.method: The authors build a simulated financial services environment with two LLM agents: a site agent trying to guide a visitor toward contacting an advisor and a visitor agent designed with psychologically realistic resistance to conversion. On top of these, they implement the Experience Orchestrator (EO), which governs the joint trajectory using: (1) a Contextual Bandit that chooses content variants (arms) calibrated from real web analytics; (2) a PID controller that enforces behavioral consistency via dynamic schema constraints on the agents; and (3) a POMDP-based belief tracker that maintains a probabilistic model of visitor intent. They then run 60,000 LLM-to-LLM simulations comparing EO-controlled conversations against a naive LLM baseline without this governance layer, and analyze overall performance and persona-level differences.
AI.result: In simulations, the EO governance layer increases the high-intent advisor contact rate by 32 percentage points compared with the naive LLM baseline (78.1% vs. 46.1%). Decomposition of variance shows that the choice of content variant by the Contextual Bandit explains 97% of between-factor outcome variance, indicating that the governance policy is the main driver of trajectory outcomes rather than initial environmental conditions. Persona-level analysis shows two regimes: (i) for visitors with low natural inclination to convert, EO turns a previously non-functional system into a functional one; (ii) for visitors already close to alignment with the site’s goals, naive LLM behavior is often adequate, with less marginal benefit from EO.
AI.conclusion: A control-theoretic governance layer can, in simulated multi-turn interactions between opposed LLM agents, effectively substitute for a missing shared goal function and dramatically improve goal achievement, primarily via well-optimized content selection policies. However, these findings are limited to LLM-to-LLM simulations; the PID controller and overall EO have not yet been tuned or validated against real human behavior. The authors conclude that deployment and testing on live human traffic is essential to confirm robustness and practical value.

title: Distribird: Literature-Informed Prior Distribution Design for Bayesian Model Calibration
summary: Bayesian calibration of process-based models requires a prior distribution for each model parameter. Despite decades of methodological work, researchers almost always fall back on uniform priors. The main reason is that building informative priors from scientific literature is slow and needs both domain and statistical expertise. We present \textbf{Distribird}, an agentic web application that automates this process. Given a parameter name, physical description, and domain context, Distribird deploys a multi-agent pipeline that searches the literature, extracts and weights reported values by domain relevance, and fits a probability distribution via AIC model selection. When no literature is available, the system falls back to sensible uninformative alternatives, and clearly reports both the evidence behind and the confidence level of every prior it produces. It is designed for the problems where the models have physically interpretable parameters, where domain knowledge exists in the published literature. We evaluate the tool on 24~parameters across 10 scientific domains comparing three open-weight models (Qwen3.6 27B, Gemma 4 31B, Mistral Small 4 119B) with a single-prompt LLM baseline. On prior quality the full pipeline \emph{matches} this baseline. Every prior is traced to the specific papers and values from which it was constructed; a built-in validity layer declines to produce priors for out-of-scope requests, whereas the single-prompt baseline returns confident but unfounded priors for them in 11 of 30~model--parameter cases; and every language-model call runs locally, so no parameter description or unpublished modelling detail is transmitted to a third-party LLM provider (only generated search terms reach the public literature databases). For scientific use, we argue these properties matter more than a marginal improvement in point-estimate accuracy.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces Distribird, an automated system that builds Bayesian priors for physically interpretable model parameters by mining scientific literature, matching the quality of a strong LLM baseline while adding transparency, traceability, and safety.
AI.motivation: Bayesian calibration needs prior distributions for parameters, but researchers often default to uniform priors because constructing informative priors from literature is time-consuming and requires both domain and statistical expertise. There is a need for a scalable, automated, and reliable way to derive informative priors from existing scientific knowledge, especially for process-based models with physically interpretable parameters.
AI.method: The authors develop Distribird, an agentic web application using a multi-agent LLM-based pipeline. Given a parameter name, its physical meaning, and the domain context, the system: (1) searches the scientific literature, (2) extracts reported parameter values, (3) weights them by domain relevance, and (4) fits a probability distribution using AIC-based model selection. If literature is missing, it falls back to sensible uninformative priors and quantifies confidence. The system includes a validity layer to reject out-of-scope queries, and it is implemented using local open‑weight models to preserve data privacy, with only search terms sent to public databases.
AI.result: On 24 parameters across 10 scientific domains, and using three open-weight models (Qwen3.6 27B, Gemma 4 31B, Mistral Small 4 119B), the complete Distribird pipeline achieves prior quality comparable to a strong single-prompt LLM baseline. However, unlike the baseline, Distribird provides transparent provenance for each prior (linking to specific papers and extracted values), declines to answer when queries are out-of-scope, and avoids sending sensitive model details to third-party API providers.
AI.conclusion: Distribird demonstrates that an automated, agentic LLM-based system can construct informative Bayesian priors from the literature with quality comparable to a strong LLM prompt baseline, while offering superior transparency, safety, and domain-of-validity checks. For scientific modeling, these reliability and governance properties are argued to be more important than small gains in numerical accuracy, suggesting that such structured, auditable pipelines are a promising direction for practical Bayesian calibration workflows.

title: A Forced-Structure Reduction and Verifiable Bounds for Conway's 99-Graph
comment: This paper is accepted to the first Conference For AI Scientists (CAISc)
summary: Conway's 99-graph problem asks whether a strongly regular graph with parameters $\mathrm{srg}(99,14,1,2)$ exists. We report a systematic, fully reproducible attack by an autonomous AI research agent, scored under the track's partial-credit metric. Our verifiable contributions are: (1) an exhaustive proof that no circulant graph on $\mathbb{Z}/99$ satisfies more than $3366/4950=68.0\%$ of the constraints ($33$ of $49$ difference-classes), with the same ceiling for the other abelian group of order $99$; (2) a forced-structure reduction: $λ=1$ makes each neighbourhood a perfect matching and $μ=2$ puts the outer vertices in bijection with non-matched neighbour-pairs, collapsing existence to a $12$-regular graph on $84$ vertices, encoded for CP-SAT and validated by recovering the unique $\mathrm{srg}(9,4,1,2)$; (3) a validated prescribed-automorphism orbit-existence framework (fixed-point-free and single-fixed-point actions, checked on $\mathrm{srg}(9,4,1,2)$ and the Paley graph $\mathrm{srg}(13,6,2,3)$), and (4) a best verified artifact at $69.43\%$, with evidence that this is a robust frontier (fourteen distinct methods, none exceeding it) entangled with the open question, since any provable bound below $4950$ is a non-existence proof.

AI.tldr: The paper uses an autonomous AI research agent to attack Conway's open 99-graph problem (existence of an srg(99,14,1,2)), giving partial but verifiable progress, strong structural reductions, and best-known computational lower bounds on violated constraints, though not a full existence or non-existence proof.
AI.motivation: Conway's 99-graph problem—whether a strongly regular graph with parameters srg(99,14,1,2) exists—has resisted traditional combinatorial and computational techniques. The authors aim to (a) push the structural and computational frontier on this specific open problem and (b) demonstrate that an autonomous AI research agent can contribute verifiably to deep unsolved questions in extremal graph theory under a partial-credit evaluation regime.
AI.method: They deploy an autonomous AI research agent that orchestrates combinatorial reasoning, algebraic structure analysis, and large-scale constraint programming (CP-SAT). First, it performs an exhaustive search over circulant graphs and graphs on the other abelian group of order 99, measuring how many of the strongly regular constraints can be satisfied. Second, it derives structural reductions from the parameters λ=1 and μ=2, showing that any such srg would induce neighbourhoods that are perfect matchings and an outer-vertex bijection with unmatched neighbour-pairs, reducing the existence question to a 12-regular graph on 84 vertices and encoding this as a CP-SAT instance, validated on the known srg(9,4,1,2). Third, it builds and validates a prescribed-automorphism orbit-existence framework for actions with no fixed points and with a single fixed point, tested on srg(9,4,1,2) and the Paley srg(13,6,2,3). Finally, it runs and cross-checks multiple independent search and optimization strategies to find graphs that maximize satisfied constraints, tracking a verified frontier.
AI.result: (1) They prove exhaustively that no circulant graph on Z/99 and no graph on the other abelian group of order 99 can satisfy more than 33 of the 49 difference-class constraints, i.e., at most 3366/4950 (68.0%) of the srg constraints. (2) They derive a strong structural reduction showing that the srg(99,14,1,2), if it exists, corresponds to a 12-regular graph on 84 vertices with a specific matching-based neighbourhood structure, and they successfully validate the reduction pipeline by recovering the unique srg(9,4,1,2) via CP-SAT. (3) They implement and validate an automorphism-orbit existence framework for fixed-point-free and single-fixed-point automorphisms, confirmed on known small SRGs. (4) They construct the best verified candidate artifact achieving 69.43% of the constraints and show via fourteen distinct methods that this appears to be a robust barrier, with no method surpassing it, implying any proof that no graph can reach 4950 constraints would settle non-existence of the sought SRG.
AI.conclusion: The work does not resolve Conway's 99-graph problem, but it significantly narrows and structures the search space and establishes strong computational and structural barriers. Their exhaustive negative results for abelian-group-based constructions, the forced-structure reduction to a 12-regular graph on 84 vertices, and the robust 69.43% frontier collectively show that further progress must overcome substantial combinatorial and algorithmic obstacles. At the same time, the study serves as a case demonstration that autonomous AI agents can make verifiable, partially creditable contributions to long-standing open problems in graph theory.

title: Detecting a Route Flip Is Easier Than Knowing Whether to Fix It: Causal Route-Mediated Damage in Quantized Mixture-of-Experts
comment: 13 pages, 2 figures, 8 tables. Pre-registered pilot study
summary: Top-k Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) routing is discontinuous, so a deployment-motivated numerical disturbance -- simulated 4-bit KV-cache quantization read by a protected BF16 gate -- pushes tokens across decision boundaries and flips which experts fire. This paper proposes no new mitigation; it supplies a causal apparatus, empirical findings, and a detection-limit result. A four-run apparatus prices the route-mediated fraction (RMF) of quantization damage, a token-level attribution decomposes it by mechanism, and pre-registered probes carry the findings across three architectures. On OLMoE-1B-7B at 4-bit KV (pilot), about a third of the damage is routing-mediated: RMF ~ 0.31 (discovery 0.31 [0.20, 0.41]; process-replicated mean 0.313 +/- 0.020; pre-registered re-execution 0.231). The deployable router margin detects that a flip occurred (AUC 0.772) but cannot tell a harmful flip from a helpful one (at chance): among the tested local, inference-observable router statistics we find no predictor of a flip's loss sign above chance -- an empirical benefit-detection barrier bounding selective repair restricted to this feature family. The signed-flip tax and sign-inseparability carry cross-model; the clean-reference remedy's payout is architecture-modulated; a controlled same-checkpoint flag-swap re-scopes the gate's normalization convention to a damage-magnitude moderator, not a route-recoverability mechanism. A real int4 KV kernel yields a fraction compatible with the fake-quant dose curve but underpowered (95% CI [-0.111, 0.394] includes zero) -- ruling out gross disagreement, not an independent replication. Hypotheses, thresholds, and evaluations were pre-registered before measurement, with misses reported; a pre-registered held-out read replicates the partition and the near-cancelling tax out of sample, while the strict impossibility exclusion narrowly misses.

AI.tldr: Studies how 4-bit KV-cache quantization indirectly harms MoE models by flipping which experts are selected, and shows such harmful vs helpful flips can’t be distinguished using simple router-side signals.
AI.motivation: In MoE LLMs, routing is discrete: small numerical changes can change which experts fire. Deployment-relevant KV-cache quantization may perturb routing, but its contribution to quality loss and the possibility of selectively fixing only harmful flips were unclear. The paper aims to quantify how much damage is mediated by routing changes and whether locally observable router statistics can be used to detect and repair only bad routing flips.
AI.method: Introduce a four-run experimental setup to isolate the fraction of performance loss specifically due to route changes under simulated 4-bit KV quantization of the KV-cache, while keeping the gating network in higher precision. Use token-level attribution to decompose damage mechanisms. Apply pre-registered probes and analysis across three architectures (including OLMoE-1B-7B) to measure the route-mediated fraction (RMF) of damage and study various router-margin-like statistics as predictors of whether a quantization-induced expert flip is helpful or harmful. Perform additional tests including a clean-reference remedy, a same-checkpoint flag-swap to change normalization conventions, and experiments with a real int4 KV kernel to compare with the simulated dose curve.
AI.result: On OLMoE-1B-7B with 4-bit KV quantization, roughly one-third of the quantization-induced degradation is mediated by routing changes (RMF around 0.31, with multiple replication runs supporting this). The router margin can detect that a flip occurred with reasonable accuracy (AUC ~0.77) but cannot predict the sign of its impact on loss: all examined inference-time router statistics fail to distinguish harmful from helpful flips better than chance. The study identifies a “signed-flip tax” and sign-inseparability that generalize across models; the benefit from using a clean reference for repair depends on architecture. A flag-swap experiment shows that normalization choices affect the magnitude of damage but not whether routes are recoverable. A real int4 KV kernel produces an RMF estimate statistically compatible with the simulated dose curve but with wide confidence intervals including zero, so it cannot serve as an independent strong replication. Pre-registered held-out evaluations replicate the main partition of damage and the near-cancelling effect of signed flips, though one strict impossibility claim narrowly fails to be excluded.
AI.conclusion: Routing changes caused by deployment-style KV-cache quantization contribute a substantial but partial share of performance loss in MoE models. However, within the family of simple, inference-observable router statistics studied, there appears to be an empirical barrier to detecting which individual routing flips are harmful versus helpful. This limits the effectiveness of selective, flip-wise repair strategies based solely on such signals, and suggests that mitigating quantization damage may require different approaches (e.g., architectural changes, better training, or richer side information) rather than simple margin-based flip detection. The work emphasizes careful causal attribution, pre-registration, and cross-model checks in evaluating MoE robustness under quantization.

title: Backtrader-Bench: Benchmarking LLM Agents on Algorithmic Trading with Self-Generated MCQs
comment: Accepted to the FinLLM Workshop at IJCAI 2026. Code and data: https://github.com/rzhao999/Backtrader-Bench
summary: Evaluating LLM coding agents in algorithmic trading is difficult because static benchmarks risk data contamination and numerical backtest outputs require ground truth from actual code execution. We present Backtrader-Bench, a framework with two complementary pipelines. A deterministic multiple-choice question (MCQ) pipeline generates questions from backtest configurations across five trading strategies, 33 templates, and three difficulty tiers, with an independent checker that re-derives every answer. A generator-solver filtering pipeline autonomously mines harder questions: a generator writes questions verified by executable code, converts them to MCQs, and discards any that a no-tool solver can answer without code execution. We evaluate 11 models without tools (10 runs each) and four with-tools configurations on a 30-question curated set. Tool-augmented agents reach 90.0% accuracy in a single pass (GPT-5.5 and Opus 4.7), outperforming the best no-tools baselines (73.0%, averaged over 10 runs) by 17 percentage points. On 38 separately mined questions, no-tools accuracy drops further, with half the models falling to roughly random-chance level (25%). Beyond evaluation, the scalable MCQ infrastructure is designed to produce a training corpus for reinforcement learning, with the ultimate goal of building a specialized agent for quantitative trading workflows.

AI.tldr: Backtrader-Bench introduces an executable-code-based benchmark for evaluating LLM coding agents in algorithmic trading via deterministic MCQs and a generator-solver pipeline that mines hard, contamination-resistant questions.
AI.motivation: Existing evaluations of LLM coding agents in algorithmic trading are unreliable: static text benchmarks risk training data contamination, and numeric backtest outputs are hard to validate without running real code and reconciling with a ground truth. The authors want a principled, scalable way to test whether LLMs can correctly reason about, implement, and interpret algorithmic trading strategies under realistic backtesting conditions, and to create a data source suitable both for evaluation and for training specialized trading agents.
AI.method: They build Backtrader-Bench, centered on a backtesting engine. First, a deterministic MCQ pipeline programmatically generates multiple-choice questions from backtest configurations that span five trading strategies, 33 question templates, and three difficulty levels; an independent checker re-derives each correct answer to avoid errors. Second, a generator-solver filtering pipeline autonomously produces more difficult questions: a generator model writes questions grounded in executable backtest code; these are validated by running the code, converted to MCQs, and then filtered out if a no-tools model can already solve them without code execution, leaving only questions that truly require tool use. They then run a systematic evaluation of 11 LLMs without tools (10 random-seed runs each) and several tool-augmented configurations on curated and mined question sets.
AI.result: On a curated 30-question benchmark, tool-augmented agents (e.g., GPT-5.5 and Opus 4.7) achieve 90.0% single-pass accuracy, outperforming the strongest no-tools baselines, which average 73.0% over 10 runs, by about 17 percentage points. On an additional 38 more challenging, mined questions, accuracy for no-tools models drops markedly, with around half of them performing near random-guess levels (~25%), demonstrating that these questions are substantially harder and expose limitations of pure reasoning without code execution.
AI.conclusion: Backtrader-Bench provides a robust, contamination-resistant framework to evaluate and train LLM coding agents in algorithmic trading by tightly coupling MCQ generation with executable backtest validation. Tool-augmented models clearly outperform no-tools variants, especially on hard questions that require actual code execution, underscoring the value of tool integration for quantitative trading tasks. The authors position the benchmark not only as an evaluation suite but also as scalable infrastructure to generate RL training data for developing specialized quantitative trading agents.

title: Poor Man's Agentic Modeling: Simulating Large LLM-Agent Societies on a Laptop
comment: 25 pages, 12 figures. Code and data at github.com/YehudaItkin/poor-mans-agentic-modeling; systematic review and pre-registration archived at Zenodo (doi:10.5281/zenodo.21198322, doi:10.5281/zenodo.21340310)
summary: Simulating societies of many large language model (LLM) agents is expensive, yet the questions asked of such simulations are usually macroscopic: phase behaviour, stylised facts, and scaling with the number of agents $N$, not the cognition of any single agent. We turn a statistical-physics observation into a method: replace each LLM agent by a low-parameter model fitted from a few hundred to a few thousand cheap queries, then run the society at any $N$ on a laptop. Whether this works is decided before the simulation runs, chiefly by what each agent perceives. We introduce an [interaction order x memory] taxonomy that maps perception and memory to an effective theory and a predicted $N$-trend of the surrogate error. We validate it on a faithful reimplementation of the LLM macroeconomy EconAgent and seven further named LLM simulations, with agent decisions cloned from genuine LLM elicitations (primarily DeepSeek) for a few dollars; the predicted error trends hold cell by cell, and the two refuted predictions, both on a strongly saturating response and traced to its curvature, are themselves matched quantitatively by the theory with no free parameters.

AI.tldr: They propose replacing expensive large language model (LLM) agents in multi-agent simulations with cheap, low-parameter surrogate models learned from a small number of LLM queries, enabling large-scale simulations on modest hardware while predicting how approximation error scales with the number of agents.
AI.motivation: Running societies of many LLM agents is computationally and financially expensive, yet most research questions about such systems concern aggregate, macroscopic behaviours rather than the detailed cognition of individual agents. There is a need for a principled way to approximate these agents so that researchers can study large-N behaviour, phase transitions, and stylised facts without incurring huge costs.
AI.method: They leverage an analogy to statistical physics: each LLM agent is replaced with a low-parameter surrogate model that approximates the LLM’s decision rule, learned from a few hundred to a few thousand cheap queries. They then introduce a taxonomy based on interaction order and memory that classifies agents according to what they perceive and remember, which in turn determines the appropriate effective theory and a prediction for how the surrogate’s error should scale with the number of agents N. They test this on a faithful reimplementation of the EconAgent macroeconomic LLM simulation and seven other named LLM simulations, cloning agent decisions primarily from DeepSeek outputs.
AI.result: The surrogate models, once fitted, allow full multi-agent simulations to be run at arbitrary scale N on a laptop, with predicted error trends that match theoretical expectations. In the validation tasks (EconAgent plus seven other LLM simulations), the empirically observed cell-by-cell error scaling with N agrees with the taxonomy’s predictions. Two cases where the initial prediction is refuted are explained by strongly saturating response curves; after accounting for curvature, the theory quantitatively matches the observed deviations without introducing additional free parameters.
AI.conclusion: Low-parameter surrogate models can reliably stand in for expensive LLM agents in many-agent simulations, provided one accounts for the agents’ perception and memory structure via the proposed interaction-order-by-memory taxonomy. This framework both enables cheap, large-scale simulations and offers predictive control over how approximation errors scale with system size N, making it practical to study macroscopic behaviours of LLM societies without running all agents as full LLMs.

title: Retrofitting Recurrent Depth into a Pretrained Language Model: Installation, Extrapolation, Transfer, and Retention at Two Parameter Budgets
summary: A dense, pretrained language model can be retrofitted with recurrent depth and learn an iterative latent transition that persists after outcome-only annealing. Qwen2.5-0.5B-Instruct is split into a Prelude, a weight-tied Recurrent Block, and a Coda, with an identity-preserving one-loop path and a re-entry bridge on later loops. At loop 1 the retrofit remains non-inferior to its base on a preregistered ARC battery. Three findings. First, the mechanism is a reusable procedure rather than terminal-answer lookup, and installs at two budgets: 6M trained parameters over frozen base weights and 180M full-block. With intermediate-step supervision, the model computes one task step per loop and persists when only final answers are graded. The adapter matched the full block overall (83.8% versus 84.0%), led through depth 11, and trailed beyond. Verbal fine-tuning reached 79-86% on controlled verbal renderings (zero-shot transfer was minimal), and adapter verbal training begun from the installed mechanism outpaced matched fresh training by 18.6 points, including on a held-out test set. Second, the operation extrapolates to roughly 1.5 times its supervised depth, holding 70% accuracy through depth 18. Third, a same-size scratchpad-trained model matched the recurrent model within its learned horizon but collapsed beyond it. The recurrent model won overall, 84% versus 72%, retained 53% versus 2.5% beyond depth 10, and answered 7.6 times faster. An iterative transformer can therefore perform deeper reasoning in latent space faster than comparable or larger models fine-tuned on the same task, in a system-level comparison. A second task, running the rule in reverse, exposed the limits: the inverse was learnable in isolation, but no continuation acquired it while preserving the installed mechanism and general capability, a catastrophic-interference boundary. Learned depth selection remains open.

AI.tldr: The paper retrofits a small pretrained transformer (Qwen2.5-0.5B) with a recurrent depth mechanism so it can iteratively reason in latent space over multiple loops, achieving deeper, faster reasoning than comparable fine-tuned models while keeping base capabilities largely intact.
AI.motivation: Standard dense pretrained language models often struggle with systematically extending their reasoning depth, and scratchpad-style fine-tuning can be slow, brittle, and may not generalize beyond the seen reasoning horizon. The authors want to test whether adding explicit recurrent depth on top of a frozen pretrained model can yield an iterative internal procedure that generalizes to deeper reasoning, is reusable across tasks or prompts, and is more efficient and robust than traditional fine-tuning, without sacrificing the base model’s competence.
AI.method: They take Qwen2.5-0.5B-Instruct and structurally decompose it into three parts: a Prelude (initial processing), a weight-tied Recurrent Block (executed multiple times as loops), and a Coda (final decoding). They add an identity-preserving one-loop path and a re-entry bridge that lets the model re-enter the recurrent block on subsequent loops while maintaining latent consistency. They train this recurrent layer under two parameter budgets: (1) a small adapter of ~6M parameters on top of frozen base weights, and (2) a larger 180M-parameter full recurrent block. Training first uses intermediate-step supervision (“one reasoning step per loop”), then they anneal to outcome-only supervision (grading only final answers) to see if the learned iterative mechanism persists. They evaluate on a preregistered ARC-style reasoning battery with controlled depth, compare against a scratchpad-trained model of similar size and horizon, and also run a second “inverse” task that requires running the learned rule in reverse to probe interference and limits of compositionality.
AI.result: 1) The recurrent mechanism behaves as a reusable latent procedure rather than memorizing final answers, and can be installed effectively with both a small adapter (6M) and a larger full block (180M). Under intermediate-step supervision, the model performs one task step per loop and continues to do so even when training is switched to outcome-only. The small adapter closely matches the full block overall (83.8% vs 84.0% accuracy), is better up to depth 11, and only falls behind at greater depths. Verbal fine-tuning on structured verbal formats obtains 79–86% accuracy but with poor zero-shot transfer; however, initializing adapter verbal training from the installed recurrent mechanism gives an 18.6-point improvement over training from scratch, including on held-out data. 2) The learned operation extrapolates to around 1.5× the supervised depth, maintaining ~70% accuracy through depth 18, showing nontrivial depth generalization. 3) A comparably sized scratchpad-trained model matches the recurrent model only within the depth it was trained for, but fails sharply beyond that horizon. The recurrent model achieves higher overall accuracy (84% vs 72%), retains 53% accuracy beyond depth 10 vs 2.5% for the scratchpad model, and is 7.6× faster in inference for the tasks considered.
AI.conclusion: Retrofitting a pretrained transformer with an explicit recurrent depth block yields an iterative latent procedure that improves depth-generalization and efficiency on reasoning tasks versus conventional scratchpad fine-tuning, while largely preserving base performance. The recurrent model can perform more steps of internal reasoning, extrapolate beyond its supervised depth, and do so faster than comparable or larger non-recurrent baselines, indicating that iterative transformers are a promising architecture for deeper reasoning. However, the mechanism has limits: attempting to learn an inverse rule on top of an already installed recurrent procedure leads to catastrophic interference—no model could acquire the inverse while retaining the original mechanism and general capabilities. This highlights current boundaries in compositional learning of multiple iterative procedures and leaves open problems such as how to select or adapt depth dynamically without interference.

title: AutoWorldModel-Bench: A State-Centric Benchmark for Automated World-Model Research
summary: World modeling is an unsettled field: architectures, training objectives, and state representations interact in complex ways, and no single recipe dominates across environments. This makes it an ideal testbed for AI coding agents acting as autonomous researchers--a setting in which the improvement direction is not specified in advance, unlike the engineering-to-spec tasks that dominate current agent benchmarks. We introduce AutoWorldModel-Bench, a closed-loop benchmark in which frontier coding agents autonomously improve a provided world-model starter under a fixed compute budget. The benchmark spans eight game environments under a unified structured-state representation--ground-truth entity state extracted from each game and consumed through a shared tensor format--which isolates dynamics modeling from perception and enables minutes-per-run iteration. Across 64 sessions, Codex-5.4 and Claude Opus 4.6 improve their starter on 63; in 91% of sessions the winning edit is a non-trivial research-style modification--a new objective, representation, rollout procedure, or architectural change--rather than a hyperparameter tweak. Our benchmark offers a setting in which frontier coding agents can be evaluated on open-ended research rather than engineering-to-spec problems.

AI.tldr: The paper presents AutoWorldModel-Bench, a closed-loop benchmark where AI coding agents autonomously improve a given world-model under compute constraints, enabling evaluation on open-ended research rather than fixed-spec engineering tasks.
AI.motivation: World modeling lacks a dominant architecture or training paradigm, with many interacting design choices and no clear best practice across environments. This makes it a challenging and realistic setting for assessing autonomous AI coding agents. Existing benchmarks mostly test agents on well-specified engineering tasks, not on open-ended research where the improvement direction is unknown in advance. The authors want a benchmark that captures the latter.
AI.method: The authors design AutoWorldModel-Bench, a benchmark where coding agents start from a baseline world-model implementation and iteratively modify it under a fixed compute budget. The benchmark covers eight different game environments that all share a unified, structured state representation: ground-truth entity states from each game are transformed into a common tensor format. This focuses the task on dynamics modeling instead of perception and allows fast, minutes-scale training/evaluation cycles. Agents like Codex-5.4 and Claude Opus 4.6 are run in closed-loop sessions where they propose and test code edits to improve model performance.
AI.result: In 64 benchmark sessions, Codex-5.4 and Claude Opus 4.6 successfully improve upon the starter world model in 63 sessions. Furthermore, in 91% of sessions, the best-performing change is a substantive, research-like modification—such as introducing a new training objective, representation scheme, rollout strategy, or model architecture—rather than simply tuning hyperparameters. This shows that the agents can produce meaningful algorithmic innovations within the benchmark setting.
AI.conclusion: AutoWorldModel-Bench provides a practical, fast-iteration testbed to evaluate frontier coding agents on open-ended research tasks in world modeling. The results suggest that current agents can consistently improve a baseline model and often do so via non-trivial, research-grade changes. The benchmark thus moves evaluation beyond narrow engineering-to-spec problems toward more realistic, creative research scenarios.

title: TRACE Bench: Task-driven Roleplay Agentic Checklist Evaluation
summary: Roleplay evaluation should do more than assign a single score: it should reveal which role requirements were tested, which failed, and which dialogue evidence supports the judgment. We propose TRACE Bench, a task-driven agentic checklist evaluation framework. It decomposes each role profile offline into a fixed checklist, then uses a User Agent to converse naturally with the target roleplay model while privately updating checklist states from model responses. Scores therefore trace back to checklist items and supporting dialogue turns rather than a black-box holistic impression. For coverage cross-validation, we audit released M2 free-dialogue transcripts from the MiniMax Role-play Benchmark against the same role-derived checklist. The released free-chat transcripts cover only 73.74% of key role-profile points, whereas TRACE Bench reaches 99.91% coverage in fewer turns. Robustness experiments show stable rankings under repeated runs and User Agent replacement. Across 26 models, TRACE Bench reports overall rankings together with capability breakdowns and checklist traces. It also supports Closed-Loop Benchmark Evolution, distilling verification methods proven effective in failed traces so later evaluations can more reliably elicit and examine observed failure modes.

AI.tldr: TRACE Bench is a checklist-based, task-driven framework for evaluating roleplay models that outputs traceable, fine-grained scores instead of a single opaque rating.
AI.motivation: Existing roleplay evaluations typically yield a single holistic score or impression, which fails to show what specific role requirements were tested, which ones failed, and what dialogue evidence supports those judgments. There is also concern about whether free-form benchmark conversations adequately cover the intended role specifications and about the stability and robustness of evaluation rankings.
AI.method: The authors introduce TRACE Bench, which first decomposes each target role profile into a fixed checklist of requirements offline. During evaluation, a dedicated User Agent interacts naturally with the roleplay model while privately updating the checklist states based on the model’s responses. Each checklist item is linked to specific dialogue turns as evidence. They cross-validate coverage by auditing existing MiniMax Role-play Benchmark (M2) free-dialogue transcripts with the same checklists, compare coverage to TRACE Bench runs, and conduct robustness experiments, including repeated runs and swapping different User Agents. They apply TRACE Bench to 26 models and support Closed-Loop Benchmark Evolution by reusing verification methods that were effective in previous failed traces.
AI.result: TRACE Bench attains 99.91% coverage of key role-profile points in fewer dialogue turns, versus 73.74% coverage for the released M2 free-chat transcripts. The evaluation rankings of models are stable across repeated runs and under different User Agents. For each of the 26 evaluated models, TRACE Bench produces overall rankings, detailed capability breakdowns, and traceable checklist-item-level evidence drawn from specific dialogue turns.
AI.conclusion: TRACE Bench provides a more transparent, fine-grained, and coverage-efficient way to evaluate roleplay models than prior free-dialogue approaches. By tracing scores to checklist items and dialogue evidence, it enables better diagnosis of strengths and weaknesses. Its robustness to evaluator changes and its Closed-Loop Benchmark Evolution mechanism suggest it can serve as a scalable, evolving framework for reliably uncovering and re-testing roleplay failure modes over time.

title: MaSRead: Content-Addressed Reading of Replicated Latent Stores
summary: Independent agents that reason in latent space can share computed state as key-value cache fragments rather than text. Merged by a conflict-free replicated data type, these fragments form a store that converges under any delivery order or duplication. Yet a later query, unknown at encode time, cannot reliably read the merged cache: colocated fragments interfere, so colocation is not addressability. MaSRead addresses the read to content. It routes through opaque keyed tag sets derived from fragment words and decodes each selected fragment under a hard attention mask that hides the rest. Under lexical connectivity, a graph walk reaches the fragments required by a multi-hop query. Across chain, pipeline, symmetric, hub, and natural-language stores, MaSRead recovers visited fragments in isolation, remains effective as unrelated fragments accumulate, and transfers to another model family. After routing, materialized decoding depends on fragment length rather than total store size; end-to-end work still includes store-dependent routing and one read per visited fragment. The limits are explicit: lexical routing can miss disconnected evidence, and answer composition remains bounded by the frozen reader. Thus a replicated latent store becomes selectively readable for later queries when the needed fragments connect to the query through content.

AI.tldr: Method to make shared latent-state caches from independent agents selectively readable using content-based routing and masked decoding.
AI.motivation: Independent agents can share intermediate reasoning as key–value cache fragments, but once merged via CRDTs, later queries cannot reliably retrieve just the relevant fragments because colocation in the store does not provide clean addressability.
AI.method: Introduce MaSRead, a content-addressed reading mechanism that: (1) derives opaque keyed tag sets from fragment words; (2) routes queries through these tags using lexical connectivity and graph walks to locate connected fragments; and (3) decodes each selected fragment with a hard attention mask so it is read in isolation from other colocated fragments. Evaluate on different store topologies (chain, pipeline, symmetric, hub, natural-language) and across model families.
AI.result: MaSRead can recover and read in isolation the fragments that were actually visited in multi-hop reasoning, stays robust as many unrelated fragments accumulate in the store, and generalizes to a different model family. After routing, decoding cost scales with fragment length rather than global store size, though routing still depends on store size and incurs one read per visited fragment.
AI.conclusion: With MaSRead, a replicated latent store composed of CRDT-merged cache fragments becomes selectively readable for later, previously unknown queries—provided that the needed fragments are lexically connected to the query—while making explicit limits around disconnected evidence and answer composition constraints from the frozen reader.

title: Lost in Compaction: Evaluating Side-Constraint Loss under Context Compaction
summary:
When the context window is under pressure, LLM systems compact prior context to continue ongoing tasks. We identify a class of user-issued instructions, Session Constraints (SCs), such as "do not delete any emails until I confirm," that are meant to constrain LLM's behavior for the remainder of a session but are silently dropped during compaction. To quantify this loss, we introduce COMPINT, an evaluation suite that evaluates compactors across three long-context scenarios: multi-turn chat, agentic trajectory, and long-horizon research.
  Current compactors retain only 17% of injected SCs on average, and most perform worse than running the same task without compaction. Retention varies sharply with compactor, prompt, context length, SC phrasing, and injection location, showing that the loss is systematic rather than tied to any single setting. We propose an SC-aware extractor that runs alongside the compactor as a plug-and-play module, achieving over 90% retention across all three scenarios without modifying the compactor or LLM. The COMPINT evaluation suite and accompanying implementation are available at https://github.com/ZhiqiEliWang/compaction-integrity.

AI.tldr: The paper shows that when large language models compress long conversations, they often drop persistent user instructions (Session Constraints), and introduces an evaluation suite (COMPINT) plus a plug-in extractor that preserves these instructions with high reliability.
AI.motivation: LLM applications with long-running sessions rely on compaction to stay within context limits, but users frequently state persistent constraints like "don’t do X until I say so." These constraints are intended to hold for the rest of the session. Existing compaction methods may silently discard them, causing LLMs to violate user expectations and safety requirements. There was no standardized way to measure or mitigate this failure mode, motivating a systematic study and benchmark.
AI.method: The authors (1) define Session Constraints (SCs) as user instructions intended to remain in force for the rest of the session; (2) construct COMPINT, an evaluation suite covering three realistic long-context scenarios: multi-turn chat, agentic trajectories, and long-horizon research, where SCs are injected into the interaction history; (3) test existing compaction methods on how well they retain SCs after compaction, measuring both SC retention and downstream task performance; and (4) design an SC-aware extractor that runs in parallel with the compactor to identify and preserve SCs as a plug-and-play module without changing the underlying compactor or LLM.
AI.result: Across the three scenarios, existing compactors on average keep only about 17% of injected SCs, and many configurations perform worse than having no compaction at all. Retention rates depend strongly on the specific compactor, prompt template, context length, wording of the SC, and where in the conversation the SC is injected, indicating a systemic problem. The proposed SC-aware extractor, when used alongside existing compactors, achieves over 90% SC retention in all scenarios without modifying the LLM or compactor architecture.
AI.conclusion: Session Constraints—user instructions intended to persist over an entire session—are frequently lost during context compaction in long LLM interactions, posing reliability and safety risks. The COMPINT benchmark exposes how severe and systematic this problem is across settings. A simple, modular SC-aware extractor can largely fix the issue, boosting SC retention above 90% while remaining compatible with existing compaction pipelines. COMPINT and the released implementation provide practical tools for evaluating and improving compaction integrity in LLM systems.

title: From Monolithic to Modular: Segment-level Automatic Prompt Optimization
comment: Accepted at the IJCAI-ECAI 2026 Workshop on Robustifying Generative AI for Reliable, Safe, and Human-Centric Systems (RobustifAI)
summary: Automatic Prompt Optimization (APO) often rewrites prompts monolithically, which can improve one behavior while degrading others. We present SAPO, a segment-level APO method that decomposes prompts into role, context, tasks, and output format, then applies targeted improvements based on top-5 and bottom-5 examples. The optimization loop uses one LLM with static meta-prompts and structured outputs for segmentation, weakness analysis, and candidate generation. We describe a train/validation protocol and a two-stage generation process: (1) segment-level diagnosis and recommendation extraction, (2) candidate synthesis constrained by weak/strong segment signals. Using the evaluation setup across SQuADv2, TweetEval, XSUM, CommonGen, and GSM8K on GPT-3.5-Turbo and GPT-4o-mini, SAPO achieves the best average score against Zero-shot and strong APO baselines including APE, OPRO, EvoPrompt, GEPA, and StraGO.

AI.tldr: SAPO is a segment-level automatic prompt optimization method that decomposes prompts into functional parts and improves weak segments using performance data, outperforming strong APO baselines across multiple benchmarks and models.
AI.motivation: Existing automatic prompt optimization methods typically rewrite the entire prompt as a single block. This monolithic optimization can fix one behavior but unintentionally harm others because it lacks fine-grained control over different functional components of the prompt (e.g., role, context, task description, and output format). There is a need for a more structured, interpretable, and controllable way to improve prompts that can leverage feedback from good and bad examples while avoiding regressions on previously strong behaviors.
AI.method: SAPO first segments a prompt into four components: role, context, tasks, and output format. Using a single LLM guided by static meta-prompts and structured outputs, it runs an optimization loop over a train/validation split. The loop consists of two stages. Stage 1 performs segment-level diagnosis by analyzing the top-5 best-performing and bottom-5 worst-performing examples, extracting weaknesses and recommendations for each segment. Stage 2 synthesizes new candidate prompts by selectively modifying weak segments while preserving or reinforcing strong ones, constrained by the diagnostic signals. The same LLM is used for segmentation, weakness analysis, and candidate generation under a unified, structured prompting scheme.
AI.result: Across five benchmarks (SQuADv2, TweetEval, XSUM, CommonGen, GSM8K) and with two LLMs as the target models (GPT-3.5-Turbo and GPT-4o-mini), SAPO achieves the best average performance compared with zero-shot baselines and several strong automatic prompt optimization baselines, including APE, OPRO, EvoPrompt, GEPA, and StraGO.
AI.conclusion: Segment-level, structure-aware prompt optimization can outperform monolithic APO by enabling targeted, interpretable modifications to different prompt components. By diagnosing strengths and weaknesses at the segment level using a single LLM and structured meta-prompts, SAPO can reliably improve overall performance across diverse tasks and models while reducing the risk of harming already-strong behaviors. This suggests that future APO research should emphasize prompt decomposition, diagnostic feedback, and constrained candidate synthesis rather than holistic rewriting alone.

title: Diffuse to Compress: Leveraging Diffusion LMs for Lossless Compression
comment: 18 pages, 11 figures, 2 tables. Main paper: 9 pages (7 pages text + 2 pages references). Includes 9 pages of supplementary material
summary:
We study the problem of lossless text compression, motivated by the rapid growth in the collection and storage of digital textual data - including plain text, source code, and structured formats such as XML - and by recent advances in neural language model-based compression. In particular, recent LLM-based approaches, whether built on symbol-ranking pipelines or paired with a statistical compressor, have demonstrated compression ratios significantly superior to general-purpose compressors such as zstd, gzip, or bzip on text and code. However, these neural approaches suffer from severe throughput limitations, making them not yet practically usable.
  For the first time in the context of lossless neural text compression, we introduce Diffusion Language Models (DLMs) as an alternative inference paradigm to autoregressive LLM-based approaches. We argue that replacing autoregressive LLMs with DLMs within the same compression framework could overcome the throughput bottleneck caused by their one-symbol-per-step limitation. However, achieving these improvements requires addressing algorithmic challenges introduced by applying DLMs to lossless compression, where the architecture allows the number and positions of symbols encoded at each forward pass to be decided independently. We design efficient and effective strategies to solve these challenges and evaluate them experimentally against LLM-based and general-purpose compressors on enwik8, a well-established textual benchmark.
  Our results show that the newly proposed DLM-based framework advances the state of the art in lossless text compression. Moreover, as DLMs are still a relatively young paradigm, recent advances toward increasingly capable and efficient models suggest substantial room for further improvements.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes using Diffusion Language Models (DLMs) instead of autoregressive LLMs for lossless text compression, achieving better compression ratios and much higher throughput than existing neural and general-purpose compressors on text benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Existing neural language model-based compressors (largely autoregressive LLMs) can outperform traditional compressors like zstd, gzip, and bzip in compression ratio for text and code, but they are too slow for practical use because they encode one symbol per decoding step. With the growth of massive textual datasets and the need for efficient storage, there is a strong incentive to find models that retain high compression performance while dramatically increasing throughput.
AI.method: The authors introduce Diffusion Language Models (DLMs) as an alternative inference paradigm for lossless text compression. Instead of the strictly sequential, one-symbol-at-a-time decoding of autoregressive models, DLMs allow flexible encoding of multiple symbols at each forward pass, with the number and positions of these symbols decided dynamically. The paper addresses the algorithmic challenges this flexibility brings—such as deciding which positions to encode when, and how to guarantee losslessness—by designing specialized encoding strategies and integrating DLMs into an existing neural compression framework. They then implement and compare this DLM-based compressor against autoregressive LLM-based compressors and standard tools on the enwik8 benchmark.
AI.result: On the enwik8 textual benchmark, the proposed DLM-based compression framework achieves state-of-the-art lossless compression performance. It surpasses both previous neural LLM-based compressors and general-purpose compressors in compression ratio, while also alleviating the throughput bottleneck that hampers autoregressive approaches. The experiments indicate significant speedups without sacrificing, and indeed improving, compression effectiveness.
AI.conclusion: The work demonstrates that Diffusion Language Models can serve as a powerful and more efficient alternative to autoregressive LLMs for lossless text compression, setting a new state of the art on a standard benchmark. Because DLMs are still a developing modeling paradigm, the authors expect further architectural and algorithmic advances to yield even better compression ratios and throughput, suggesting a promising future direction for practical neural text compression systems.

title: LLMs in Process Diagram Engineering: From Optimal PFDs to Validated P&IDs
summary: Nowadays, the creation of a process flow diagram (PFD) and its subsequent transformation into a piping and instrumentation diagram (P&ID) is predominantly performed manually. Applying artificial intelligence in the task could potentially lead not only to process automation and time savings, but also to financial gains by exploring numerous diagram's topology options and reducing manual labor. This research presents P&ID Pilot - a practical end-to-end AI pipeline capable of handling flowsheet developing for both stages. The first stage focuses on PFD synthesis, whereas the second is directed toward modifying the generated PFD into P&ID. After comparing four different methods, the hybrid approach combining genetic algorithms (GA) and large language models (LLM) is shown to generate the optimal valid PFD topology, achieving the lowest loss value among all the methods, while satisfying the required outlet flow parameters without engineering-rule violations. For the second stage, the proposed LLM-based agent successfully transforms the generated PFD into a source-grounded P&ID by producing validated, executable modifications through a restricted engineering software development kit, achieving 100% execution success while maintaining compliance with domain-specific rules and reference graph structures. This unified pipeline - coupling GA/LLM-driven synthesis with an LLM-based transformation agent - offers a feasible path toward end-to-end process design automation by producing validated, deployable outputs and substantially reduces manual engineering effort.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes an end-to-end AI pipeline, P&ID Pilot, that automatically generates process flow diagrams (PFDs) and converts them into piping and instrumentation diagrams (P&IDs) using a hybrid GA+LLM approach and an LLM-based transformation agent.
AI.motivation: Creating PFDs and converting them into P&IDs is currently a manual, time-consuming, and labor-intensive engineering task. Manual workflows limit how many topology options can be explored and increase design costs. The authors aim to automate and optimize this process using AI to save time, reduce costs, and enable exploration of many valid design alternatives while ensuring adherence to engineering rules and target process specifications.
AI.method: The paper introduces P&ID Pilot, an end-to-end AI pipeline with two main stages. Stage 1 performs PFD synthesis and compares four methods, ultimately using a hybrid approach that combines genetic algorithms (GA) with large language models (LLMs) to search over and generate valid flowsheet topologies that satisfy outlet flow requirements and engineering rules. Stage 2 uses an LLM-based software agent to transform the synthesized PFD into a P&ID. This agent interacts with a restricted, domain-specific engineering SDK to propose, validate, and execute modifications that are grounded in the source PFD and compliant with domain rules and reference graph structures.
AI.result: In PFD synthesis, the hybrid GA+LLM method achieves the best performance among the four evaluated methods, producing valid PFD topologies with the lowest loss values while meeting outlet flow requirements and avoiding engineering-rule violations. In the P&ID transformation stage, the LLM-based agent successfully converts generated PFDs into executable, source-grounded P&IDs with 100% execution success using the constrained engineering SDK, while maintaining compliance with domain-specific constraints and reference graph structures.
AI.conclusion: The study demonstrates that a unified AI pipeline combining GA/LLM-driven PFD synthesis with an LLM-based P&ID transformation agent can feasibly automate end-to-end process design. The resulting system produces validated, deployable diagrams, satisfies engineering constraints, and significantly reduces manual engineering effort, suggesting a practical route toward industrial-scale process design automation.

title: Gloss-Free Representation Learning for Cross-Dataset Sign Spotting
comment: Accepted at the 4th LIMIT Workshop (Representation Learning with Very Limited Resources), ECCV 2026. The abstract was shortened to comply with arXiv's 1,920-character limit
summary: Sign-language research for resource-constrained languages is often limited by the cost of dense linguistic labels such as glosses, temporal boundaries, and sign order. Broadcast news offers a practical alternative by pairing continuous signing with spoken-language transcripts, but this supervision is weak since text and signing are loosely aligned. Morphologically rich languages such as Turkish add further difficulty, as the same lexical meaning can appear in many inflected forms while some derived forms should remain distinct. We study whether weak transcript-based supervision can pretrain a reusable sign encoder in this setting, where poor text normalization can fragment pseudo-gloss targets and weaken representation learning. Unlike prior pseudo-gloss pipelines designed mainly to improve translation, we test whether the pretrained encoder transfers as a reusable representation for cross-dataset sign spotting. We pretrain on TSL-News, a new Turkish broadcast corpus, using pseudo-gloss labels derived from transcripts rather than manual annotation, comparing rule-based morphological lemmatization with constrained LLM-assisted normalization over a fixed vocabulary. We evaluate the learned representations via cross-dataset sign spotting on a new TSL Spotting Benchmark built from the TSL Dictionary corpus. The LLM-assisted encoder raises top-5 temporal localization mean IoU from 0.235 to 0.465, with 56.2% of examples reaching an IoU of at least 0.50; a frequency analysis suggests this gain is not mainly driven by memorizing frequent pseudo-gloss labels. In a downstream translation check, the same pretraining improves BLEU-4 from 9.60 to 11.04 and ROUGE from 23.48 to 27.43. These results show that loosely aligned broadcast data can provide effective weak supervision for learning sign representations that capture both lexical content and temporal structure.

AI.tldr: They pretrain a sign-language encoder for Turkish Sign Language using weak supervision from broadcast news transcripts, show that better text normalization via LLM-based pseudo-glosses dramatically improves cross-dataset sign spotting and also helps translation, demonstrating that loosely aligned broadcast data can yield strong reusable sign representations.
AI.motivation: Dense manual annotation for sign languages (glosses, temporal boundaries, sign order) is costly, especially for resource-constrained and morphologically rich languages like Turkish. Existing work focuses on pseudo-gloss pipelines mainly to improve translation, not to learn reusable sign encoders. There is a need to understand whether weak supervision from loosely aligned broadcast news transcripts can pretrain sign encoders that transfer across datasets, and how text normalization quality (lemmatization vs. LLM-based normalization) affects representation learning under heavy morphology.
AI.method: They construct TSL-News, a Turkish Sign Language broadcast news corpus with continuous signing and spoken-language transcripts. From transcripts, they derive pseudo-gloss labels without manual sign annotation, exploring two normalization strategies over a fixed vocabulary: (1) rule-based morphological lemmatization and (2) constrained LLM-assisted normalization designed to better handle Turkish morphology and maintain necessary distinctions. They use these pseudo-glosses as weak supervision to pretrain a sign encoder. Then they evaluate this encoder as a reusable feature extractor on cross-dataset sign spotting using a new TSL Spotting Benchmark built from the TSL Dictionary corpus, measuring temporal localization IoU. They also run a downstream sign language translation experiment to see how pretraining affects BLEU and ROUGE. Frequency analysis is used to test whether gains come simply from memorizing frequent pseudo-glosses.
AI.result: The encoder pretrained with LLM-assisted pseudo-gloss normalization significantly outperforms the rule-based lemmatization encoder on cross-dataset sign spotting: top-5 temporal localization mean IoU improves from 0.235 to 0.465, and 56.2% of examples achieve IoU ≥ 0.50. Frequency analysis suggests these gains are not mainly due to memorizing frequent pseudo-gloss labels. In downstream translation, the same pretraining boosts BLEU-4 from 9.60 to 11.04 and ROUGE from 23.48 to 27.43, indicating better lexical and structural capture in the learned representations.
AI.conclusion: Weak supervision from loosely aligned broadcast news transcripts can effectively pretrain sign-language encoders, even in morphologically rich, low-resource settings like Turkish Sign Language. Careful pseudo-gloss normalization, particularly via constrained LLM assistance rather than simple rule-based lemmatization, substantially enhances the learned representations, leading to large gains in cross-dataset sign spotting and measurable improvements in translation quality. This demonstrates that broadcast data can yield reusable sign representations that encode both lexical meaning and temporal structure without requiring dense manual labeling.

title: A Conceptual Framework for Refining Influence Knowledge from Simulation Evidence in Cyber-Physical Systems
summary: Cyber-physical systems (CPS) are typically developed by multiple stakeholders who produce artefacts tailored to their specific domains of expertise. The behaviour of these systems emerges from the interaction between those artefacts and their operational environment. Simulation and co-simulation have become essential approaches for analysing CPS behaviour and, through simulation campaigns, developers can explore system responses under changing conditions, including interactions with the environment. However, the lack of details and understanding of some environmentmediated interactions (typically the ones beyond direct sensing and actuation), which remain unmodelled due to their complexity, a lack of time, or a lack of domain experience, hinders the proper comprehension and exploitation of simulation results. To address these limitations, we propose a conceptual framework leveraging the novel concept of Influences to support the iterative and incremental refinement of simulation campaigns and deepen the understanding of the system behaviour. We demonstrate the proposed approach through a case study involving a mobile robot implemented using Simulink/Gazebo co-simulation.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a conceptual framework using the notion of 'Influences' to iteratively refine CPS simulation campaigns and better understand emergent behaviour, demonstrated on a Simulink/Gazebo mobile robot case study.
AI.motivation: Cyber-physical systems are built by multiple stakeholders, resulting in heterogeneous artefacts whose combined behaviour with the environment is hard to predict. Simulation and co-simulation are widely used, but their effectiveness is limited because many environment-mediated interactions (beyond direct sensing/actuation) are not modeled due to complexity, time constraints, or lack of domain expertise. This leads to incomplete understanding and suboptimal use of simulation results. The authors want a structured way to capture and refine these missing environmental interactions over time.
AI.method: They introduce a conceptual framework centred on the new concept of 'Influences'—abstractions that represent environment-mediated interactions affecting system behaviour. The framework guides developers in iteratively and incrementally refining simulation campaigns by identifying, modelling, and incorporating these Influences into existing simulation/co-simulation setups. The approach is instantiated and illustrated on a CPS case study: a mobile robot co-simulated with Simulink (control) and Gazebo (environment/robot dynamics).
AI.result: The authors show—via the mobile robot Simulink/Gazebo co-simulation case study—that their Influences-based framework can be applied in practice to refine simulation campaigns. As Influences are iteratively identified and modelled, the simulations capture more of the relevant environment-mediated behaviour, providing richer and more informative results about the CPS’s responses under varying conditions.
AI.conclusion: The paper concludes that using Influences as a central concept enables more systematic, incremental refinement of CPS simulations and better comprehension of emergent system behaviour, particularly regarding complex environment-mediated interactions that are usually left unmodelled. The demonstrated case study suggests the framework is feasible and beneficial, and it can support developers in more effectively exploiting simulation and co-simulation for CPS analysis.

title: Better, Faster, Stronger: Programmatic Skill Learning Best Reduces Agent Cost
summary: Recently, the practice of augmenting LLM agent capability with skills has gained prevalence. We explore the cost effective adaptation of agents to novel domains by means of learning skills. Existing works focus on performance gain over cost effectiveness. As a result, little is known about what skill learning strategies save cost. We argue that among all the different skill learning methods, those that view skills as programs can achieve the best cost reduction. By executing sequences of actions deterministically, a program-augmented agent can reliably and cheaply achieve goals that would otherwise require trial and error and risk degenerate behavior over long horizons. An agent can learn at inference time by incrementally discovering these programs and equipping them for future tasks. We hypothesize that past trajectories contain enough signal to guide skill learning, even without replay or validation, provided the agent can learn to analyze them. To test our claims, we propose SpeedRunner, a coding agent that analyzes trajectories and refactors skills for better performance on future tasks. Across three different embodied environments, we show that SpeedRunner consistently achieves the frontier in learning and cost reduction while remaining robust against distribution shifts and environmental randomness.

AI.tldr: The paper presents SpeedRunner, a coding-based skill-learning framework that reduces the cost of adapting LLM agents to new domains by treating skills as deterministic programs extracted from past trajectories.
AI.motivation: Most work on LLM agents with skills prioritizes performance and task success over cost efficiency, leaving open how to systematically reduce inference-time cost and prevent long-horizon trial-and-error. The authors want to understand which skill learning strategies are most cost-effective and argue that program-like skills may offer the greatest cost savings and reliability, especially in long-horizon embodied tasks.
AI.method: The authors conceptualize skills as deterministic action programs that can be executed reliably once discovered. They propose SpeedRunner, a coding agent that, at inference time, analyzes its own past trajectories, discovers reusable programs (skills), and refactors them for future use. SpeedRunner does this without explicit replay buffers or external validation, relying instead on trajectory analysis to identify and refine skill programs. They evaluate this approach in three embodied environments and compare to existing skill-learning baselines on both performance and cost metrics.
AI.result: Across three embodied environments, SpeedRunner attains state-of-the-art or frontier results in both learning progress and cost reduction compared to prior skill-learning approaches. It reliably solves tasks with fewer costly interactions and is less prone to degenerate long-horizon behaviors, while maintaining strong performance under distribution shifts and environmental randomness.
AI.conclusion: Treating skills as deterministic programs and learning them directly from past trajectories at inference time is an effective and cost-efficient way to adapt LLM agents to new domains. SpeedRunner, the proposed coding agent, demonstrates that trajectory-based program refactoring can simultaneously improve performance, reduce cost, and enhance robustness to distribution shifts and stochastic environments.

title: Harnessing agent memory to build lifelong AI partners for materials scientists
summary: Materials research advances through accumulated experience - scripts that work, protocols that are trusted, warnings attached to failed calculations or experiments, and judgement that links a new question to an old result. This experience is essential for reproducibility and knowledge transfer, yet it is usually fragmented across notebooks, repositories, job logs and individual memory, and it is rarely portable across artificial-intelligence agents. Here we argue that a lifelong AI partner for materials science can be designed around persistent memory rather than around a particular agent implementation. We introduce a self-evolving memory framework that stores scientific experience as inspectable facts and executable skills, so that observations, failure boundaries, protocols and validation checks can be retrieved, revised and migrated across models. We evaluate the idea in three computational settings that expose different layers of materials-research competence. In 49 real-world materials-tool-use questions comprising 138 executable subtasks, memory nearly doubles GPT-5.2 task success without model-parameter updates. In elemental-solid equation-of-state calculations, memory converts a wavefunction-initialization failure into a pre-execution guardrail, improving outcomes from 22/1/4 to 25/2/0 Correct/Partial/Error and avoiding 92% of repeated errors. In 13 practical material simulation workflows, remembered skills and failure facts halve the aggregate trace burden (tokens) and reduce tool calls by over a factor of two by the third round, while preserving physically meaningful outputs in band-gap, phonon, vacancy and work-function analyses. These results show that agent memory can serve as a durable scientific asset; a portable, self-improving record of materials-research experience that outlives any single model or agent stack.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a persistent, self-evolving memory framework for AI agents in materials science that captures reusable experience (facts and skills) to improve reliability, efficiency, and transferability across models and workflows.
AI.motivation: In materials research, valuable experience—working scripts, trusted protocols, and known failure modes—is scattered across notebooks, repositories, logs, and human memory, and is not readily shared or reused by different AI agents. This fragmentation harms reproducibility, slows knowledge transfer, and prevents AI systems from continuously improving across tasks and model generations. The authors aim to create an AI partner whose core asset is a durable, inspectable memory of scientific experience, rather than any specific model instance.
AI.method: They design a self-evolving memory framework that stores scientific experience as two main elements: (1) inspectable facts (e.g., observations, failure boundaries, validation checks) and (2) executable skills (e.g., protocols, workflows, tool-use patterns). This memory can be retrieved, revised, and migrated across different AI models and agent stacks without updating model parameters. They evaluate the framework in three computational settings: (a) real-world tool-use questions decomposed into executable subtasks, (b) elemental-solid equation-of-state calculations focusing on wavefunction initialization failures and guardrails, and (c) multi-round practical materials-simulation workflows (band gaps, phonons, vacancies, work functions), tracking task success, error reduction, trace tokens, and tool-call counts over rounds.
AI.result: 1) On 49 real-world materials-tool-use questions comprising 138 executable subtasks, adding memory nearly doubles GPT-5.2’s task success without any fine-tuning. 2) In equation-of-state calculations for elemental solids, the system turns recurrent wavefunction-initialization failures into pre-execution guardrails, improving Correct/Partial/Error outcomes from 22/1/4 to 25/2/0 and preventing 92% of repeated errors. 3) Across 13 practical simulation workflows, remembered skills and failure facts cut aggregate token traces roughly in half and reduce tool calls by more than a factor of two by the third interaction round, while maintaining physically meaningful results in typical materials properties analyses.
AI.conclusion: A persistent, self-evolving memory layer can function as a long-lived scientific asset for AI agents in materials science. By encoding reusable facts and executable skills, the memory substantially improves reliability, efficiency, and error avoidance without retraining the underlying models. Because this memory is inspectable, revisable, and portable across agents and model versions, it enables a form of cumulative, sharable scientific experience that can outlast any single AI implementation and supports the vision of a lifelong AI partner for materials research.

title: Self-Evolving Embodied Agents via Skill-Harness Evolution
summary: Embodied agents are increasingly built as systems around foundation models, where performance depends not only on model weights but also on the skills, context, action interfaces, and execution harness surrounding the model. While supervised fine-tuning and reinforcement learning can adapt agents to new environments, they require additional data, rewards, and training runs; meanwhile, many train-free code-centric approaches rely on programmable robot APIs that may be unavailable in fixed-interface settings. We propose SHAPER, a self-evolving framework for train-free embodied adaptation that keeps model parameters frozen and improves the non-parametric agent system by evolving reusable skills and a context-code harness through target-environment rollouts. In SHAPER, the same frozen model can serve as both planner and optimizer, refining its external skills and context-code harness without parameter updates. We evaluate SHAPER on VLABench and ESI-Bench, covering embodied agents with different low-level action interfaces, and compare against pure execution, supervised fine-tuning, and test-time-scaling baselines such as verifier-free selection and voting. Our results suggest that skill-and-harness optimization is a practical route to self-evolving embodied agents when model training is expensive, unavailable, or undesirable.
