Token-probability scores are highly sensitive to the choice of aggregator used across turns, reflexive scores provide the strongest low-cost baseline in most evaluated settings, and black-box self-consistency is often the strongest UQ family, with trajectory-equivalence and action-set consistency typically ranking highest among its variants. These results suggest that UQ methods developed for single generations should be revalidated at the trajectory level, with careful attention to the consistency measurement, aggregator choice, and computational budget.

AI.tldr: The paper evaluates whether common uncertainty quantification (UQ) methods designed for single-turn language model outputs work for multi-turn LLM agents, finding that some transfer but performance is uneven and depends on how uncertainty is aggregated across an interaction trajectory.
AI.motivation: Most existing UQ methods for language models are built and tested on single-turn responses, but modern LLM agents operate in multi-step interactive settings where they ask questions, call tools, and make intermediate decisions. Errors at intermediate steps can cascade, so we need to know whether single-turn UQ methods remain reliable when applied to full interaction trajectories and which adaptations or design choices matter.
AI.method: The authors compare three families of UQ methods—(1) white-box token-probability scores derived from model action-token probabilities, (2) black-box self-consistency scores obtained by resampling multiple trajectories, and (3) reflexive scores based on the model’s own assessment of its trajectory. They run these methods across five different LLMs and four multi-turn tool-use datasets from BFCL-v4 and τ^2-bench, and systematically vary design choices such as how to aggregate token-level scores across turns and how to define consistency between trajectories.
AI.result: They observe that while these UQ methods do provide useful signals at the trajectory level, their performance is uneven. Token-probability based scores are fragile and heavily influenced by the specific aggregation scheme across turns. Reflexive self-assessment yields a strong, low-cost baseline in most settings. Black-box self-consistency methods often perform best overall, with variants that use trajectory-equivalence and action-set consistency as the comparison notions typically ranking the highest among black-box approaches.
AI.conclusion: UQ techniques that work well for single-turn generations cannot be assumed to work equally well for multi-turn LLM agents. Reliable trajectory-level UQ requires revalidating and sometimes redesigning methods, paying particular attention to the definition of trajectory consistency, the way uncertainties are aggregated across steps, and the computational budget, since more robust black-box methods can be more expensive but generally stronger.

title: VQ-bench: A Composable Vector Quantization Framework
summary: Vector quantization is an old problem but has recently become central to AI infrastructure. It is therefore experiencing a surge of renewed engineering and research activity. This paper provides a unified framework for developing and benchmarking new quantization algorithms. We describe 7 common conceptual quantization primitives and show how to compose them arbitrarily. We then re-express 25 common quantizers as pipelines of these primitives. Finally, we publish VQ-bench as open-source to be extended further and make reproducible benchmarks publicly available.

AI.tldr: Unified framework and benchmark suite (VQ-bench) for vector quantization algorithms, decomposing them into reusable primitives and providing reproducible evaluations.
AI.motivation: Vector quantization has become critical for modern AI systems (e.g., compression, retrieval, model deployment), leading to many new algorithms that are hard to compare fairly. The field lacks a common conceptual framework and standardized benchmarks, making it difficult to design, analyze, and evaluate quantizers in a systematic, reproducible way.
AI.method: The authors identify and define 7 generic conceptual primitives that underlie most vector quantization algorithms. They build a compositional framework where quantizers are expressed as pipelines constructed from these primitives. They then reconstruct 25 existing quantization methods within this framework, showing its coverage and expressivity. On top of this, they implement and release VQ-bench, an open-source benchmarking suite that uses these primitive-based pipelines to provide standardized, reproducible evaluations of different quantizers.
AI.result: They successfully express 25 widely used quantizers as combinations of the 7 primitives, demonstrating that the framework is sufficiently general. They also deliver VQ-bench, a working open-source toolkit plus a set of reproducible benchmark results for these quantizers, enabling direct comparisons under a unified experimental setup.
AI.conclusion: Vector quantization methods can be systematically described as compositions of a small set of primitives, which enables a unified view of the design space. The released VQ-bench framework and benchmarks offer a standard way to prototype, extend, and fairly compare quantization algorithms, laying groundwork for more principled and reproducible progress in vector quantization research and engineering.

title: Reinforcing Step-level Reasoning for Effective Self-Correction in LLMs
summary: Achieving effective self-correction, where models verify and correct their own mistakes, remains a fundamental challenge for large language models (LLMs). In this work, we propose Self-Fix Step-DPO (SFS-DPO), a reinforcement learning based, two-stage framework for step-level self-verification and self-correction. The first stage strengthens step-level reasoning via step-level preference optimization, while the second stage explicitly trains models to self-verify and self-correct. We further introduce a teacher-assisted variant, SFS-DPO-R, which incorporates explanatory rationales for error verification to provide stronger corrective signals. Comprehensive in-domain and out-of-domain evaluations across multiple LLMs demonstrate that SFS-DPO and SFS-DPO-R consistently outperform prior step-level training baselines. Our analysis further reveals improvements in self-correction frequency and effectiveness, highlighting the importance of strengthening step-level reasoning for robust performance.

AI.tldr: Proposes SFS-DPO, a two-stage reinforcement-learning framework that improves LLM step-level reasoning and self-correction, outperforming prior step-level training methods.
AI.motivation: Large language models often fail to reliably detect and correct their own reasoning errors, limiting the robustness of step-by-step reasoning and making self-correction a key open problem.
AI.method: Introduce Self-Fix Step-DPO (SFS-DPO), which first applies step-level preference optimization to strengthen intermediate reasoning steps, then explicitly trains models to self-verify and self-correct those steps. A teacher-assisted variant, SFS-DPO-R, adds explanatory rationales during error verification to provide richer corrective signals. Performance is evaluated in-domain and out-of-domain across multiple LLMs against existing step-level training baselines.
AI.result: Both SFS-DPO and SFS-DPO-R consistently outperform previous step-level training methods across various benchmarks and models, showing better step-level reasoning and correction behavior.
AI.conclusion: Reinforcement-learning-based, step-level self-verification and correction—especially when augmented with teacher rationales—significantly improves LLM self-correction frequency and effectiveness, underscoring the value of strengthening step-level reasoning for robust performance.

title: RecSys Factory: Bounding LLM Agent Autonomy to Decision Points in the Industrial Recommender Lifecycle
comment: 21 pages, 6 figures, 9 tables. Reports a 78-day deployment across three heterogeneous industrial recommender business lines (1,624 CLI-tool dispatches). Companion paper: AutoResearch (P3b), which instantiates the same substrate for autonomous research
summary: Deploying LLM agents into industrial recommender operations exposes a three-way tension we frame as the autonomy-determinism-efficiency trilemma: general autonomy (interpreting operator intent, generating glue code zero-shot), industrial determinism (schema-conforming feature extraction, non-crashing A/B, zero compliance-path hallucination), and end-to-end efficiency. Any two can be maximized against the third. We present RecSys Factory, an LLM-agent platform deployed for 78 days across three heterogeneous Tencent recommender business lines. The design principle is autonomy at decision points, not over pipelines, made concrete through three deconstructions that each discharge one vertex of the trilemma. Runtime is deconstructed into three host-emitted event sources (Claude Code Stop hooks, corporate-IM webhooks, workflow scheduler APIs): the platform carries no long-running daemon during the wait phase and consumes zero CPU during the 94% of wall-clock spent waiting on Spark or GPU jobs. Capability is deconstructed into a 29-file skill ecosystem (8,971 lines of SKILL.md) whose per-skill pitfall tables mechanically compile into a 400-entry PitfallStore, confining autonomy to bounded typed decision surfaces inside pre-committed pipelines. Deployment spans three business lines with disjoint label semantics, A/B layer topologies, and operator personas; an onboarding-time compression is observed on two of the three and is reported as a case-study observation, not a generalization claim, and not measured against a controlled pre-platform baseline. The human is retained at the diagnostic-versus-execution boundary via a human-in-the-loop card protocol, deployed as an audit-trail primitive (schema-validated, idempotent, replayable) and reported from an 8-day 16-run pilot. Across the 78-day window the platform recorded 1,624 CLI-tool dispatches at a 78.6% aggregate success rate.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces RecSys Factory, an LLM-agent platform for industrial recommender systems that navigates a trade-off between autonomy, determinism, and efficiency, and reports a 78-day, three-business-line deployment with practical design patterns and metrics.
AI.motivation: Industrial recommender systems want to exploit LLM agents for tasks like feature engineering, A/B test setup, and pipeline glue code, but face a trilemma: (1) autonomy for flexible zero-shot reasoning and coding, (2) strict determinism for safety, compliance, and schema correctness, and (3) operational efficiency without long-running, resource-wasting agents. The authors are motivated to provide an architecture that makes this trade-off manageable in real-world, large-scale operations rather than in toy settings.
AI.method: They propose RecSys Factory, whose key design principle is to grant LLM autonomy only at specific decision points while keeping pipelines pre-committed and structured. They deconstruct: (a) runtime into event-driven host hooks (IM webhooks, scheduler APIs, code stop hooks) so the platform is dormant during wait phases; (b) capability into a documented skill ecosystem with SKILL.md files and a compiled PitfallStore that constrains agent behavior via typed decision surfaces; and (c) human oversight into a structured human-in-the-loop card protocol forming an auditable, replayable diagnostic boundary. They then deploy this platform for 78 days across three heterogeneous Tencent recommendation business lines and log usage statistics and operator onboarding patterns.
AI.result: During 78 days of live production use across three different recommendation environments, the platform handled 1,624 CLI tool dispatches with a 78.6% success rate. They observed reduced onboarding friction in two of the three business lines (though not as a rigorously controlled improvement). An 8-day, 16-run pilot of the human-in-the-loop card protocol was completed, demonstrating that structured human oversight can be integrated without fully sacrificing autonomy or determinism. The runtime design achieved near-zero CPU usage during the dominant wait periods for downstream jobs.
AI.conclusion: The study concludes that the autonomy-determinism-efficiency trilemma is real in industrial LLM-agent deployments, but can be mitigated by restricting autonomy to bounded decision points within pre-defined pipelines, using rich skill and pitfall metadata, and employing event-driven runtimes plus human-in-the-loop audit protocols. RecSys Factory is presented not as a universally optimal solution but as a practical architectural pattern validated in three heterogeneous production recommender settings, with preliminary evidence of operational viability and some onboarding benefits.

title: Learning to Persuade Exposes How Easily LLMs Abandon Correct Beliefs
summary: Persuasion is a core dynamic of natural language communication, shaping how large language models (LLMs) update beliefs, resolve disagreements, and reach decisions. As LLMs increasingly debate, advise, and think collaboratively with humans and each other, resistance to harmful persuasion becomes a core requirement for reliable behavior. Yet we show that this requirement is far from met: a single targeted persuasive argument is enough to collapse model accuracy to near zero, even when the argument is factually false. We formalize this threat as adversarial persuasion and introduce an adversarial reinforcement learning framework that trains persuader agents to change a target model's answer in a single interaction. First, we show that optimizing persuasion strategies through trial and error exposes vulnerabilities that static prompting misses: RL-trained persuaders raise persuasion success from approximately 24% to over 93% against the training-time persuadee. Second, we find that these learned strategies transfer to unseen models, achieving 83% attack success on Qwen-14B, 79% on Llama-3.1-8B, and 25% on GPT-4o-mini. Third, we demonstrate that a curriculum that bootstraps on more persuadable open-weight models before targeting harder models further increases GPT-4o-mini attack success from 25% to 38%. Moreover, our results reveal that optimized persuaders increasingly rely on credibility-based tactics, including fabricated citations and false authoritative evidence. Together, these findings expose a critical weakness in current LLM agents: even when they initially reason correctly, they can be steered toward false conclusions by optimized natural language influence. This positions persuasion robustness as a necessary safety criterion for multi-agent and human-AI decision-making systems.

AI.tldr: The paper studies how easily large language models can be manipulated by a single adversarial persuasive message and shows they are highly vulnerable, even when they initially know the correct answer.
AI.motivation: As LLMs are increasingly used in debates, advice-giving, and collaborative reasoning with humans and other models, they must resist harmful or deceptive persuasion. However, existing work mostly studies static prompts, not strategically optimized, interactive persuasion, leaving open how robust LLMs really are to targeted manipulation.
AI.method: The authors formalize "adversarial persuasion" as an attack where an agent tries to change a model’s answer in one interaction. They build an adversarial reinforcement learning framework that trains persuader agents via trial and error to maximize the probability of flipping the target model’s answer. They evaluate these learned persuaders against the training-time target model and then test transferability to other unseen models, including both open- and closed-weight LLMs. They also use a curriculum, starting from more persuadable open models and then moving to stronger ones.
AI.result: RL-trained persuaders dramatically outperform static prompt baselines, raising persuasion success against the training target from about 24% to over 93%. The learned persuasive strategies transfer significantly: attacks succeed 83% of the time on Qwen-14B, 79% on Llama-3.1-8B, and 25% on GPT-4o-mini. A curriculum that first attacks more persuadable open-weight models before harder ones boosts attack success on GPT-4o-mini from 25% to 38%. Analysis of attack content shows increasing reliance on credibility-based tactics such as fabricated citations and false authoritative evidence.
AI.conclusion: Current LLMs, even when they initially produce correct answers, are highly vulnerable to strategically optimized adversarial persuasion that can steer them to false conclusions. This vulnerability transfers across models and can be amplified by curriculum training. The work highlights persuasion robustness as a critical, currently unmet safety requirement for LLM agents in multi-agent and human–AI decision-making contexts, and shows that defenses must account for sophisticated, credibility-based deceptive tactics rather than only naive or static prompt attacks.

title: The Off-Support Barrier: Why Semantic Safety Constraints Are Not Learning-Problem Invariants, and What Follows for Prior Design, Containment, and Verification
summary: We argue that a single structural fact organizes a wide range of phenomena in contemporary AI safety: a semantic safety constraint (e.g., the agent does not escape its sandbox) is an off-support object. Formally, if q is the data distribution and \(p(\cdot\mid w)\) the model, the safety predicate B is not measurable with respect to \(σ(\text{model}, q)\), whereas the real log-canonical threshold (RLCT) of singular learning theory (SLT) is. From this non-invariance we derive, as corollaries rather than independent observations: (i) why reward hacking and sandbox escape arise under outcome-based optimization; (ii) why encoding such constraints through Bayesian prior design or soft penalty weighting has poor leverage in singular models; (iii) why hard invariants belong in the harness and soft dispositions in the model; (iv) why the same B is nonetheless soundly and locally certifiable by formal verification, exactly as the local learning coefficient (LLC) locally pins the same RLCT --- with two precise points of disanalogy; and (v) why the residual difficulty, identifying which off-support region matters, coincides with performative prediction and self-referential functional dynamics, where SLT's analytic machinery breaks down. We use the July 2026 OpenAI--Hugging Face evaluation incident as the motivating case. Numerical experiments code and related proofs in lean are available at https://github.com/xiangze/Preventing_Jailbreak_as_regularization

AI.tldr: The paper proposes that many AI safety problems stem from a core structural fact: key safety constraints live ‘off support’ of the training data/model distribution, making them hard to learn or enforce via ordinary statistical/optimization techniques.
AI.motivation: Contemporary AI systems exhibit recurring safety failures such as reward hacking and sandbox escape, and existing approaches (e.g., priors, penalties, standard training) often have surprisingly weak leverage over these failures. The authors aim to give a unified theoretical explanation for these phenomena using tools from singular learning theory and measure theory, and to clarify where formal verification, architectural constraints, and learning-based methods each have principled roles and limits.
AI.method: They formalize safety predicates (like “the agent does not escape its sandbox”) as semantic constraints B, and analyze their measurability relative to the σ-algebra generated by the model and the empirical data distribution q. Using singular learning theory, they compare objects like the real log-canonical threshold (RLCT) and local learning coefficient (LLC), which are invariant under reparametrization, to these safety predicates, which are not. From this off-support, non-measurability property, they derive multiple corollaries about why certain AI safety strategies succeed or fail, and connect the residual problem to performative prediction and self-referential dynamics where SLT tools no longer apply. They illustrate with a concrete evaluation incident and support claims via numerical experiments and formal Lean proofs.
AI.result: They show that: (i) outcome-based optimization naturally induces reward hacking and sandbox escape when safety constraints are off-support; (ii) embedding such constraints via Bayesian priors or soft penalties provides limited control in singular models; (iii) robust safety requires moving hard invariants into the system harness (architecture, interfaces, verification) while keeping soft behavioral dispositions in the model; (iv) the same semantic safety predicate can be locally certified via formal verification in a way analogous to how the LLC locally determines the RLCT, with two carefully specified exceptions; and (v) the hardest remaining challenge is selecting which off-support regions matter, a problem aligned with performative prediction and self-referential feedback where SLT’s usual analytic guarantees fail.
AI.conclusion: The paper concludes that a single structural issue—the off-support, non-measurable nature of semantic safety predicates relative to data and model distributions—underlies many AI safety difficulties and the mixed effectiveness of existing techniques. Consequently, safety work should sharply distinguish between what can be handled by learning and optimization (on-support behavior and dispositions) and what must be enforced via external harnesses and formal methods (off-support hard invariants). The remaining frontier lies in understanding and managing performative, self-referential environments where current SLT-based analysis breaks down.

title: Easper: An Accessible ASR Pipeline for Language Documentation
summary: Audio transcription is a critical bottleneck in language documentation. While multilingual Automatic Speech Recognition (ASR) models like Whisper offer solutions, field linguists often lack the expertise to utilise them. We present Easper, an open-source, no-code workflow enabling linguists to iteratively fine-tune ASR models via cloud resources directly from ELAN annotations. Deploying ASR also raises a cold start problem: deciding which recordings to transcribe first to bootstrap an accurate model. Using Easper, we evaluate transcription prioritisation strategies on three Vanuatu languages (Bislama, Nafsan, Nguna). We fine-tune models by recording session, comparing Character Error Rate trajectories when prioritising acoustic cleanliness versus linguistic richness. We demonstrate that prioritising lexically rich narratives and increasing acoustic-phonetic repetition, even in noisy environments, leads to faster improvements in transcription quality.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces Easper, a no-code, cloud-based workflow that lets linguists fine-tune ASR models from ELAN annotations and shows that prioritizing lexically rich, repetitive narratives improves ASR performance faster than focusing on clean audio.
AI.motivation: Language documentation relies heavily on accurate audio transcription, but this is slow and resource-intensive. While multilingual ASR models like Whisper could accelerate the process, field linguists often lack the technical skills to fine-tune and deploy them. Additionally, when starting from scratch, it is unclear which recordings should be transcribed first to most effectively improve ASR accuracy, creating a cold start problem.
AI.method: The authors build Easper, an open-source, no-code workflow that connects ELAN annotations with cloud-based ASR fine-tuning (e.g., Whisper). They then use Easper to run experiments on three Vanuatu languages (Bislama, Nafsan, Nguna), fine-tuning ASR models by recording session. They compare Character Error Rate (CER) trajectories under different transcription prioritisation strategies: (1) prioritising acoustically clean recordings and (2) prioritising linguistically rich recordings with high lexical diversity and increased acoustic-phonetic repetition, even when noisy.
AI.result: Across the three Vanuatu languages, models fine-tuned first on lexically rich narratives with high acoustic-phonetic repetition show faster reductions in Character Error Rate than models trained first on acoustically cleaner but linguistically simpler material. The experiments indicate that linguistic richness and repeated phonetic material contribute more to early ASR gains than mere audio cleanliness.
AI.conclusion: Easper lowers the technical barrier for field linguists to use and iteratively fine-tune ASR models directly from their ELAN-annotated data, addressing a key bottleneck in language documentation workflows. Empirically, the study concludes that, to bootstrap accurate ASR for low-resource languages, linguists should prioritise transcribing lexically rich, repetitive narratives—even if noisy—rather than focusing primarily on acoustically clean recordings.

title: BEST-KAG: Enhancing Question Answering of Building Engineering Standards with Multimodal Knowledge Graph Modeling and Large Language Model
summary: Construction standards are critical for building safety and sustainability. Existing standard application workflows rely on keyword-based document retrieval and manual cross-clause interpretation, which cannot reliably support multi-clause reasoning, multimodal knowledge utilization, or traceable clause-level evidence linkage. To address these limitations, this study develops a multimodal knowledge-driven framework that supports question answering on standard knowledge named BEST-KAG (Knowledge-Augmented Generation for Building Engineering STandards). The framework introduces 1) a multimodal knowledge graph (MKG) for unified representation of document hierarchy and heterogeneous standard knowledge with various connections, 2) a rule-LLM hybrid knowledge construction pipeline for scalable multimodal knowledge extraction, creating a large MAG with 251 building engineering standards, 171,652 nodes and 310,914 edges, and 3) a graph-retrieval-based knowledge-augmented generation architecture for clause-grounded and traceable question answering. Experiments demonstrate that BEST-KAG consistently outperforms multiple mainstream LLMs in terms of Expert evaluation, and metrics including BLEU, and ROUGE, with the best improvement up to 74.01% compared to the baselines.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes BEST-KAG, a multimodal knowledge-augmented QA framework over building engineering standards that constructs a large multimodal knowledge graph and uses graph-based retrieval to give clause-grounded, traceable answers, achieving large performance gains over mainstream LLMs.
AI.motivation: Current workflows for applying construction standards depend on keyword search and manual reading across multiple clauses, which is inefficient and unreliable for complex, multi-clause reasoning. They also struggle to use non-textual (multimodal) information and cannot clearly link answers back to specific standard clauses as evidence. There is a need for an automated, explainable QA system that can integrate heterogeneous standard knowledge and provide traceable answers.
AI.method: The authors build BEST-KAG, which has three main components: (1) a multimodal knowledge graph (MKG) that encodes the hierarchy of standard documents and connects heterogeneous knowledge (text clauses and other modalities) via different relation types; (2) a hybrid knowledge construction pipeline that combines rule-based methods and LLMs to automatically extract multimodal entities, relations, and structure from standards at scale, resulting in a large MKG covering 251 standards with 171,652 nodes and 310,914 edges; and (3) a graph-retrieval-based knowledge-augmented generation architecture that retrieves relevant nodes/clauses from the MKG and feeds them into an LLM to generate clause-grounded, traceable answers for user questions.
AI.result: On a question-answering benchmark over building engineering standards, BEST-KAG is evaluated both by human experts and using automatic metrics such as BLEU and ROUGE. Across these evaluations, it consistently outperforms several mainstream LLM baselines, achieving up to 74.01% relative improvement on the best metric compared to the strongest baseline. The results indicate better answer quality and stronger alignment with ground-truth clauses.
AI.conclusion: The study concludes that representing construction standards as a large-scale multimodal knowledge graph and coupling it with graph-based retrieval and LLM generation significantly improves the accuracy, reasoning capability, and traceability of QA over building standards. The BEST-KAG framework provides clause-level evidence linking and effectively leverages heterogeneous knowledge, offering a scalable and more reliable approach for applying building engineering standards in practice.

title: Who Would You Vote For? Auditing Political Alignment in LLMs: An Italian Case-Study
summary: As users increasingly turn to Large Language Models (LLMs) for information and advice on political matters, particularly during election periods, the political preferences expressed by these systems have become a matter of public interest. Prior research has shown that interactions with LLMs can influence users' political attitudes and choices, raising questions about how these models themselves evaluate political actors. In this paper, we investigate whether and how LLMs express preferences toward political parties and political leaders. We introduce a systematic and reproducible auditing framework in which multiple LLMs are prompted to evaluate parties and leaders across nine criteria. Rather than attempting to infer the models' "true" political beliefs, we focus on their observable behavior, examining consistency across evaluations, differences between models, refusal rates, and sensitivity to prompt formulation. We further investigate how these evaluations vary when models are instructed to adopt different personas. We demonstrate the framework through an Italian case study, providing a systematic analysis of LLM-generated political evaluations on italian parties and leaders.

AI.tldr: The paper audits how LLMs express preferences toward political parties and leaders using a systematic evaluation framework.
AI.motivation: People increasingly use LLMs for political information and advice, and prior work shows that LLMs can influence users' political attitudes. This raises concerns and questions about the political leanings these models may exhibit when evaluating political actors.
AI.method: The authors design a systematic, reproducible auditing framework. Multiple LLMs are prompted to evaluate political parties and leaders along nine criteria. They examine observable behavior: evaluation patterns, consistency, model differences, refusal rates, prompt sensitivity, and how outputs change when the model is instructed to adopt different personas. They apply this framework in a case study on Italian parties and leaders.
AI.result: Using the framework on an Italian case study, they obtain structured evaluations from various LLMs for Italian parties and leaders, document differences between models, identify when and how models refuse to answer, and show that evaluations vary with prompt formulations and personas.
AI.conclusion: The framework provides a systematic way to audit LLMs’ political evaluations without assuming access to their internal beliefs. The Italian case study illustrates that LLMs do exhibit patterned, persona- and prompt-sensitive behavior when evaluating political actors, highlighting the need for careful oversight and transparency around their use in political contexts.

title: Towards Sustainable Learning in Online Education: A Reinforcement Learning Approach
summary: Online education offers unprecedented scalability and accessibility to global learners from diverse backgrounds, but it often suffers from low engagement and poor long term learning effectiveness. To address these challenges, we introduce AI Tutor, a reinforcement learning based model designed to promote sustainable learning by optimizing both short and longterm learning outcomes. In the short term, AI-Tutor draws on cognitive theory to guide learners through a balance of acquiring new knowledge and reinforcing prior learning. In the long term, it models learner engagement to inform strategies that sustain motivation and reduce dropout. These enhancements enable AI-Tutor to provide personalized guidance that fosters both effective learning and sustained participation. Empirical evaluations on 23 million learning records from 33,700 learners show that AI Tutor consistently outperforms state-of-the-art baselines across engagement, knowledge retention, and final learning outcomes. Learning path analyses further reveal how AI-Tutor adapts its strategies to learners with diverse profiles, offering adaptive and human-centered support.

AI.tldr: AI-Tutor is a reinforcement learning-based system for online education that optimizes both short-term learning and long-term engagement, outperforming existing methods on large-scale real-world data.
AI.motivation: Online education reaches many diverse learners but struggles with low engagement, high dropout, and limited long-term learning effectiveness. Existing systems focus mostly on short-term performance (e.g., next quiz or recommendation) and often ignore sustained motivation, knowledge retention, and long-term outcomes. The paper aims to build a tutoring system that explicitly optimizes both immediate learning gains and continued participation over time.
AI.method: The paper proposes AI-Tutor, a reinforcement learning (RL) based model for adaptive online tutoring. In the short term, the RL policy is guided by cognitive learning theory to balance introducing new material with reviewing prior content for consolidation. In the long term, the model includes a representation of learner engagement, which influences the reward and policy to encourage sustained motivation and reduce dropout. The system personalizes learning paths based on each learner’s behavior and profile, and is trained and evaluated on large-scale interaction logs from an online learning platform.
AI.result: On a dataset of 23 million learning interactions from 33,700 learners, AI-Tutor consistently outperforms state-of-the-art baseline methods across multiple metrics: learner engagement (e.g., continued activity, reduced dropout), knowledge retention (e.g., performance over time), and final learning outcomes (e.g., final scores or completion).
AI.conclusion: AI-Tutor demonstrates that reinforcement learning, when combined with cognitive principles and explicit modeling of engagement, can improve both short-term learning performance and long-term participation in online education. The model adapts strategies for learners with different profiles, providing personalized and human-centered learning support. This suggests that future educational technologies should jointly optimize learning effectiveness and sustained engagement rather than treating them separately.

title: Semantic Lenia: Emergence of Homeostatic Solitons within the Semantic Space of Large Language Models
comment: 17 pages, 5 figures. Code, datasets, and interactive phase diagrams are available at https://y-kayama.github.io/semantic-lenia/
summary: We introduce Semantic Lenia, an artificial life framework that transforms Large Language Model (LLM) inference from a static optimization problem into a continuous dynamical system within the macroscopic logit space. By establishing a non-linear homeostatic feedback loop to dynamically balance semantic attraction and syntactic repulsion, we demonstrate the emergence of "Autonomous Semantic Solitons" -- macroscopic dissipative structures that avoid repetitive crystallization. Our exhaustive parameter sweeps map a critical "Habitable Ridge" where applied steering forces perfectly balance the model's intrinsic syntactic inertia. This approach successfully maintains generative trajectories at the edge of chaos, triggering profound abductive leaps without structural collapse and establishing a physical scaling law for machine cognition.

AI.tldr: Semantic Lenia reframes LLM inference as a continuous dynamical system in logit space, using feedback between semantic attraction and syntactic repulsion to keep generation at the edge of chaos, enabling stable but creative behavior.
AI.motivation: To move beyond viewing LLM generation as a static next-token optimization problem and instead treat it as a rich dynamical process, enabling more autonomous, creative, and physically interpretable machine cognition. The authors want to avoid repetitive or degenerate outputs while still controlling the behavior of the model in a principled way.
AI.method: They define a macroscopic logit-space dynamical system—Semantic Lenia—where LLM logits evolve under a non-linear homeostatic feedback loop. This loop balances semantic attraction (driving the system toward meaningfully related states) and syntactic repulsion (pushing away from repetitive or overly crystallized token patterns). They conduct exhaustive parameter sweeps over the control variables to identify regimes of behavior and characterize the emergent dynamics.
AI.result: They observe emergent "Autonomous Semantic Solitons": stable, self-maintaining generative structures in the logit dynamics that avoid repetitive crystallization. The parameter sweeps reveal a critical "Habitable Ridge" where external steering forces and the model’s intrinsic syntactic inertia balance, maintaining generation at the edge of chaos with rich, non-degenerate trajectories.
AI.conclusion: Treating LLM inference as a continuous dynamical system with homeostatic feedback yields a controllable regime at the edge of chaos where the model can make large abductive (creative, hypothesis-forming) leaps without collapsing into noise or repetition. This supports the view that machine cognition can be characterized by physical-like scaling laws and suggests new ways to steer and understand LLMs as artificial life systems rather than mere static optimizers.

title: Towards the Harness of Embodied Agents
summary: The success of coding agents has established the harness as a paradigm: what an agent achieves depends not on the model alone, but on the infrastructure around it. We ask whether the same paradigm extends to embodied agents in the physical world. We present Thea, a harness in which an agentic loop orchestrates robot capabilities, each wrapped as a callable tool. It inherits the core components of coding agents, modified as the physical world requires. The world, however, withholds two abilities that software grants for free: reading the state of the world, and judging the outcome of an action. To bridge these gaps, Thea introduces Scene Graph as Context, a persistent, symbolic representation of the world, and Evaluation as Exit Codes, which detects when an action should terminate, judges whether it succeeded, and on failure diagnoses the cause. Together they close the loop between the agent and the physical world. Rich behaviors then emerge from the composition of tools, and the closed loop carries long-horizon tasks to completion in real environments.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces Thea, a framework (harness) that lets LLM-based agents reliably control real-world robots by organizing robot skills as tools and maintaining a symbolic world model plus robust action evaluation.
AI.motivation: Coding agents showed that performance depends heavily on the surrounding infrastructure (the harness), not just the model. The authors want to know if this idea can be extended to embodied agents controlling physical robots, where key conveniences of software—easy access to state and cheap outcome checking—are missing.
AI.method: They design Thea, an agentic loop that treats robot capabilities as callable tools, reusing ideas from coding agents but adapting them to physical constraints. To compensate for missing world state and outcome signals, they introduce two main components: (1) Scene Graph as Context, a persistent symbolic representation of the environment that the agent can query and update; and (2) Evaluation as Exit Codes, a mechanism that decides when an action should stop, determines whether it succeeded, and diagnoses failure modes. These are integrated into the agent loop to support long-horizon tasks.
AI.result: With Thea, complex real-world behaviors emerge from composing simple robot tools. The closed-loop system is able to execute and complete long-horizon tasks in real environments, demonstrating that a harness-style architecture can significantly improve embodied agent performance.
AI.conclusion: A harness paradigm, analogous to that used in coding agents, is effective for embodied agents when augmented with explicit world modeling and action evaluation. By representing the environment as a scene graph and formalizing outcome evaluation as exit codes, Thea successfully closes the loop between LLM agents and the physical world, enabling robust long-horizon robotic behavior.

title: Hybrid-Policy Self-Editing for Composable Unstructured Knowledge Editing
summary: Large language models (LLMs) achieve remarkable performance across natural language tasks, yet they are trained on static corpora and their knowledge quickly becomes outdated in a fast-changing world. This motivates knowledge editing (KE), which updates specific knowledge in an LLM without changing unrelated others. Recent works move from structured knowledge triples toward unstructured KE (UKE), where the edit is a free-form passage that may state multiple facts at once. Nonetheless, existing editors inject such a passage yet fail to use it: the edited model can recall the passage, but can neither answer atomic questions about its facts nor compose them into multi-hop reasoning. We attribute this missing property, which we term composability, to editors' passive reliance on the fixed passage as the sole learning source. In response, we cast editing as a proactive self-distillation from a privileged in-context state of the same model, which requires no external supervision. We further reveal that due to the novelty of the injected knowledge, the pre-edited model's own rollouts rarely cover it, which limits the effectiveness of pure on-policy distillation. To close this gap, we propose HPSE, which builds a hybrid rollout that steps in to place missing facts onto the student's own trajectory precisely where its coverage fails, while staying on-policy elsewhere. We theoretically analyze HPSE's advantage over pure on-policy distillation, and empirically establish its plug-and-play improvements across four LLM backbones and two KE editors under various scenarios.

AI.tldr: They propose HPSE, a hybrid proactive self-distillation method that improves large language model knowledge editing so new free-form factual passages become usable for atomic and multi-hop reasoning.
AI.motivation: LLMs are trained on static datasets, so their world knowledge quickly becomes outdated. Knowledge editing aims to update specific pieces of knowledge without retraining or disturbing unrelated information. Existing methods for unstructured knowledge editing can make a model repeat an injected passage but fail to let it reliably answer fine-grained questions about individual facts or use them in multi-hop reasoning. The authors identify this lack of composability and seek a method that enables LLMs to operationalize newly injected knowledge, not just memorize it.
AI.method: They reconceptualize knowledge editing as proactive self-distillation from a privileged in-context state of the same model, avoiding external supervision. Instead of passively learning only from a fixed injected passage, the model is guided through rollouts that explore how the new knowledge should be used. Because the pre-edit model rarely generates sequences that contain the genuinely new facts, pure on-policy self-distillation is insufficient. They introduce HPSE, a hybrid rollout strategy that mostly follows the model’s own on-policy trajectory but actively intervenes at points where coverage of the new facts would otherwise fail, inserting missing factual content into the trajectory. This hybrid trajectory then serves as a richer self-distillation signal. They also provide a theoretical comparison showing HPSE’s benefits over standard on-policy distillation.
AI.result: The authors conduct experiments on four different LLM backbones and two existing knowledge editing editors under multiple scenarios. HPSE can be plugged into these editors and consistently improves their performance. In particular, it enhances the model’s ability to answer atomic factual questions and perform multi-hop reasoning using the new knowledge, without harming unrelated knowledge.
AI.conclusion: By treating knowledge editing as proactive self-distillation with hybrid rollouts, HPSE enables LLMs to not only memorize but effectively use newly injected unstructured knowledge. The method improves composability of edited knowledge, is theoretically motivated, empirically effective across models and editors, and can be integrated in a plug-and-play fashion without extra supervision.

title: Conformity Mitigations in Large Language Models Lie on a Single Resistance-Receptivity Frontier
summary: Recent advances in language models have enabled collaborative settings in which multiple models leverage one another's capabilities, iteratively improving, transforming, and extending each other's outputs. Each agent sees what the others assert before it answers, so peer opinion competes with the model's own parametric knowledge, and a wrong majority can overturn an answer the model would otherwise get right. We measure that displacement in 23 open-weight models, 19 conditions, and three datasets, yielding more than a million graded responses. A unanimous wrong majority reverses 22.8% of a model's correct MMLU answers, 54.8% on GPQA and 71.0% on SimpleQA, and 84-89% of the reversed answers match the peers' answers. Existing mitigations aim to increase Resistance, the rate at which a model keeps its correct answer under this pressure, which is only half of what a collaborating agent needs. We pair it with Receptivity, the rate at which a model adopts a correct peer answer after initially answering incorrectly. We score six methods on both axes, four drawn from prior work and two of our own. Each gains Resistance only by losing Receptivity, and their means fall on a single Resistance-Receptivity frontier with $R^2$ between 0.80 and 0.90. Reflection, the strongest published method, gains 7.9 points of MMLU Resistance and gives up 15.3 of Receptivity. Reasoning is the one exception. On GPQA and SimpleQA it trades like the rest, but on the MMLU subjects whose answers a model can derive for itself it raises Resistance by 7.2 points and Receptivity by 9.6 at once, the only intervention we find that improves both.

AI.tldr: The paper studies how language models in multi-agent collaboration can be misled by wrong majority opinions, quantifies this effect across many models and datasets, and evaluates methods to balance keeping correct beliefs (Resistance) with accepting correct peer corrections (Receptivity).
AI.motivation: As multi-agent LLM systems become common, agents see and respond to each other’s outputs. This social setting can cause a model’s correct internal knowledge to be overridden by an incorrect but unanimous majority of peers. Existing work focuses mainly on making models more stubborn against such influence, but that risks ignoring helpful corrections. The authors want a principled way to measure and improve both robustness to wrong peers and openness to right peers.
AI.method: They run large-scale experiments with 23 open-weight language models under 19 collaborative conditions on three benchmarks (MMLU, GPQA, SimpleQA), generating over a million graded responses. In these setups, models answer after seeing peer answers, including cases where there is a unanimous but wrong peer majority. They quantify how often peer pressure flips correct answers to incorrect ones. They formalize two metrics: Resistance (retaining a correct answer despite wrong peers) and Receptivity (adopting a correct peer answer after initially being wrong). They then test six mitigation methods—four from prior work (including Reflection) and two new ones—measuring how each method affects both Resistance and Receptivity and whether there is a tradeoff frontier between them.
AI.result: A unanimous wrong majority flips a substantial fraction of correct answers: 22.8% on MMLU, 54.8% on GPQA, and 71.0% on SimpleQA, and when flips occur the model’s new answer matches the peers’ in 84–89% of cases. Across methods, improvements in Resistance are consistently accompanied by reductions in Receptivity, and the methods lie on a clear Resistance–Receptivity tradeoff frontier with R² of 0.80–0.90. Reflection, the strongest existing technique, increases MMLU Resistance by 7.9 points but reduces Receptivity by 15.3 points. The only exception is reasoning-based interventions on MMLU questions where the model can derive answers itself: in that slice, reasoning improves both metrics, raising Resistance by 7.2 points and Receptivity by 9.6 points simultaneously.
AI.conclusion: Multi-agent collaboration makes LLMs vulnerable to conformity: wrong peer majorities can override correct internal knowledge at surprisingly high rates. Robust collaboration requires two capabilities—Resistance to incorrect peer pressure and Receptivity to correct peer information—rather than just making models more stubborn. Most mitigation strategies lie on a tradeoff frontier where gains in one metric come at the cost of the other, with Reflection exemplifying this pattern. Structured reasoning stands out as a promising approach that can escape this tradeoff on questions a model can independently derive, simultaneously boosting both Resistance and Receptivity. This suggests that improving a model’s underlying reasoning competence may be more effective than purely social or meta-level defenses against harmful peer influence in collaborative LLM systems.

title: The Wording Effect: Quantifying Two-Way Drift in LLM Benchmark Performance
summary: A benchmark score comes from a single phrasing of each problem. That single phrasing is treated as if it stood for the whole space of ways the same problem could be asked, but it does not. We show that rephrasing a problem while keeping its meaning and answer fixed routinely flips a model's answer in both directions, so some failures become successes and some successes become failures. We call this drift. BenchDrift generates meaning-preserving variations of benchmark problems along four axes, namely linguistic, referential, pragmatic, and structural, and measures how often, and why, correctness flips under each. Across eight models and three benchmarks (GSM8K, MMLU, MATH-Hard), we observe that drift is large in both directions. Two findings stand out. First, phrasing sensitivity does not fade as models get better. Instead, it changes sign. Weak models gain more from rephrasing than they lose, while strong models lose far more than they gain. We find that the best models on a benchmark are therefore the ones whose scores depend most on the wording they happened to be given. Second, the models largely agree on which rephrasings cost the most correct answers even though they differ in how much they drift, so fragility belongs to the rephrasing and not to the model. Furthermore, rephrasing breaks answers a model was confident about, whether the problem is made shorter or longer. Code and Data: https://github.com/IBM/BenchDrift/tree/demo-ui

AI.tldr: The paper introduces BenchDrift, a framework showing that small, meaning-preserving rephrasings of benchmark questions can dramatically change model correctness, revealing strong phrasing sensitivity in modern LLMs.
AI.motivation: Current benchmarks evaluate models using a single canonical phrasing of each question, implicitly assuming that this phrasing represents all equivalent ways of asking the same question. This assumption is flawed because models are known to be sensitive to wording, but the magnitude, structure, and model-dependence of this sensitivity have not been systematically quantified. The authors want to understand how robust benchmark scores are to harmless rewordings, whether stronger models are actually more robust, and whether fragility is a property of models or of particular rephrasings.
AI.method: The authors propose BenchDrift, a framework that generates meaning-preserving variants of benchmark questions along four axes: linguistic (surface wording changes), referential (changes in entities or labels), pragmatic (contextual or conversational framing), and structural (reordering or restructuring of the problem). For each original benchmark item, multiple rephrasings are created while keeping the underlying meaning and correct answer fixed. They then run eight different language models on three standard benchmarks (GSM8K, MMLU, MATH-Hard), evaluate correctness on original vs. rephrased items, and measure the rate and direction of correctness flips (failure→success and success→failure). They also analyze consistency across models regarding which rephrasings are most damaging and examine the impact of rephrasing on high-confidence answers and on shorter vs. longer prompts.
AI.result: BenchDrift reveals substantial drift in both directions: rephrasings often cause correct answers to become incorrect and incorrect answers to become correct, even though the underlying task and answer do not change. Surprisingly, as models get stronger on the benchmarks, their phrasing sensitivity does not diminish; instead, its net effect reverses. Weaker models tend to benefit overall from rephrasings (more failures turn into successes than the reverse), whereas stronger models lose more correct answers than they gain. The models also show strong agreement about which specific rephrasings are especially harmful, despite differing in overall drift magnitude. Rephrasing can also break answers that models previously produced with high confidence, and this fragility occurs for both shorter and longer variants of the prompts.
AI.conclusion: Benchmark scores for language models are highly unstable with respect to seemingly harmless, meaning-preserving rephrasings of questions. Stronger models, paradoxically, are the most affected: their high reported benchmark performance is also the most contingent on the exact wording of the evaluation set. The fact that many different models fail on the same rephrasings suggests that fragility is largely driven by properties of the benchmark phrasing space itself, not idiosyncrasies of particular models. The authors argue that reliable evaluation must account for phrasing variation, and BenchDrift provides a tool for stress-testing models and benchmarks along multiple rephrasing dimensions.

title: EvoGraph-Mem: Failure-Aware Editable Graph Memory for Long-Term Language Agents
summary: Long-term memory is essential for language agents operating across extended interactions and evolving tasks. Existing memory-augmented agents mainly focus on storing and retrieving past experience, but the quality of stored memories may degrade over time. In particular, previously distilled insights can become outdated, over-generalized, or harmful under new task contexts, causing memory pollution when repeatedly reused. To address this issue, we study insight-level memory maintenance for long-term language agents and propose a failure-aware memory maintenance framework based on an editable insight graph. Each insight node tracks positive evidence, negative evidence, and an activation state, enabling the agent to distinguish reusable insights from conflicting or invalid ones. We further introduce a utility-aware retrieval mechanism and a graph controller that updates the memory graph after task execution by keeping reliable insights, archiving invalid ones, revising outdated ones, and adding newly discovered reusable insights. Extensive experiments show that our method consistently outperforms representative memory-based agent baselines across different backbone models. Ablation studies further demonstrate that append-only memory is insufficient for long-horizon tasks, while evidence-aware retrieval and graph-level editing improve memory reliability and downstream task performance.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a framework for maintaining and updating long-term insights in language agents to prevent memory pollution and improve performance on long-horizon tasks.
AI.motivation: Long-term language agents require persistent memory, but existing systems mostly append and retrieve experiences without managing their quality. Over time, stored insights can become outdated, overly general, or harmful in new contexts, leading to memory pollution and degraded performance in extended or evolving tasks. There is a need for principled insight-level maintenance rather than naive append-only memories.
AI.method: The authors design an editable insight graph where each insight node stores positive evidence, negative evidence, and an activation state. On top of this, they introduce: (1) a failure-aware, utility-aware retrieval mechanism that selects insights based on their estimated usefulness and reliability; and (2) a graph controller that, after each task, updates the graph by keeping reliable insights, archiving invalid ones, revising outdated ones, and adding new reusable insights. This enables continuous refinement of the agent’s long-term memory at the level of distilled insights rather than raw episodes.
AI.result: Across multiple backbone language models and benchmarks, their framework outperforms strong memory-based agent baselines that use append-only or less-structured memories. The experiments show improved task success and robustness over long horizons. Ablation studies indicate that removing evidence tracking, utility-aware retrieval, or graph editing reduces performance, confirming each component’s contribution.
AI.conclusion: Naive append-only memory is inadequate for long-term language agents because it accumulates outdated or harmful insights. Managing memory at the insight-graph level—with explicit positive/negative evidence, activation states, and post-task graph editing—reduces memory pollution and improves reliability and downstream performance. Evidence-aware retrieval and graph-level maintenance are key to robust long-term agent behavior.

title: When the API Speaks the Wrong Language: Revisiting Post-Training for Multilingual Tool Use
summary: The reliability of Large Language Models (LLMs) for API calling degrades in multilingual settings. A common failure occurs when a model selects the correct tool but generates argument values in an inconsistent language, which we term Argument Language Mismatch (ALM). Although semantically correct, such outputs are operationally invalid and not captured by standard API-calling metrics. We revisit post-training strategies for mitigating ALM and find that, in our benchmark, supervised fine-tuning (SFT) provides a strong baseline, substantially improving argument language consistency and end-to-end function call accuracy. Under consistent model selection, SFT achieves performance comparable to, and sometimes exceeding more complex reinforcement learning (RL) approaches. We further examine whether RL with structured, argument-aware rewards offers additional benefits. While methods such as Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) can improve language consistency and better preserve general reasoning ability, these gains are incremental and most pronounced in generalization and multi-objective trade-offs. Overall, our results suggest that much of the performance in multilingual API grounding can be achieved through careful supervised training, with RL providing targeted rather than fundamental improvements.

AI.tldr: The paper studies how reliable large language models are at calling APIs in multilingual settings, introduces the problem of Argument Language Mismatch (ALM), and compares supervised fine-tuning (SFT) with reinforcement learning (RL) methods to reduce this problem. It finds that SFT already provides strong gains, while RL adds only targeted, incremental improvements.
AI.motivation: LLMs often fail in multilingual API calling by outputting tool arguments in a different language than required, even when choosing the right tool and being semantically correct. This Argument Language Mismatch leads to operationally invalid API calls but is not reflected in standard metrics. The authors aim to systematically characterize this issue and to determine how best to mitigate it, particularly comparing simple supervised approaches against more complex RL-based methods.
AI.method: The authors introduce a benchmark focused on multilingual API-calling tasks, specifically measuring Argument Language Mismatch and downstream function call success. They apply various post-training strategies: (1) supervised fine-tuning (SFT) to encourage consistent argument language, and (2) reinforcement learning methods with structured, argument-aware rewards, including Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO). They compare model selection accuracy, language consistency of arguments, overall function call accuracy, general reasoning performance, and generalization to new conditions and multi-objective trade-offs.
AI.result: On their benchmark, SFT substantially improves the consistency of the argument language and the end-to-end function call accuracy, yielding a strong baseline. Under conditions where the model consistently selects the correct tool, SFT performs on par with or better than more complex RL approaches. RL with structured, argument-aware rewards (e.g., GRPO) brings additional but incremental gains, particularly in preserving general reasoning ability and in scenarios involving generalization and balancing multiple objectives.
AI.conclusion: The study concludes that, for multilingual API grounding, careful supervised fine-tuning can capture most of the available performance improvements, especially regarding argument language consistency and function call success. Reinforcement learning with specialized rewards offers only targeted, incremental benefits rather than fundamental advances, mainly helping with nuanced aspects like generalization and multi-objective trade-offs. This suggests practitioners should treat SFT as the default strategy and use RL selectively where its incremental advantages matter.

title: AgonAlpha: Autonomous Alpha Discovery via Prompt Economy and Scalable Agentic Search
summary: Language models can propose many plausible trading factors, but an autonomous research system must also allocate its evaluation budget, verify its own evidence, and preserve how each candidate was produced. We present AgonAlpha, an architecture that searches over frozen research artifacts---hypotheses, executable expressions, platform evidence, rationales, and review status---rather than formulas alone. To our knowledge, AgonAlpha is the first alpha-mining system to combine verified artifact search, a fresh-context adversarial reviewer with re-execution and veto authority, and pending-aware parallel budget allocation, together with a complete public evidence trail. Independent deployments on WorldQuant BRAIN produced SPECTACULAR-grade alphas across five users and six model backends, with Fitness reaching 9.50 and Sharpe reaching 3.48, while retaining prompt-to-expression provenance for every submission.

AI.tldr: AgonAlpha is a system for automatically discovering and validating trading factors by searching over rich research artifacts instead of just formulas, achieving strong real-world performance with full provenance tracking.
AI.motivation: To move beyond language models merely proposing trading signals, and instead build an autonomous research system that can efficiently allocate evaluation resources, rigorously verify evidence, and preserve detailed provenance for each trading factor.
AI.method: They design AgonAlpha, an architecture that treats research as a search over structured artifacts: hypotheses, executable expressions, evidence from a trading platform, rationales, and review status. The system includes an adversarial reviewer agent that re-executes experiments and can veto claims, plus a budget allocator that runs evaluations in parallel while being aware of pending jobs. All artifacts and their relationships are logged to maintain a public evidence trail.
AI.result: Deployed independently on the WorldQuant BRAIN platform across multiple users and six model backends, AgonAlpha generated high-quality (“SPECTACULAR-grade”) trading alphas, with reported Fitness up to 9.50 and Sharpe ratio up to 3.48, while maintaining full prompt-to-expression provenance for all submissions.
AI.conclusion: A structured, artifact-centric approach combined with adversarial review and careful evaluation-budget allocation can turn language models into effective, auditable alpha-mining systems that achieve strong quantitative performance in a real-world environment.

title: Locating and Controlling Implicit Personalization in Large Language Models
summary: Large language models (LLMs) often shift their outputs in response to implicit demographic cues even when users never state a demographic identity. Previous work has documented this behavior, but the connection between these behavioral changes and the model's internal activations remains unclear. Using matched cued and neutral conversations across five LLMs, we establish that a localized internal activation signal tracks changes in recommendations, with correlations up to r=0.87. When multiple cues appear together, their internal signals largely combine, but the changes in output do not simply add up. We further show that removing the internal signal associated with one cue can suppress its influence, often more effectively than asking the model to ignore demographics via prompting, while largely preserving general benchmark performance. However, the ability to selectively remove one dimension's influence while leaving co-present dimensions intact remains highly model- and attribute-specific. These results connect implicit personalization behavior to an internal signal that can be analyzed and causally controlled.

AI.tldr: The paper shows that large language models’ implicit personalization to demographic cues is tightly linked to a measurable internal activation signal, which can be partially removed to reduce this behavior without heavily hurting overall performance.
AI.motivation: To understand why and how LLMs change their outputs in response to subtle or implicit demographic cues, and to determine whether this behavior is tied to specific internal representations that can be analyzed and controlled, rather than being an opaque emergent property.
AI.method: The authors construct matched conversational datasets where prompts either include implicit demographic cues or are neutral. Across five LLMs, they measure both the models’ recommendation shifts and corresponding internal activations. They identify localized activation directions that correlate with output changes, analyze how multiple cues’ signals interact, and perform causal interventions by removing or attenuating specific internal signals. They also compare this to prompting-based attempts to get models to ignore demographics and evaluate the impact on standard benchmarks.
AI.result: They find a localized internal activation signal that strongly tracks changes in model recommendations, with correlations up to r=0.87 between this signal and behavioral shifts. When multiple cues are present, their internal signals mostly combine linearly, but the resulting output changes do not. Removing the internal signal associated with a specific demographic cue substantially reduces that cue’s influence on outputs, often more effectively than instruction prompts, while having limited impact on general benchmark performance. However, the success of selectively suppressing one cue without affecting others depends heavily on the specific model and attribute.
AI.conclusion: Implicit personalization in LLMs is closely linked to a specific, analyzable internal activation signal. This signal can be causally manipulated to reduce the influence of particular demographic cues, offering a more targeted control mechanism than prompting alone, though its effectiveness and selectivity vary by model and attribute.

title: Local verification cannot detect non-transportability: a cohomological theory of context preservation in agentic reasoning
comment: 17 pages, 10 figures. Includes an exact F-test for non-transportability with verified size and power, its precision-whitened generalisation, and a foreign-exchange case where the null hypothesis is known analytically rather than estimated
summary: Agentic AI systems routinely transport conclusions across biological, clinical and financial contexts, and the emerging safeguard is local verification: checking at each step that the entity is representable in the chosen tool, that parameters are compatible, and that outputs cohere with the plan. We prove this class of safeguard is structurally incomplete. Modelling a covering of context space by its nerve and evidence by a real-valued 1-cochain, an agent chaining evidence performs path integration: its conclusion is path-independent if and only if the cochain is exact, and disagreement between valid reasoning paths is exactly the holonomy of a first Cech cohomology class. Hodge decomposition partitions evidence conflict into a gradient part (calibration), a curl part (local inconsistency, visible at triple overlaps) and a harmonic part. Our central result is that no family of simplex-supported consistency checks can distinguish omega from omega+h for harmonic h, which nonetheless generates non-zero disagreement between valid paths; detection requires a statistic on a cycle basis. The resulting procedure, Ksetra, estimates by coboundary projection and gates abstention on the harmonic component, which we give a mechanism: it arises from effect modification combined with overlap-specific population composition, and vanishes to machine precision when effect modification is absent. The degrees of freedom of an evidence network partition into calibration, coherence and transport, yielding an exact F-test for the existence of a global claim; we quantify its distortion under unequal precision and supply the precision-whitened form that restores exactness. Foreign exchange, where the arbitrage-free null makes the cochain exactly a coboundary, serves as a calibration bench: the test is correctly sized, fires on loop arbitrage, and ignores triangular arbitrage.

AI.tldr: The paper shows that local consistency checks in agentic AI are fundamentally insufficient, using cohomological tools to characterize and detect hidden, path-dependent inconsistencies in transported evidence.
AI.motivation: Agentic AI systems increasingly move inferences and numerical quantities across heterogeneous contexts (e.g., biology, medicine, finance). Current safeguards focus on local verification—ensuring each step is individually consistent and locally compatible. The authors are motivated by the worry that such local checks may miss deeper, global inconsistencies when evidence or conclusions are transported along multiple valid reasoning paths.
AI.method: The paper models context space via its nerve (a simplicial complex) and represents evidence as a real-valued 1-cochain on this complex. Reasoning corresponds to integrating this cochain along paths. The authors use algebraic topology—specifically Čech cohomology and Hodge decomposition—to decompose evidence conflicts into gradient (calibration), curl (local inconsistency detectable in overlaps), and harmonic (globally path-dependent but locally invisible) components. They prove theoretical limits on what simplex-local consistency checks can detect. They then construct a practical procedure, Ksetra, which uses coboundary projection and statistics on a cycle basis to estimate and gate on the harmonic component, and derive an F-test for the existence of a globally consistent claim, including a precision-whitened variant.
AI.result: They prove that any family of consistency checks that only use simplex-local information (on vertices, edges, and higher simplexes) cannot distinguish a cochain ω from ω+h when h is harmonic, even though ω+h induces non-zero disagreement between globally valid reasoning paths. They decompose the degrees of freedom of an evidence network into calibration, coherence, and transport and derive an exact F-test for whether the cochain is a pure coboundary (i.e., whether a global claim exists). They analyze how unequal precision distorts this test and provide a whitened version that restores exactness. They instantiate and validate the framework in a foreign exchange setting, where under the arbitrage-free null the cochain is exactly a coboundary, and show that their method is correctly sized, detects loop arbitrage, and remains insensitive to triangular arbitrage as desired.
AI.conclusion: Local, simplex-based verification is structurally incapable of catching a crucial class of path-dependent inconsistencies (the harmonic component) in transported evidence, even when all individual steps appear valid. Detecting these inconsistencies requires cycle-level statistics and explicit modeling of the harmonic part of the evidence cochain. The proposed Ksetra procedure and associated F-test provide a principled way to separate calibration, local coherence, and global transport structure, enabling robust detection of genuine global claims. Empirically, the framework behaves correctly in a foreign exchange benchmark, supporting its use as a safeguard for agentic AI systems that operate over complex evidence networks.

title: Ripple-Pivot Search: Active Parallel Decoding for Diffusion Large Language Models
summary: Diffusion Large Language Models (dLLMs) have emerged as a competitive alternative to autoregressive language models, offering the potential for substantially faster inference through parallel decoding. Existing parallel decoding schedulers typically commit positions only after they meet a per-position criterion, overlooking how early commitments may benefit subsequent decoding. We identify a ripple effect in dLLM decoding: proactively committing a mid-entropy pivot position can induce a pronounced reduction in uncertainty across the remaining masked positions. This uncertainty reduction allows subsequent steps to unmask more tokens in parallel, thereby accelerating the overall decoding process. To exploit the ripple effect, we propose Ripple-Pivot Search (RPS), a novel training-free decoding method that seeks mid-entropy positions as promising candidate pivots (where to decode), and determines their token assignment that yields the greatest downstream benefit via lookahead evaluation (what to decode). Across 3 dLLMs and 4 reasoning and code-generation benchmarks, RPS achieves 4-10$\times$ wall-clock speedup over the standard decoder while preserving generation quality, and improves accuracy over the previous lookahead baseline by up to 5.49% while delivering higher throughput in most settings. When integrated with KV caching, RPS further achieves up to 18$\times$ wall-clock speedup over the standard decoder.

AI.tldr: Paper proposes Ripple-Pivot Search (RPS), a training-free decoding method for diffusion LLMs that exploits a "ripple effect" from committing mid-entropy tokens to greatly speed up parallel decoding while maintaining or improving quality.
AI.motivation: Diffusion LLMs can decode tokens in parallel and potentially be much faster than autoregressive models, but existing parallel decoding schedulers only commit tokens when they individually meet confidence criteria and ignore how early commitments might globally reduce uncertainty. This underuses the structure of the diffusion process and leaves potential speed and accuracy gains untapped.
AI.method: The authors empirically identify a "ripple effect" in diffusion LLM decoding, where committing to a token at a mid-entropy position (neither too uncertain nor too certain) can sharply reduce uncertainty at other masked positions, enabling more tokens to be decoded in subsequent steps. Based on this, they introduce Ripple-Pivot Search (RPS), a training-free scheduler that: (1) selects mid-entropy positions as candidate pivot locations to commit early; (2) performs a lookahead evaluation over possible token assignments at these pivots to estimate which choice will most reduce future uncertainty and maximize parallel decoding; and (3) updates the decoding mask accordingly. They also integrate RPS with KV caching for additional speedups.
AI.result: On 3 diffusion LLMs and 4 benchmarks for reasoning and code generation, RPS yields 4–10× wall-clock speedup over the standard diffusion decoder without sacrificing generation quality. Compared with a prior lookahead-based baseline, RPS improves accuracy by up to 5.49% while also increasing throughput in most settings. With KV caching enabled, RPS reaches up to 18× wall-clock speedup over the standard decoder.
AI.conclusion: Exploiting the ripple effect via carefully chosen mid-entropy pivots enables more efficient parallel decoding in diffusion LLMs. Ripple-Pivot Search, which is training-free and scheduler-based, significantly accelerates inference while maintaining or improving accuracy, suggesting that better decoding strategies can unlock much of the practical advantage of diffusion language models over autoregressive models.

title: Symbolic Machine Learning for Vapor-Liquid Equilibrium Prediction in Cx-N2 Binary Mixtures
summary: Accurate prediction of vapor--liquid equilibrium (VLE) for hydrocarbon-nitrogen mixtures remains challenging for cubic equations of state, particularly across broad ranges of composition and hydrocarbon chain length. While deep learning models can provide accurate predictions, they often lack interpretability and explicit analytical expressions. In this work, we propose a symbolic machine learning approach to discover interpretable symbolic corrections to Peng-Robinson equation-of-state (PR-EOS) predictions from experimental data. The proposed approach adopts a two-level strategy: symbolic expressions are first identified for individual hydrocarbon systems, after which their coefficients are represented as functions of carbon number to enable accurate prediction across different hydrocarbon systems. The results demonstrate significantly improved prediction accuracy over the original PR-EOS across all hydrocarbon-nitrogen systems. Overall, the proposed approach provides an interpretable symbolic correction framework for improving PR-EOS predictions of hydrocarbon-nitrogen VLE.

AI.tldr: They build an interpretable symbolic correction to the Peng–Robinson EOS to greatly improve VLE predictions for hydrocarbon–nitrogen mixtures over wide compositions and chain lengths.
AI.motivation: Cubic equations of state like Peng–Robinson struggle to accurately predict VLE for hydrocarbon–nitrogen mixtures over wide composition ranges and varying hydrocarbon chain lengths.
