Pure deep learning models can fix accuracy but are black boxes and lack explicit analytical forms, which limits trust, extrapolation, and use in conventional thermodynamic calculations. The paper is motivated by the need for a method that improves accuracy while preserving interpretability and analytical structure.
AI.method: They use symbolic machine learning to learn closed-form correction terms to the PR-EOS VLE predictions directly from experimental data. The workflow is two-level: (1) For each individual hydrocarbon–nitrogen system, they identify a symbolic expression that corrects the PR-EOS predictions. (2) They then model the coefficients of these symbolic expressions as functions of the hydrocarbon carbon number so that a unified, chain-length-dependent correction is obtained, enabling predictions across different hydrocarbons with a single interpretable formula.
AI.result: The learned symbolic corrections significantly reduce prediction errors of PR-EOS for all examined hydrocarbon–nitrogen systems over broad composition and chain-length ranges. The corrected PR-EOS consistently outperforms the uncorrected version while retaining a compact analytical form. Quantitative improvements are not listed in the abstract but are described as substantial and systematic.
AI.conclusion: Symbolic machine learning can discover simple, interpretable correction formulas that upgrade classical cubic EOS like Peng–Robinson for complex mixtures. By parameterizing correction coefficients versus carbon number, one obtains a generalized, chain-length-aware correction that yields much more accurate VLE predictions for hydrocarbon–nitrogen systems while maintaining analytical transparency and compatibility with existing thermodynamic workflows.

title: LabelFusion-TS: Fusing Large Language Models, Transformer Encoders, and Financial Time Series for Monetary-Policy Stance Classification
summary: Financial text is produced and interpreted within a market environment, yet financial text classifiers almost always receive text alone. We study whether financial time series are useful as an additional input on the task of classifying sentences from Federal Reserve communication as hawkish, dovish, or neutral. Our system, \lfts{}, extends the \lf{} architecture with this modality: a small voting network combines three independently trained components, a fine-tuned RoBERTa encoder, a prompted large language model (LLM), and a fused ensemble of time-series transformers over the market series of the months preceding publication. Because only about a thousand annotated sentences are available for training, the RoBERTa encoder is first pre-trained on sentences annotated automatically by the LLM and only then fine-tuned on the human labels. Trained on Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC) communication up to 2015 and evaluated on 2015--2022, the fused system achieves 70.2\% weighted F1 -- against 64.1\% for the zero-shot LLM -- and overtakes it with as few as 240 human-labelled sentences. We take this as initial evidence for market time series as an input modality in financial text classification.

AI.tldr: They enhance financial text classification (hawkish/dovish/neutral Fed sentences) by combining language models with financial time-series transformers, showing that adding market data and weak supervision beats a strong zero-shot LLM baseline, even with few human labels.
AI.motivation: Existing financial text classifiers generally ignore the fact that financial language is produced and interpreted within a market context; they only use the text, despite traders relying heavily on recent market behavior to interpret central bank communication. Moreover, labeled data for nuanced stances like hawkish/dovish is scarce, making it hard to fine-tune powerful text encoders effectively. The paper aims to test whether including market time series as an additional input modality, and leveraging LLM-generated weak labels, can improve sentence-level stance classification of Federal Reserve communications in an out-of-sample time period.
AI.method: They build \lfts{}, an extension of the Label-Free Distillation (\lf{}) architecture, which combines three components through a small voting network: (1) a RoBERTa encoder fine-tuned for hawkish/dovish/neutral classification; (2) a prompted large language model used as a zero-shot classifier and weak labeler; and (3) a fused ensemble of time-series transformer models operating on market time series from the months prior to each communication. Due to limited human-annotated data (~1,000 sentences), they first pre-train RoBERTa on LLM-annotated sentences (weak supervision) and then fine-tune it on the human labels. The time-series transformers ingest multiple financial series and produce class predictions that are then combined with the text-based components via a learned voting module. They train on FOMC communication up to 2015 and evaluate on 2015–2022 data.
AI.result: The fused multimodal system reaches a 70.2% weighted F1 score on 2015–2022 FOMC sentences, outperforming the zero-shot LLM baseline at 64.1% weighted F1. The approach becomes superior to the LLM with as few as 240 human-labeled sentences, showing strong label efficiency. These results indicate that both the use of LLM-generated weak labels for pre-training RoBERTa and the inclusion of financial time-series transformers contribute to performance gains in stance classification of Fed communications.
AI.conclusion: The study provides initial empirical evidence that incorporating financial market time series as an additional input modality improves financial text classification of central bank communication. By combining a weakly supervised RoBERTa encoder, a prompted LLM, and time-series transformers in a voting framework, the system outperforms a strong zero-shot LLM baseline, even in low-label regimes. This suggests that future financial NLP systems should consider multimodal architectures that account for the market context in which texts are produced and interpreted, especially when labeled data is scarce.

title: Adaptive Hybrid Particle Swarm Optimization with Gradient Descent
comment: 11 pages, 8 figures, 8 tables, 25 references. 14,700+ independent optimization runs
summary: Gradient injection helps Particle Swarm Optimization (PSO) only when the swarm has identified a basin with smooth local structure, not universally. We propose Adaptive Hybrid PSO (AHPSO), which uses a sigmoid function on swarm diversity to automatically modulate gradient influence: near-zero during exploration, near-maximum during exploitation, with no manual phase-switching. Under budget-normalized comparison (PSO given equivalent total function evaluations), PSO wins 52.5% of 40 configurations versus AHPSO's 20% (p = 7.0e-5, Friedman). AHPSO retains advantage specifically on problems with smooth local basins (F8, F24-F27) where directed descent outperforms undirected sampling even at equal cost. Under iteration-matched comparison across 29 functions (42 configurations, 14,700 runs), AHPSO-Adadelta ranks first of 9 methods including CMA-ES (p = 9.75e-4). The contribution is a principled characterization of when gradient injection provides value in swarm-based search, not a claim of universal superiority.

AI.tldr: Study introduces Adaptive Hybrid PSO (AHPSO), which selectively injects gradient information into Particle Swarm Optimization only when swarm diversity indicates convergence to smooth basins, showing that gradients help in specific scenarios rather than universally.
AI.motivation: Understand when and how gradient information actually benefits Particle Swarm Optimization, given empirical evidence that naive or constant gradient injection does not always improve performance and may harm exploration. The authors aim to formalize conditions under which gradient-based refinement is valuable in swarm search.
AI.method: Propose AHPSO, a hybrid PSO algorithm that uses a sigmoid function of swarm diversity to adaptively scale the influence of gradient information: negligible when diversity is high (exploration) and strong when diversity is low (exploitation). They compare AHPSO variants against standard PSO and other optimizers under two evaluation protocols: (1) budget-normalized (matching total function evaluations) and (2) iteration-matched across multiple benchmark functions, using statistical tests (Friedman) for ranking significance.
AI.result: In budget-normalized tests over 40 configurations, standard PSO outperforms AHPSO in win-rate (52.5% vs. 20%, statistically significant with p = 7.0e-5), indicating that gradient injection is not broadly superior when accounting for its evaluation cost. However, AHPSO shows clear advantages on problems with smooth local basins (e.g., benchmarks F8, F24–F27), where directional gradient steps are more efficient than undirected swarm sampling. In iteration-matched tests on 29 functions (42 configurations, 14,700 runs), the AHPSO variant with Adadelta achieves the best overall rank among 9 algorithms, including CMA-ES, with statistically significant superiority (p = 9.75e-4).
AI.conclusion: Gradient injection should not be viewed as a universally beneficial enhancement to PSO but as a tool that yields value under specific landscape conditions—particularly smooth basins suited to local descent. AHPSO offers a principled, diversity-driven mechanism to switch between exploration-dominated and gradient-dominated behavior without manual phase scheduling, and the empirical results clarify the regimes where such hybridization is advantageous.

title: AWARe: Mitigating Catastrophic Forgetting via Activation-Weighted Adaptive REtention
summary: Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) exhibit strong generalization and reasoning abilities due to large-scale multimodal pre-training. However, fine-tuning these models on downstream tasks often leads to catastrophic forgetting, where newly learned task-specific knowledge degrades previously acquired capabilities. This issue arises because gradient updates for new tasks overwrite parameters critical to prior knowledge, limiting the practical deployment of MLLMs. To address this challenge, we propose Activation-Weighted Adaptive REtention (AWARe), a fine-tuning method that mitigates catastrophic forgetting by dynamically controlling parameter updates based on activation patterns. AWARe assigns activation-based importance scores to parameters, selectively freezing those essential for preserving prior capabilities while allowing less important parameters to adapt to new tasks. Importantly, AWARe operates without modifying model architectures, ensuring compatibility with existing inference engines. Extensive experiments demonstrate that AWARe effectively preserves upstream capabilities while achieving superior downstream performance compared to existing methods. Code is available at https://github.com/kaln27/AWARe.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces AWARe, a fine-tuning method for Multimodal Large Language Models that reduces catastrophic forgetting by adaptively freezing important parameters based on their activation patterns, thus preserving prior capabilities while improving downstream task performance without changing model architecture.
AI.motivation: Fine-tuning Multimodal Large Language Models on specific downstream tasks often causes catastrophic forgetting, where new task learning harms previously acquired general capabilities, limiting their practical use. There is a need for a method that allows effective adaptation to new tasks while preserving upstream, pre-trained knowledge, and that works without altering model architectures or inference pipelines.
AI.method: The paper proposes Activation-Weighted Adaptive REtention (AWARe), which analyzes activation patterns during fine-tuning to compute importance scores for model parameters. Parameters deemed highly important for existing capabilities are selectively frozen to retain prior knowledge, while less critical parameters are allowed to update to learn new tasks. The method is applied during standard fine-tuning and does not require architectural modifications, making it plug-and-play with existing inference engines.
AI.result: Experiments show that AWARe significantly alleviates catastrophic forgetting in Multimodal Large Language Models, maintaining strong upstream performance while also achieving better results on downstream tasks than competing fine-tuning techniques. The empirical evaluation suggests that activation-based parameter importance is effective for balancing retention and adaptation.
AI.conclusion: AWARe provides an architecture-agnostic fine-tuning strategy for MLLMs that dynamically controls parameter updates using activation-based importance, effectively preserving pre-trained capabilities while enhancing downstream performance and integrating seamlessly with existing systems.

title: Glance, Scrutinize, and Think: Advancing Video Anomaly Detection from Training-Free to Agentic Reasoning
comment: 34 pages, 8 figures, 8 tables. Journal extension of our AAAI 2026 paper (arXiv:2507.21507)
summary: Video Anomaly Detection (VAD) aims to identify anomalous events and localize their temporal intervals. Existing approaches exhibit a "when-what" dissociation: traditional DNN-based methods localize when anomalies occur but lack semantic understanding, whereas LLM-based methods explain what happens but neglect precise temporal grounding. We attribute this to the absence of a unified reasoning paradigm. Inspired by how humans inspect surveillance videos - glancing globally to form temporal hypotheses, scrutinizing suspicious segments, and thinking iteratively to correct errors - we study this global-to-local paradigm from two perspectives. We first propose Glance then Scrutinize (GtS), a training-free framework using static and dynamic textual guidance for coarse-to-fine anomaly grounding and understanding, balancing accuracy and speed. To break the ceiling imposed by frozen external modules, we further propose a tool-augmented agentic VAD method, where a multimodal large language model learns to invoke a video cropping tool, inspect densely resampled frames, and self-correct mislocalized hypotheses, via cold-start supervised fine-tuning followed by reinforcement learning with a joint answer-grounding reward. For training and evaluation, we extend our prior VAGU benchmark into VAGU-T (Video Anomaly Grounding, Understanding, and Thinking), comprising 7,567 real-world videos over 21 anomaly categories with human-validated grounding, explanations, QA pairs, and chain-of-thought tool-calling traces. We further introduce JeAUG, a metric jointly evaluating semantic interpretability and temporal precision. Experiments show that GtS substantially surpasses training-free baselines, while the agentic model delivers both higher accuracy and faster inference.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a unified, human-inspired global-to-local reasoning framework for video anomaly detection that combines precise temporal localization with semantic explanation, enabled by a training-free method and a tool-augmented multimodal LLM agent, evaluated on an expanded benchmark and a new joint metric.
AI.motivation: Current Video Anomaly Detection methods are split: DNN-based models can detect when anomalies occur but lack semantic understanding, while LLM-based methods provide rich descriptions of what happens but fail to temporally localize events accurately. There is no unified reasoning paradigm that jointly handles temporal grounding and semantic interpretation in a human-like, iterative way. The authors aim to bridge this "when-what" dissociation and improve both accuracy and efficiency in anomaly detection, grounding, and explanation.
AI.method: The authors introduce two complementary approaches under a global-to-local, human-inspired reasoning paradigm. (1) Glance then Scrutinize (GtS): a training-free framework that first performs a global glance over the video using static and dynamic textual guidance to generate coarse anomaly hypotheses, then scrutinizes suspicious temporal segments for finer-grained grounding and understanding, balancing speed and accuracy. (2) A tool-augmented agentic VAD method: a multimodal large language model is trained as an agent that can call a video cropping tool, densely inspect resampled frames, and iteratively self-correct mislocalized anomaly hypotheses. This agent is trained via a two-stage process: cold-start supervised fine-tuning on curated traces, followed by reinforcement learning using a combined reward that accounts for both answer correctness and temporal grounding quality. They support this with an extended benchmark, VAGU-T, and a new evaluation metric, JeAUG, that jointly assesses semantic interpretability and temporal precision.
AI.result: On the extended VAGU-T benchmark, GtS outperforms other training-free baselines in both temporal grounding and anomaly understanding. The tool-augmented multimodal LLM agent further improves over GtS and prior methods, achieving higher accuracy and faster inference by effectively invoking tools, refining temporal localization, and providing coherent explanations. Quantitatively, the proposed JeAUG metric shows that the new methods better balance semantic interpretability with precise temporal localization than existing approaches.
AI.conclusion: A unified global-to-local reasoning paradigm can effectively address the "when-what" dissociation in video anomaly detection. The proposed GtS framework and tool-augmented multimodal LLM agent jointly enable more accurate, temporally precise, and semantically rich anomaly detection and explanation, while also improving inference efficiency. The new VAGU-T benchmark and JeAUG metric provide comprehensive infrastructure for training and evaluating such systems, supporting future research on agentic, tool-using models for video understanding.

title: Causal Structure is Inducible but Functionally Decoupled: The Routing/Readout Boundary of a Typed Mechanism Library
summary: When a language model answers an interventional question, the computation it must perform depends on the type of evidence the query requires. We report a decoupling in how a transformer organizes causal knowledge: slot-by-type structure induced by type-level supervision organizes routing, yet remains functionally decoupled from answer readout. We establish this with a typed mechanism library -- discrete mechanism slots partitioned by evidence type, auditable at the state level -- on a causal-world benchmark with exact interventional ground truth, under a frozen protocol, at two scales (22.6M and 125M). Four preregistered findings. (i) Origin. Slot-by-type organization is induced by type-level supervision: absent in architecturally identical unsupervised controls, not buyable by content-free gating labels, and statistically attributable to the supervision signal, replicating at 125M under a powered preregistered protocol (all nine cells passed). (ii) Boundary. The induced structure is a typed routing index with a sharp routing/readout boundary: slot codes scaffold routing but do not drive answer readout ($|Δ\hat{y}| \le 3.4\times10^{-6}$, zero collateral, three seeds, stable across a 5.6x scale window) -- we therefore make no behavioral-editability claim. (iii) Cost. The structure is free: LM quality matches a parameter-matched monolith within 0.0082 nats. (iv) Trust. The library state is exactly local under edit and bit-exactly revertible -- 250 single-edit and 1,000 stacked reverts per seed, zero failures. We further find that the unsupervised null itself moves with scale, so comparisons reusing a null calibrated at one scale may be confounded at another. Every claim is tied to a preregistered, machine-checkable criterion archived before the data it governs; the full audit trail, including one criterion we failed and how the frozen protocol handled it, is released as an appendix.

AI.tldr: The paper studies how transformers internally organize causal knowledge for answering interventional questions, and finds a clean separation between routing by evidence type and answer readout using a typed mechanism library on a controlled causal benchmark.
AI.motivation: To understand and audit how language models compute answers to interventional causal questions, especially how different types of evidence are internally routed and used. Current interpretability work often lacks exact ground truth, strong experimental control, and preregistered, machine-checkable claims; this work aims to provide a rigorously controlled setting to study the internal structure that supports causal reasoning.
AI.method: The authors build a causal-world benchmark with exact interventional ground truth and train transformer language models (22.6M and 125M parameters) under a frozen protocol. They introduce a typed mechanism library: discrete mechanism slots partitioned by evidence type, which allows state-level auditing. They compare supervised models (with type-level supervision) against unsupervised controls and models with content-free gating labels. They analyze the learned slot structure, quantify its impact on routing vs answer readout, measure performance cost relative to a monolithic baseline, and test how locally editable and revertible the library states are, using preregistered, machine-checkable evaluation criteria across multiple seeds and scales.
AI.result: 1) Origin: Slot-by-type structure appears only when type-level supervision is present; it is absent in unsupervised controls, not inducible by content-free gating, and statistically attributable to the supervision signal, replicating at 125M with all preregistered tests passing. 2) Boundary: The resulting structure acts as a typed routing index with a sharp separation from answer readout; modifying slot codes affects routing but not outputs (Δŷ ≤ 3.4×10^-6) over multiple seeds and a 5.6x scale range, so it does not constitute a behavioral-editable handle. 3) Cost: Adding this typed mechanism library incurs essentially no performance penalty; language model quality is within 0.0082 nats of a parameter-matched monolithic model. 4) Trust: The mechanism library states are exactly local and bit-exactly revertible under edits, with extensive tests (250 single-edit and 1,000 stacked reverts per seed) showing zero failures. They also find that the unsupervised null model’s internal behavior shifts with scale, warning that cross-scale comparisons using a fixed null can be confounded.
AI.conclusion: Transformers answering interventional questions can be made to organize causal knowledge into a slot-by-type mechanism library where type-level supervision induces discrete, evidence-type-partitioned routing codes that are sharply decoupled from answer readout. This typed routing index is effectively free in performance cost, highly auditable, and precisely editable/revertible at the state level, but does not itself provide direct behavioral control of outputs. The work underscores the importance of scale-aware null baselines and preregistered, machine-checkable evaluation protocols for reliable interpretability claims.

title: Deployment Decision Reliability: A Generalizability-Theory Framework for Sizing Long-Horizon Agent Evaluations
comment: 11 pages, 1 figure, 1 table. Code and reproducibility artifacts: https://github.com/vasundras/agent-reliability-engineering-lab
summary: Enterprise practitioners read agent leaderboards as if they ranked agent capability. We show, across three open agent-trace benchmarks (TheAgentCompany, $τ^2$-bench, and AppWorld), that the agent main effect accounts for less than 3% of total variance in every dataset and check type, while the agent-by-task interaction accounts for 7-23%. Leaderboards rank specialization, not capability. We arrive at this through a four-facet Generalizability Theory variance decomposition, fit with three estimators (Henderson Method-I, REML via lme4, and a Bayesian binomial GLMM) that agree to three decimal places. Four further findings sharpen what the leaderboard is hiding. First, aggregate reliability collapses on the hardest task quartile: $Eρ^2$ on $τ^2$ action_checks falls from 0.752 to 0.000. Second, training-cell reliability negatively correlates with held-out reliability ($r = -0.90$ on $τ^2$), meaning the designs that look most reliable replicate worst. Third, population-level diagnostics transfer across enterprise benchmarks (capability-gap ratio stable at 0.35-0.40) but per-family agent rankings invert. Fourth, on the MAST failure taxonomy, trace-level mode profiles are idiosyncratic (MAE = 0.261) while cell-level profiles generalise (MAE = 0.056, $r = 0.83$). We package these into Deployment Decision Reliability (DDR), a one-page reporting discipline that turns the variance-component table into five decisions an enterprise buyer can defend. All code, data loaders, and fit artifacts are released under an open-source license.

AI.tldr: The paper shows that current multi-agent leaderboards mainly measure task specialization rather than overall agent capability, using Generalizability Theory to decompose variance and proposing a practical reporting framework (DDR) for more reliable deployment decisions.
AI.motivation: Enterprise users often treat agent leaderboards as if they provide a reliable, general ranking of agent capability. However, agents may perform very differently across tasks and conditions, so a single aggregate score can be misleading for deployment decisions. There is a need to rigorously quantify what portion of performance variation is due to inherent agent capability versus task-specific effects and interactions, and to turn those insights into a form that practitioners can use when selecting agents for real-world applications.
AI.method: The authors analyze three open agent-trace benchmarks (TheAgentCompany, τ^2-bench, and AppWorld) using a four-facet Generalizability Theory (G-Theory) framework. They perform variance decomposition to partition total performance variance into components for agent main effects, task effects, and agent-by-task interactions (among others). They fit this G-Theory model using three independent estimators—Henderson Method-I, REML via lme4, and a Bayesian binomial generalized linear mixed model (GLMM)—and verify agreement to three decimal places. They further compute reliability metrics (e.g., generalizability coefficients Eρ^2) across task difficulty quartiles, correlate training-cell reliability with held-out reliability, examine transfer of diagnostics across benchmarks, and analyze error patterns using the MAST failure taxonomy at both trace and cell levels. Finally, they summarize these diagnostics into a Deployment Decision Reliability (DDR) template—a one-page reporting discipline grounded in the variance components.
AI.result: Across all three benchmarks and check types, the agent main effect explains less than 3% of the total performance variance, whereas the agent-by-task interaction explains between 7% and 23%, indicating strong specialization. Aggregate leaderboard reliability collapses on the hardest quartile of tasks; for example, Eρ^2 on τ^2 action_checks drops from 0.752 overall to 0.000 for the most difficult tasks. Reliability estimated on training cells is strongly negatively correlated with held-out reliability (r = -0.90 on τ^2), so the designs that look most reliable in-sample generalize worst. Population-level diagnostics, such as the capability-gap ratio, are stable across enterprise benchmarks (around 0.35–0.40), yet rankings of agent families invert between benchmarks. In the MAST taxonomy, failure mode profiles at the trace level are highly idiosyncratic (MAE = 0.261), while profiles aggregated at the cell level generalize well (MAE = 0.056, r = 0.83). These findings are consolidated into the DDR framework, and the authors release code, data loaders, and fitted models as open source.
AI.conclusion: The paper concludes that current agent leaderboards do not measure a single stable notion of agent capability; instead, they primarily reflect task-specific specialization and agent–task interactions. Aggregate scores can give a false sense of reliability, especially on harder tasks and when judged only on training splits. Reliable deployment decisions require variance-aware evaluation: understanding where variance comes from, how reliability behaves across task difficulty, and how well diagnostics transfer across settings. The proposed Deployment Decision Reliability (DDR) reporting discipline turns technical variance decomposition into a small set of defensible, practitioner-facing decisions, offering a more robust basis for enterprise agent selection and evaluation. The open-source release enables others to reproduce, extend, and apply this methodology to their own agent benchmarks.

title: Diagnosis Before Recovery: Turning Agent Failures into Selective Self-Correction
summary: Self-correction is particularly useful when a failure constrains the next repair. Coding agents benefit from this property because compilers, tests, and execution traces turn many failures into typed recovery signals, but broad language-agent tasks often expose only a coarse task failure. This creates a tension for generic recovery playbooks: they broaden the agent's context precisely when the system needs a narrower repair interface, mixing incompatible signals for invalid actions, missing procedures, and strict-format errors. Our insight is that development-set failures can recover part of the missing diagnostic substrate by deciding which recovery interventions are admissible before test-time correction. We propose DARC, a diagnosis-guided recovery harness that profiles task-family failure modes, prunes mismatched interventions from a shared recovery library, and freezes a verifier-selected success-cost policy for deployment. This causal order makes correction selective: the harness first determines what kind of failure can be repaired, then decides how much recovery evidence to spend. In ALFWorld, AppWorld, and XBRL Finance, the same protocol yields an action-validity harness, a procedural-recovery fallback, and a format-precision retrieval policy; in each evaluated setting it improves average task performance over base agents and broad playbooks while reducing environment steps or retrieval budget. Our experiments show that failures need not trigger uniformly more context: DARC turns self-correction from prompt expansion into recovery-interface design. DARC provides a practical route toward more reliable agents in domains where compiler-like feedback is absent: making failures actionable before making contexts larger.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces DARC, a diagnosis-guided recovery framework that profiles failure modes in development to choose targeted self-correction strategies, improving agent reliability without always expanding context.
AI.motivation: Existing language agents often rely on coarse task-level failure signals, unlike coding agents that get rich, typed feedback from compilers and tests. Generic recovery strategies tend to add more context and mixed signals when what’s really needed is a precise, structured repair interface. The authors aim to recover some of the benefits of compiler-like diagnostics in domains where such feedback is absent, by making self-correction more selective and structured rather than uniformly expanding prompts.
AI.method: They propose DARC, a diagnosis-guided recovery harness that: (1) profiles failure modes on a development set for a given task family; (2) identifies which kinds of failures are actually repairable; (3) prunes incompatible or unhelpful interventions from a shared recovery library; and (4) fixes a verifier-driven policy that trades off success gains vs. recovery cost for deployment. This establishes a causal order: first decide which failures can be repaired, then decide how much recovery evidence or effort to invest, effectively turning self-correction into a designed recovery interface tailored to the task domain.
AI.result: Using the same DARC protocol, they instantiate three different harnesses across ALFWorld, AppWorld, and XBRL Finance: an action-validity harness, a procedural-recovery fallback, and a format-precision retrieval strategy. In all evaluated settings, DARC improves average task performance compared to both base agents and broad, generic recovery playbooks, while also reducing environment interaction steps or retrieval budget.
AI.conclusion: Self-correction for language agents does not need to default to adding more context; instead, it can be reframed as designing a domain-specific recovery interface informed by observed failures. DARC demonstrates that profiling failures ahead of time and constraining admissible interventions yields more reliable, efficient agents in domains lacking compiler-like feedback, by making failures actionable before expanding context.

title: Apodex Discovery: Reality Benchmarks and Environments for Evaluating and Building Discoverative Artificial Intelligence
summary:
Apollo did not reach the Moon merely because its engineers could solve difficult equations. It succeeded by turning a distant ambition into a mission architecture of explicit objectives, simulation, verification, and repeated correction. AI now faces a similar transition: frontier models can solve difficult tasks once the problem, tools, and success criteria are specified, yet consequential real-world challenges rarely arrive in an executable or verifiable form.
  We introduce Apodex Discovery, a framework for building and evaluating discoverative AI through the heavy-duty solver, a system comprising a foundation model, harness, tools, and control policies that pursues extended, stateful, verifiable investigations. It has three core components. First, a problem-scouting process surveyed 561 industries across 16 sectors, assembled 423 high-value real-world problems, and selected 20 for the initial release. Second, a common environment-task-episode abstraction provides data, tools, constraints, feedback, trajectory recording, and verification of intermediate artifacts and final submissions. Third, HDS6 evaluates Tools, Repair, Alternatives, Coherence, Evidence, and Scope independently of final-task success.
  In AAV capsid design, Apodex surpassed the published state of the art by 7% across viability, tropism, structure prediction, and generative design. In drug repurposing and reformulation, a task-specific biomedical environment improved the mean normalized prediction score of GPT-5.5 and GPT-5.6-sol by 2.5 and 7.6 points over the same closed-book backbone. Controlled ablations show that the fixed TRACES episode interface enables attribution of performance differences to specific solver components. Apodex Discovery moves AI evaluation beyond predefined benchmarks toward verifiable investigations aimed at genuine discovery.

AI.tldr: Introduces Apodex Discovery, a framework and benchmark suite for “discoverative AI” that evaluates AI systems on extended, verifiable scientific and industrial discovery tasks rather than narrow benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Frontier AI models excel once problems are well-specified, but most impactful real-world challenges are messy: goals are under-defined, not easily executable, and success is hard to verify. Current benchmarks don’t capture this, so there is a need for a framework that (1) identifies high-value, real-world discovery problems, (2) provides rich environments where models can work in a stateful, tool-using, and verifiable way, and (3) evaluates not just final answers but the quality and robustness of the investigative process.
AI.method: The authors build Apodex Discovery around a “heavy-duty solver” architecture combining a foundation model with a harness, tools, and control policies to run extended, stateful investigations. They: (1) conduct a large-scale “problem-scouting” process over 561 industries to collect 423 high-value problems and select 20 initial tasks; (2) define a standardized environment-task-episode abstraction that supplies data, tools, constraints, feedback, trajectory logging, and verification for intermediate artifacts and final outputs; and (3) design the HDS6 evaluation scheme (Tools, Repair, Alternatives, Coherence, Evidence, Scope) to assess solver behavior independently of whether the final task was solved, enabling controlled ablations via a fixed TRACES episode interface.
AI.result: On AAV capsid design, Apodex Discovery solvers beat the previous published state of the art by 7% across multiple biological criteria (viability, tropism, structure prediction, generative design). In drug repurposing and reformulation, equipping GPT-5.5 and GPT-5.6-sol with a dedicated biomedical environment improved their mean normalized prediction scores by 2.5 and 7.6 points compared to the same models in a closed-book setting. Controlled ablation experiments show that, because of the fixed TRACES episode interface, performance differences can be cleanly attributed to particular solver components (e.g., tools or control policies).
AI.conclusion: Apodex Discovery provides a concrete framework and benchmark suite to move AI evaluation from narrow, pre-specified benchmarks to richer, verifiable discovery workflows. By combining curated high-value tasks, standardized interactive environments, and process-focused evaluation criteria (HDS6), the framework supports building and diagnosing “discoverative AI” systems that can conduct long-horizon, tool-using investigations and achieve state-of-the-art results in domains such as protein engineering and drug discovery.

title: Language-Conditional Dequantization: Recovering What Quantization Steals from Non-English Languages
summary: Aggressive quantization disproportionately harms multilingual capability: in the sub-4B INT3 GPTQ regime, we measure 2-4x larger perplexity degradation on non-English languages than on English. We propose Language-Conditional Dequantization (LCD), a post-hoc method that attaches per-language rank-2 LoRA corrections to the linear layers of an already-quantized model, adding 0.12% parameters per language and training in under 20 minutes on a single GPU. Across Qwen2.5-3B and Llama-3.2-3B, LCD recovers 70-83% of the perplexity gap for non-Latin script languages and 17-28% of the GlobalMMLU accuracy gap, outperforming a language-agnostic correction of equal capacity by 3-9 points on typologically distant languages and a data-free low-rank baseline (LQER) by an order of magnitude. We further identify a perplexity-accuracy disconnect and trace it to where quantization concentrates damage: early-depth errors (Llama) propagate downstream and resist local correction, while late-depth errors (Qwen) do not. A layer-restricted variant of LCD validates this mechanism directly.

AI.tldr: The paper shows that aggressive low-bit quantization harms non-English languages much more than English in small LLMs, and introduces a lightweight, per-language LoRA-based dequantization method that largely recovers this lost performance and reveals where quantization damage occurs in model depth.
AI.motivation: To deploy small, aggressively quantized LLMs efficiently while preserving strong multilingual performance. Existing quantization schemes disproportionately degrade non-English language capability, especially for non-Latin scripts, and generic, language-agnostic correction methods are insufficient. The authors want a simple, cheap, post-hoc fix that restores multilingual quality without retraining or significantly increasing model size.
AI.method: They first empirically measure how INT3 GPTQ quantization affects perplexity across many languages for sub-4B parameter models. They then propose Language-Conditional Dequantization (LCD), which attaches a small, rank-2 LoRA adapter per language to the linear layers of an already-quantized model. These language-specific corrections are trained quickly (under 20 minutes on a single GPU), adding only 0.12% parameters per language. They compare LCD against language-agnostic corrections of the same capacity and against a data-free low-rank correction baseline (LQER). Finally, they perform layer-restricted LCD experiments to analyze how error location in depth (early vs. late layers) explains the observed perplexity-accuracy disconnect and the differing behavior between Qwen and Llama.
AI.result: In the INT3 GPTQ regime for sub-4B models, quantization increases perplexity for non-English languages 2–4x more than for English, confirming strong multilingual degradation. LCD recovers 70–83% of the quantization-induced perplexity gap for non-Latin script languages on Qwen2.5-3B and Llama-3.2-3B, and recovers 17–28% of the GlobalMMLU accuracy gap. It outperforms equally sized language-agnostic corrections by 3–9 accuracy points on typologically distant languages and surpasses the data-free LQER baseline by an order of magnitude. Layer-restricted variants show that in Llama models, quantization errors in early layers propagate and are hard to fix locally, whereas in Qwen models quantization damage is concentrated in later layers and is more amenable to local correction.
AI.conclusion: Aggressive low-bit quantization is not language-neutral: it disproportionately harms multilingual performance, especially for non-Latin script languages, even when English performance appears acceptable. Lightweight, per-language LoRA-based dequantization (LCD) can largely restore this lost capability at minimal parameter and compute cost, and is substantially more effective than language-agnostic or data-free low-rank corrections. The depth-wise distribution of quantization error matters: early-layer damage in some architectures causes a perplexity-accuracy disconnect and resists simple local fixes, while late-layer damage in others is easier to correct, informing where and how to apply dequantization strategies.

title: Can Frontier LLMs Match Natively Multimodal Embeddings? A Comparison on Hard-Negative Text-to-Image Retrieval
summary: Multimodal retrieval and classification across different types of media, spanning text, images,video and audio, has traditionally relied on dual-encoder models that align visual and textual representations through contrastive learning. The March 2026 release of Gemini Embedding 2, Google's first natively multimodal embedding model to map text, images, video, audio, and documents into a single shared space, raises competition among multimodal retrieval systems. Simultaneously, frontier Large language models (LLMs) have also demonstrated strong visual understanding, raising the question of whether they can serve as effective zero-shot rankers. Our study provides the first direct comparison of native multimodal embeddings against LLM-based visual ranking on Flickr30k. We observe that GPT-4.1 and Claude Sonnet 4.6 perform on par with Gemini Embedding 2. Additionally, once embeddings are precomputed, multimodal embeddings are better suited for low-latency applications.

AI.tldr: The paper compares native multimodal embedding models with LLM-based visual rankers for multimodal retrieval, finding similar performance but different latency profiles.
AI.motivation: To understand whether frontier LLMs with strong visual abilities can replace or rival dedicated multimodal embedding models for retrieval and ranking tasks, especially in zero-shot settings.
AI.method: Conduct a direct empirical comparison on the Flickr30k dataset between Gemini Embedding 2 (a natively multimodal embedding model) and LLMs like GPT-4.1 and Claude Sonnet 4.6 used as zero-shot visual rankers, focusing on retrieval and ranking quality and latency once embeddings are precomputed.
AI.result: GPT-4.1 and Claude Sonnet 4.6 achieve ranking performance comparable to Gemini Embedding 2 on Flickr30k, while multimodal embedding models show clear advantages in low-latency scenarios when embeddings are precomputed.
AI.conclusion: LLMs can act as competitive zero-shot visual rankers compared to state-of-the-art multimodal embeddings, but dedicated multimodal embedding models remain preferable for low-latency retrieval systems where precomputed embeddings are used.

title: GRPO for Financial Advice Generation: Outperforming Commercial LLMs under CATE Evaluation
summary:
Generating actionable financial advice from business records demands that models integrate numerical reasoning, domain knowledge, and sound judgment, while avoiding recommendations that could harm the business. Direct supervision is difficult: historical decisions are not necessarily optimal, and high-quality free-form labels are expensive to obtain. We formulate financial advice generation as a reinforcement learning problem and fine-tune an open-weight language model using Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO). Our reward is an LLM-as-a-judge rubric that scores each recommendation across multiple binary dimensions of advice quality, augmented with a safety gate for harm prevention.
  Since LLM-based evaluation alone cannot confirm whether improvements reflect genuine business value rather than adaptation to the judge, we complement it with a judge-independent audit based on a standard doubly-robust Conditional Average Treatment Effect (CATE) estimator. Under this observational off-policy audit, our trained LLM achieves approximately twice the estimated gross-profit lift of the strongest evaluated commercial baseline ($0.0228$ vs.\ $0.0104$), together with the lowest downside rate and the least negative tail risk of any policy evaluated. Notably, the two evaluations do not rank the baselines identically: the untrained base model places last on the judge rubric but second on the causal audit, indicating that the audit captures a signal the judge does not. Our results demonstrate that GRPO with a finance-grounded reward signal can produce substantially more useful business recommendations than commercial LLMs, and that a judge-independent causal audit is a valuable complement to, rather than a confirmation of, LLM-as-a-judge assessment in financial NLP.

AI.tldr: They train an open-weight LLM with RL to give safer, more profitable financial advice from business records, and validate it both with an LLM judge and an independent causal audit based on observed profits.
AI.motivation: Producing financial recommendations from business data requires numerical reasoning, domain knowledge, and safety, but supervised labels are scarce, biased, and not guaranteed to be optimal. Existing LLM evaluation via LLM-as-a-judge may reward gaming the judge rather than real business value. There is a need for a training and evaluation framework that aligns LLM advice with actual financial outcomes and risk profiles, not just with heuristic labels.
AI.method: They cast financial advice generation as a reinforcement learning problem and fine-tune an open-weight language model via Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO). The reward is computed by an LLM-as-a-judge using a rubric that evaluates multiple binary dimensions of advice quality and includes a safety gate to block harmful recommendations. For evaluation, beyond the judge scores, they perform a judge-independent audit using an observational off-policy evaluation method: a standard doubly-robust Conditional Average Treatment Effect (CATE) estimator that infers the expected profit lift and downside risk of following the model’s recommendations from historical business data.
AI.result: In the causal audit with the doubly-robust CATE estimator, the RL-trained LLM achieves about double the estimated gross-profit lift compared to the strongest commercial baseline (0.0228 vs. 0.0104), while also exhibiting the lowest downside rate and the smallest negative tail risk among all evaluated policies. However, LLM-judge and causal audit rankings differ: the untrained base model scores worst on the judge rubric but comes second on the causal audit, implying that the causal estimator captures aspects of true business value missed by the judge-based reward.
AI.conclusion: Finance-grounded GRPO fine-tuning guided by an LLM-as-a-judge reward can produce financial advice that is substantially more profitable and safer, by causal metrics, than commercial LLMs. Yet, LLM-as-a-judge evaluations are not sufficient proxies for real-world impact; a judge-independent causal audit using off-policy CATE estimation provides complementary information and is necessary to understand true business value and risk of LLM-generated financial recommendations.

title: Inverse Theory of Mind Modeling for Content Recommendation: From Web Browsing to Dynamic Intelligent Interfaces
comment: Preprint for conference full paper at 20th ACM Conference on Recommender Systems (RecSys '26), Minneapolis, MN, USA
summary: Modern recommender systems treat observed actions as reliable proxies for user preferences, yet interactions often reflect exploration or comparison rather than stable preference expression. As interfaces evolve from static layouts toward generative UIs and immersive extended reality (XR), the need for deeper, modality-agnostic user understanding grows: these adaptive environments must decide not only what to present but where, when, how prominently, and most importantly why a user acts. We propose an Inverse Theory of Mind (IToM) pipeline that reasons backward from observed interactions to infer the beliefs, preferences, and decision-making traits that explain behavior. The pipeline reconstructs each user's decision context, including what was chosen and what alternatives were available, applies LLM-driven counterfactual reasoning to produce evidence-grounded natural-language belief statements, and synthesizes these beliefs through multi-hypothesis abductive inference into a structured user persona. We evaluate on the OPeRA dataset against ground-truth personality assessments, attitudinal surveys, and interview-based personas across four tasks: next action prediction, shopping attitude alignment, Big Five personality inference, and held-out category prediction. Results show that inferred personas match or exceed ground-truth personas and that multi-hypothesis reasoning is essential for accurate personality prediction. We further demonstrate cross-modal transferability with a persona-driven spatial banking application on VisionOS.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces an inverse theory-of-mind pipeline that infers users’ beliefs, preferences, and traits from their interactions, building structured personas that improve prediction and transfer across modalities.
AI.motivation: Current recommender systems assume that logged interactions directly reveal preferences, but in reality many actions are exploratory or comparative. As interfaces move toward generative UIs and XR, systems must understand not just what a user did, but why they did it, in a way that is agnostic to modality and presentation. This motivates a method that can reconstruct user mental states and stable traits from sparse, ambiguous interaction traces.
AI.method: The authors propose an Inverse Theory of Mind (IToM) pipeline. It (1) reconstructs each interaction’s decision context, including chosen items and available alternatives; (2) uses a large language model for counterfactual reasoning, generating natural-language statements about possible user beliefs that could explain the observed choices; and (3) aggregates these via multi-hypothesis abductive inference into a structured user persona capturing beliefs, preferences, and decision-making traits. They evaluate IToM on the OPeRA dataset across multiple behavioral and psychological prediction tasks, and also test a cross-modal scenario in an XR banking interface (VisionOS).
AI.result: On OPeRA, personas inferred by IToM perform as well as or better than ground-truth personas (from surveys and interviews) for next-action prediction, shopping attitude alignment, Big Five personality inference, and held-out category prediction. The experiments also show that multi-hypothesis reasoning is critical for accurate personality prediction. In a VisionOS spatial banking prototype, the inferred personas successfully transfer to a different modality, guiding interface behavior in an XR environment.
AI.conclusion: Inferring structured user personas via inverse theory-of-mind reasoning from interaction logs is feasible and can outperform traditional persona sources in predictive tasks. Multi-hypothesis, LLM-based counterfactual reasoning is key to capturing nuanced personality traits, and the resulting personas generalize across UI modalities, suggesting a path toward more adaptive, explanation-aware recommender and XR systems.

title: TELLME: Test-Enhanced Learning for Language Model Enrichment
comment: Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: EACL 2026
summary: Continual pre-training (CPT) has been widely adopted as a method for domain adaptation in large language models. However, CPT has consistently been accompanied by challenges, such as the difficulty of acquiring large-scale domain-specific datasets and high computational costs. In this study, we propose a novel method called Test-Enhanced Learning for Language Model Enrichment (TELLME) to alleviate these issues. TELLME leverages the TestEnhanced Learning (TEL) principle, whereby the model's training efficiency is improved using quizzes during training. It integrates this principle with CPT, thereby promoting efficient domain-specific knowledge acquisition and long-term memory retention. Experimental results demonstrate that TELLME outperforms existing methods by up to 23.6% in the financial domain and achieves a 9.8% improvement in long-term memory retention.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces TELLME, a quiz-based continual pre-training method that makes domain adaptation of language models more data- and compute-efficient while improving long-term memory, with large gains shown in the financial domain.
AI.motivation: Continual pre-training for domain adaptation of large language models requires large, domain-specific corpora and substantial computational resources, creating barriers to practical deployment. Additionally, existing methods may not sufficiently reinforce long-term retention of newly acquired domain knowledge. The authors are motivated to find a more efficient training paradigm that can better consolidate domain-specific knowledge with fewer data and lower computational cost.
AI.method: The authors propose TELLME (Test-Enhanced Learning for Language Model Enrichment), which integrates the principle of Test-Enhanced Learning (TEL) into continual pre-training. Instead of relying solely on passive exposure to domain text, the model is trained using quiz-like testing during CPT. These quizzes are designed to actively retrieve and reinforce domain-specific knowledge, thereby improving training efficiency and long-term retention compared with standard CPT procedures.
AI.result: On benchmarks in the financial domain, TELLME achieves up to 23.6% performance improvement over existing domain-adaptation methods, and it yields a 9.8% improvement in long-term memory retention, indicating that the model better preserves acquired domain-specific knowledge over time.
AI.conclusion: Incorporating quiz-style test-enhanced learning into continual pre-training offers a more efficient and effective way to adapt large language models to specific domains. TELLME both boosts domain performance and enhances long-term retention of domain knowledge while mitigating the data and computational burdens of traditional CPT approaches.

title: From Numbers to Judgment: Specialist LLM Agents and Reinforcement Learning for European Listed Real Estate
summary: We study whether the localized numerical operations and integrative judgments of financial analysis benefit from the same form of LLM specialization. Larix maps a 16-lens European listed-real-estate analysis framework to eight lens-aligned specialists; we compare a frontier LLM under monolithic versus specialist-decomposed prompting while holding the model, source evidence, task instructions, output schema, and scoring fixed. Across 19 firms spanning seven regulatory wrappers, decomposition improves the numerical-task aggregate by 15.8 percentage points but does not reliably improve, and can reduce, performance on judgment tasks, a pattern stable across four frozen-template dispatches; a single-agent control given the complete framework does not reproduce the numerical gain. Post-training Qwen3.5-9B with GRPO using task-aligned structured rewards then raises the development-split score by 12.0 points and the judgment aggregate by 14.2 points, with gains on all four sub-ceiling tasks; the gains transfer to unseen firms (+15.2 points overall; +40.4 on covenant stress) and to unseen regulatory wrappers (+4.3), with positive transfer on all three anti-memorization splits. Prompt-level decomposition thus improves modular numerical execution, whereas targeted parameter adaptation improves integrative financial judgment.

AI.tldr: The paper evaluates how specialized prompting vs. model fine-tuning affect financial analysis tasks with large language models, finding that prompt-level decomposition improves numerical sub-tasks while parameter training improves integrative judgment.
AI.motivation: To understand whether breaking complex financial analysis into specialist components or adapting model weights is more effective for numerical accuracy and higher-level judgment, particularly in structured, high-stakes domains like listed real-estate analysis.
AI.method: They design Larix, which maps a 16-lens European real-estate analysis framework into eight lens-aligned specialist prompts. Using a single frontier LLM, they compare monolithic prompting vs. specialist decomposition while holding model, evidence, instructions, schema, and scoring constant across 19 firms and seven regulatory regimes. They also run a single-agent control with full framework. Then they post-train Qwen3.5-9B with GRPO using task-aligned structured rewards and evaluate on development, held-out firms, and unseen regulatory wrappers, including anti-memorization splits.
AI.result: Prompt decomposition boosts numerical task performance by 15.8 percentage points but does not improve—and may reduce—performance on judgment tasks, and the effect is robust across multiple dispatch templates; the numerical gain is not replicated by a single agent given the full framework. GRPO post-training of Qwen3.5-9B improves development-split scores by 12.0 points overall and 14.2 points on judgment aggregates, with improvements across all sub-ceiling tasks. These gains generalize to unseen firms (+15.2 overall; +40.4 on covenant stress) and unseen regulatory wrappers (+4.3), with consistent positive transfer across anti-memorization splits.
AI.conclusion: Prompt-level specialist decomposition is effective for modular, localized numerical operations but not for complex integrative financial judgments, whereas targeted parameter adaptation via reinforcement-style training substantially improves judgment and generalizes across firms and regulatory contexts.

title: Hybrid Gated Attention
summary: Gated attention is an effective approach to mitigate attention sinks and enhance the representational capacity of attention. To further extend its effectiveness-efficiency Pareto frontier, we propose a Hybrid Gated Attention (HyGA) framework that contains three types of gating strategies. Specifically, these gates leverage diverse information from multiple stages of attention, and collaboratively build element-wise/head-wise gating from multiple perspectives, capturing intra-head and cross-head information interactions. Through our hybrid gating components, HyGA could provide multi-source modulation signals, enabling more comprehensive control over information flow and improving the representational capacity of attention. We also introduce low-rank matrix decomposition and learnable attention sink to further enhance training efficiency and stability. In experiments, we evaluate HyGA on widely-used benchmarks based on different backbones. The experimental results show that our HyGA comprehensively improves both training loss and various downstream performances compared with Gated attention. HyGA has also been verified to achieve the best performance at different computation costs, with comprehensive model analyses for better understanding. The proposed HyGA sheds light on a more effective, efficient, and stable attention mechanism.

AI.tldr: Hybrid Gated Attention (HyGA) extends gated attention with multiple complementary gating strategies to better control information flow while improving efficiency and stability.
AI.motivation: Standard attention and prior gated attention mechanisms suffer from attention sinks, limited representational capacity, and suboptimal efficiency–effectiveness trade-offs. There is a need for an attention mechanism that more precisely modulates information flow across and within heads while remaining computationally efficient and stable to train.
AI.method: The paper proposes HyGA, a Hybrid Gated Attention framework with three kinds of gating strategies that act at different stages of the attention computation. These gates use diverse signals to build element-wise and head-wise gating, modeling both intra-head and cross-head interactions and providing multi-source modulation of attention outputs. The method also integrates low-rank matrix decomposition to reduce computation and a learnable attention sink mechanism to stabilize training. HyGA is plugged into different backbone architectures and evaluated on standard benchmarks.
AI.result: Across multiple benchmarks and backbone models, HyGA consistently reduces training loss and improves downstream task performance compared to existing gated attention baselines. The method achieves superior performance at various compute budgets, demonstrating a better effectiveness–efficiency Pareto frontier. Ablation and model analyses are provided to validate the contributions of the hybrid gating components and auxiliary techniques.
AI.conclusion: Hybrid Gated Attention offers a more expressive and controllable attention mechanism by combining complementary gating strategies and multi-source modulation signals, while also incorporating efficiency- and stability-oriented design choices. The framework improves performance and training behaviour over prior gated attention approaches, and points toward more effective, efficient, and stable attention mechanisms for future architectures.

title: When Self-Consistency Backfires: Majority Vote Hurts the Majority of Hard Science Problems for Small LLMs
comment: 9 pages, 4 figures, 3 tables. Accepted at the COLM 2026 Workshop on Efficient Reasoning
summary: Self-consistency (SC) via majority vote is a widely used way to spend inference-time compute: sample N chains of thought, return the plurality answer. On the full GPQA Diamond benchmark (198 graduate-level science questions), majority voting reduces per-problem accuracy on a majority of problems for two instruction-tuned models from different families: 56.6% of problems for Qwen2.5-7B and 65.7% for Llama-3-8B, with Qwen the primary demonstration and Llama corroborating the direction from a near-chance baseline. The effect was pre-registered on a 151-problem confirmatory split after being observed on 47 exploratory problems, and all four confirmatory hypotheses passed. A grid oracle that routes each problem to the best N across {1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 32, 64} marks a theoretical upper bound 14 accuracy points above N = 1 for Qwen and 17 for Llama, an oracle bound requiring ground truth rather than a deployable method. No verifier-free gate reaches it: neither a plurality-agreement gate nor a token-entropy gate moves accuracy more than 0.002 from fixed-budget voting at N = 64. The mechanism is direct: confidence does not track correctness on these problems. In the highest-agreement bin the plurality answer is correct about half the time for Qwen, and for Llama that bin is less accurate than its lowest-agreement bin. We pre-register and confirm these findings on small instruction-tuned models; we do not test reasoning-native models, which we flag as the central open question.

AI.tldr: The paper shows that majority-vote self-consistency with multiple chains of thought can actually harm accuracy on a hard science QA benchmark for small instruction-tuned models, because model confidence and agreement do not reliably indicate correctness.
AI.motivation: Self-consistency via majority vote over multiple sampled chains of thought is a popular way to use extra inference-time compute to improve reasoning accuracy. However, it is not well understood whether this reliably helps on very difficult, expert-level questions, especially for smaller instruction-tuned models. The authors want to rigorously test whether majority voting improves or degrades performance, and to what extent confidence-based gating strategies can recover any potential gains.
AI.method: They evaluate two different small instruction-tuned language models (Qwen2.5-7B and Llama-3-8B) on the full GPQA Diamond benchmark of 198 graduate-level science questions. For each question, they sample multiple chains of thought at different sample counts N in {1,2,4,8,16,32,64} and use majority vote (plurality) over the sampled answers. They measure per-problem accuracy changes as N grows and compute how often majority voting helps or hurts. They pre-register hypotheses on a confirmatory split of 151 problems after exploratory analysis on 47 problems. They also compute an oracle upper bound where each problem is routed to the best N in hindsight using ground truth. Finally, they test verifier-free gating schemes—plurality-agreement gates and token-entropy gates—to see whether they can approach the oracle bound and analyze how model agreement (confidence) correlates with correctness.
AI.result: For both Qwen2.5-7B and Llama-3-8B, majority voting over multiple chains of thought actually reduces per-problem accuracy on most problems. Specifically, accuracy decreases on 56.6% of problems for Qwen and 65.7% for Llama compared to single-sample N=1. All four pre-registered hypotheses on the confirmatory 151-problem split are confirmed. The oracle that chooses the best N per problem shows a large theoretical headroom—up to 14 percentage points higher accuracy for Qwen and 17 for Llama compared to N=1—but this oracle needs ground truth and is not deployable. Practical verifier-free gates using either answer agreement or token entropy fail to significantly improve over fixed-budget N=64 voting, changing accuracy by at most 0.002. They also find that model agreement does not reliably signal correctness: for Qwen, even in the highest-agreement bin the plurality answer is correct only about half the time, and for Llama, the highest-agreement bin is less accurate than the lowest-agreement bin.
AI.conclusion: The study concludes that, on GPQA Diamond and for small instruction-tuned models, naive self-consistency via majority vote over many chains of thought can more often hurt than help at the per-problem level, despite a large theoretical oracle upper bound. Confidence or agreement-based, verifier-free gating strategies do not close this gap, because model confidence does not align well with correctness on these difficult questions. The authors emphasize that their findings are specific to the tested instruction-tuned models and do not cover reasoning-native models, for which they highlight the effectiveness of self-consistency as an important open question.

title: Located but Not Releasable: Silent Gate Inversion and Bounded Linear Release
summary: A growing body of work reports that language models represent task-relevant latent structure that they fail to use. Whether such structure, once located, can be converted into behavior is a separate question that is rarely tested end to end. We submit the complete pipeline -- detect, localize, and release -- to a fully preregistered stress test on a 25.7M transformer trained on causal-evidence discrimination, where a known suppression phenomenon (latent causal structure present but behaviorally unused) has previously been documented. Every threshold, claim template, and decision-tree branch was hashed and archived before any corresponding data existed. Three findings. (i) Localization succeeds: interventions at observation-evidence channels of mid layers restore target behavior on otherwise-suppressed worlds (paired release advantages $0.563$ and $0.854$, 97.5% CIs excluding zero; best-site release rate $0.889$). (ii) Gating fails out of distribution: a detector calibrated to trigger on zero out-of-distribution calibration worlds triggers on 6.9-7.3% of held-out in-distribution generations and on zero of the 2,400 held-out generations that actually need it -- a complete inversion that silently reduces the gated pipeline to its base model. (iii) Linear release is capped: removing the gate and injecting a per-instance linear direction unconditionally yields a monotone dose-response that plateaus far below the preregistered release margin (intercept $0.382 \to 0.311 \to 0.264$ vs. threshold $\le 0.08$); per-instance adaptivity adds less than $\pm 0.03$. The failure is doubly located: the detector is OOD-inverted, and the entire family of linear release directions at this site and resolution is bounded away from sufficiency. The two failures are dissociable, and neither overturns localization. Every number traces to a hashed artifact in the released audit chain.

AI.tldr: The paper stress-tests an end-to-end pipeline for turning latent knowledge in a transformer into behavior, finding that while latent causal structure can be localized and manipulated, practical gating and linear intervention mechanisms fail to reliably and sufficiently release it.
AI.motivation: Prior work suggests language models internally encode task-relevant structure that they nonetheless fail to use in their outputs. However, most studies stop at showing that such structure exists, without demonstrating that it can be reliably converted into correct behavior with a fully specified, preregistered procedure. The authors aim to rigorously test whether a complete detect-localize-release pipeline can successfully unlock suppressed causal knowledge in a controlled setting, and to identify where and how such pipelines can fail.
AI.method: The authors use a 25.7M parameter transformer trained on a causal-evidence discrimination task where a suppression phenomenon is known: the model encodes causal structure but does not use it behaviorally. They fully preregister a pipeline with hashed, archived specifications for thresholds, claim templates, and decision trees before observing any data. They then: (1) detect and localize latent causal representations, (2) intervene at specific observation-evidence channels in mid layers to attempt to restore target behavior, (3) design and test a detector-based gating mechanism intended to trigger interventions only when needed, and (4) experiment with unconditional linear interventions and per-instance adaptive linear directions, measuring dose-response behavior and comparing it with preregistered success criteria.
AI.result: (i) Localization succeeds: manipulating identified mid-layer observation-evidence channels can restore correct causal behavior on suppressed test cases, with substantial and statistically robust release advantages (0.563 and 0.854, 97.5% CIs excluding zero) and a best-site release rate of 0.889. (ii) Gating fails out of distribution: a detector tuned to avoid false positives on OOD calibration data misgeneralizes, triggering on 6.9–7.3% of held-out in-distribution generations while failing to trigger even once on 2,400 generations that actually require intervention, effectively collapsing the gated system back to the base model. (iii) Linear release is limited: removing the gate and always injecting a per-instance linear direction yields a monotone but plateauing improvement, with intercepts (0.382 → 0.311 → 0.264) that remain far above the preregistered success threshold (≤ 0.08), and per-instance adaptation provides only marginal additional gains (less than ±0.03). The failures of gating and linear release are dissociable and do not negate the success of localization.
AI.conclusion: The study shows that while task-relevant causal structure in transformers can be localized and manipulated to influence behavior, building a robust, fully specified pipeline to detect when and how to intervene is challenging. The gating mechanism fails catastrophically out-of-distribution, and linear interventions at the studied site and resolution cannot achieve the preregistered performance target. These dual failures pinpoint limitations in current mechanistic editing approaches while reinforcing that localization of latent structure is viable. The preregistered audit chain ensures that all reported results are traceable and guards against post-hoc analytic flexibility.

title: Social Chain of Thought: A Multi-Agent Architecture Grounded in Medical Differential Diagnosis Methodology
summary: Medical diagnostic reasoning is a high-impact use case for LLMs that carries significant implications for the health and wellbeing of users. When OpenAI (2026) reports that more than 5% of ChatGPT messages globally are healthcare-related, the transparency of these systems becomes a serious design concern. This is especially true for complex cases, where differential diagnosis often requires integrating multiple forms of specialist reasoning. Existing work has proposed multi-agent approaches to medical diagnosis, but it remains unclear when such systems are needed, why they help, and where they outperform monolithic inference. We introduce Social Chain of Thought (SCoT),a multi-round pipeline for medical differential diagnosis that structures multi-agent interaction as a deliberative framework for collabora. tive LLM reasoning. Evaluating SCoT against single-agent baselines, one-agent pipeline ablations, and best-of-n scaling, we show that its recall advantage is not reproduced by monolithic inference alone. SCoT is most successful in the hardest diagnostic cases, where multiple rounds of specialist conversation help recover ground-truth diagnoses and converge on a higher-recall differential.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces Social Chain of Thought (SCoT), a multi-agent, multi-round LLM framework for medical differential diagnosis that improves recall, especially on difficult cases, beyond what monolithic single-agent approaches achieve.
AI.motivation: Medical diagnostic reasoning via LLMs is already widely used and has direct impact on users’ health. Yet current systems often operate as single, opaque models with limited transparency, especially for complex cases requiring multiple specialist perspectives. Existing multi-agent approaches lack clear understanding of when and why they are beneficial, and how they compare systematically to single-agent inference. The paper aims to address these gaps to support safer, more reliable, and more transparent medical use of LLMs.
AI.method: The authors propose Social Chain of Thought (SCoT), a structured, multi-round interaction pipeline where multiple specialist LLM agents collaborate on constructing a differential diagnosis. The framework treats diagnosis as a deliberative process: agents exchange viewpoints, refine each other’s reasoning, and iteratively update the candidate differential list. They evaluate SCoT empirically against several baselines: a single-agent LLM, one-agent pipeline ablations (removing collaboration elements), and best-of-n scaling to see if simple sampling can match SCoT’s performance.
AI.result: Empirical evaluation shows that SCoT achieves higher recall of ground-truth diagnoses compared with single-agent systems, pipeline ablations, and best-of-n monolithic inference. Its advantage is particularly pronounced on the most challenging diagnostic cases, where multiple rounds of structured specialist conversation help uncover correct but non-obvious diagnoses and yield a more comprehensive differential list.
AI.conclusion: The study concludes that structured multi-agent collaboration via SCoT provides a genuine benefit over monolithic LLM inference for medical differential diagnosis, especially for complex cases. The performance gains cannot be replicated simply by scaling up single-agent sampling, indicating that the deliberative, social structure of reasoning is key. This suggests that future medical LLM systems should prioritize transparent, multi-agent deliberation frameworks for difficult diagnostic reasoning tasks.

title: When the Knowledge Base Becomes the Gold Standard: Measuring Resource-Shared Evaluation Loops in Entity-Level Machine Translation
comment: 21 pages, 3 figures. Code and model outputs: https://github.com/nepersoned/malmoi-sjw-eval
summary:
The Seungjeongwon Ilgi, a UNESCO Memory of the World record, is only 37.4% translated, and the most conspicuous failure mode in automatic translation is the person name -- a misread name corrupts the historical fact rather than merely the surface. Low-resource historical domains have no expert gold standard for entity translation, so practitioners substitute a knowledge base (KB) for the gold. That KB is the same resource injected into the system: scoring becomes self-referential and the metric measures instruction compliance rather than translation quality.
  We measure this loop. Using expert person-name annotations from the National Institute of Korean History as a gold independent of the injection pipeline, we hold the entity set fixed and vary only the provenance of the correct reading. Of 527 expert-annotated mentions, only 31.1% lie outside the injection pipeline, and the residual loop is not uniform -- in the overlapping segment the injected reading agrees with the human translation 97.8% of the time against 70.1% in the independent one, so the segment that looks healthiest is the one the loop is holding up.
  Across four models, a difference-in-differences analysis shows the gain from KB injection is confined to the segment whose gold shares the injected resource; in the independent segment it is at or below zero. Post-injection preservation clusters in a narrow 0.910-0.996 band even though baseline capability differs fivefold, so the reported gain is the complement of prior performance and weaker models appear to improve more dramatically. On an independent sample built by removing the construction filter, the measure replicates within model (overlapping intervals) while discriminating between models (non-overlapping intervals) -- it reflects a property of the model, not of the sample.

AI.tldr: The paper studies how using a knowledge base (KB) both to help machine translation and to evaluate it creates a self-referential loop, especially for person-name translation in a low-resource historical Korean corpus.
AI.motivation: In translating the Seungjeongwon Ilgi, a key Korean historical record, person names are critical: errors change historical facts. Automatic translation systems for this low-resource, historical domain lack expert gold-standard annotations for entities. Practitioners thus use the same knowledge base both as input (injected into the model) and as a stand-in for gold labels to evaluate performance. This risks creating a feedback loop where systems are rewarded for following the injected KB rather than truly improving translation quality.
