The authors aim to quantify and understand this loop and its impact on reported gains from KB injection.
AI.method: The authors obtain expert person-name annotations from the National Institute of Korean History as an independent gold standard, separate from the KB injection pipeline. They fix the set of entity mentions (527) and vary only where the "correct" reading comes from: either within or outside the injection pipeline. They compare agreement between human translations and KB-injected readings in overlapping vs independent segments, and perform a difference-in-differences analysis across four models to measure how much of the apparent gain from KB injection is confined to the segment whose gold labels share the injected resource. They also examine post-injection preservation rates and test robustness on an independently sampled dataset without the original construction filter.
AI.result: They find that only 31.1% of expert-annotated mentions fall outside the injection pipeline, showing heavy overlap between evaluation data and the injected KB. Within the overlapping segment, injected KB readings match human translations 97.8% of the time, versus 70.1% in the independent segment, indicating that the seemingly strongest performance occurs where the loop is strongest. Across four models, difference-in-differences analysis shows that gains from KB injection exist only where the gold labels share the injected resource; in the independent segment, gains are zero or negative. Post-injection preservation rates lie in a tight 0.910–0.996 band across models whose baseline abilities differ fivefold, implying that reported improvements are largely the complement of prior performance, making weaker models appear to improve more. On an independently sampled dataset, the measure is stable within models and separates models from each other, indicating it captures a model property rather than sample idiosyncrasy.
AI.conclusion: Using a KB both as a translation aid and as an evaluation gold standard creates a self-referential loop that inflates apparent improvements in person-name translation for low-resource historical texts such as the Seungjeongwon Ilgi. Most of the reported gain from KB injection is confined to data segments that share the injected resource, while segments independent of the KB show little or no benefit. The standard evaluation thus measures conformity to the injected KB rather than true translation quality, especially for weaker models. The authors highlight the need for independent expert gold standards and more robust evaluation practices in knowledge-augmented translation for historical, low-resource domains.

title: Benchmarking LLM Judges for Mobile Agent Evaluation
summary: Mobile agent benchmarks increasingly rely on LLM-based judges to evaluate task completion, yet the reliability of these judges on mobile agent trajectories remains largely unexamined. We introduce MobileJudgeBench, a benchmark for systematically evaluating LLM-as-judge methods on mobile agent trajectories. Our benchmark comprises 931 human-annotated trajectories spanning 6 mobile agent benchmarks, 4 agent models, and 68 apps. We evaluate 6 judge methods (five adapted from SPA-Bench, A3 with two modes, AndroidArena, and AgentRewardBench, plus a simple baseline we design) across multiple LLM backends. Our experiments reveal three key findings. First, a simple baseline judge with sampled screenshots is competitive with, and often exceeds, purpose-built methods, indicating that more elaborate judge pipelines do not consistently improve judge quality; among competitive methods, the LLM backbone is the primary driver. Second, benchmark quality metrics reliably predict real-world judge utility: they correlate with both agent ranking fidelity for evaluation and downstream performance when judges serve as reward signals for on-policy reinforcement learning. Third, failure analysis across two LLM backends uncovers qualitatively opposite failure profiles, one conservative and the other permissive, linked to the backbone's precision-recall characteristics.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces MobileJudgeBench, a benchmark to systematically evaluate LLM-based judges on mobile agent trajectories, showing that a simple screenshot-based judge can match or beat complex methods, benchmark metrics predict real-world utility, and different LLM backbones exhibit opposite failure profiles.
AI.motivation: LLM-based judges are increasingly used to evaluate mobile agents, but their reliability and behavior on mobile agent trajectories have not been rigorously studied. There is a need for a standardized benchmark to compare judge methods, understand what drives judge quality, and analyze their failure modes and downstream impact.
AI.method: The authors build MobileJudgeBench, a dataset of 931 human-annotated mobile agent trajectories covering 6 existing mobile agent benchmarks, 4 agent models, and 68 apps. They adapt and evaluate six judge pipelines (five from prior work plus a new simple baseline using sampled screenshots) across multiple LLM backbones. They measure how well these judges agree with human labels, how their benchmark performance correlates with real-world uses such as ranking agents and serving as reward models in on-policy RL, and conduct a failure analysis comparing error profiles across different LLM backbones.
AI.result: The simple baseline judge that relies on sampled screenshots performs competitively with, and often better than, more elaborate, purpose-built judge pipelines. Judge quality is driven more by the choice of LLM backbone than by pipeline complexity. Performance on the MobileJudgeBench metrics correlates with practical utility: judges that score better on the benchmark also better preserve agent rankings and lead to better agent learning when used as rewards. Failure analysis shows two distinct error profiles across LLM backbones: one conservative (high precision, low recall) and one permissive (higher recall, lower precision).
AI.conclusion: MobileJudgeBench provides a systematic way to evaluate LLM-based judges for mobile agents and demonstrates that simple judging strategies paired with strong LLM backbones can be highly effective. Benchmark metrics are good predictors of a judge’s usefulness in real applications, and different LLM backbones have distinct precision–recall trade-offs that lead to opposite failure modes. This highlights the importance of backbone choice and calibrated use of judges in mobile agent research and deployment.

title: Total Recall at What Cost? Benchmarking the Serving Cost of Agentic Memory Systems
summary: Long-running conversational agents increasingly rely on a memory system to avoid resending the whole conversation each turn, yet how much that costs to serve has received little systematic benchmarking. We compare three memory systems (Mem0, Hindsight, and Mastra Observational Memory) against two reference strategies -- a fixed-size rolling window and resubmitting the full transcript -- across two backbones and conversations of up to 400 turns, pairing every cost measurement with answer accuracy on 665 LoCoMo questions. First, a memory system's serving cost cannot be predicted from conversation length and message size alone: a regression that tracks the two reference strategies closely misses the memory systems by 18-69%, their cost driven instead by internal memory behavior. Second, a break-even analysis shows that whether -- and when -- a memory system becomes cheaper to serve than the full transcript is highly sensitive to the system and the backbone, from the first tens of turns for the cheapest to never within 400 turns for the most expensive. Third, no system wins on both axes: accuracy spans 21-54%, and the backbone choice drives cost as much as the memory system does.

AI.tldr: This paper benchmarks the serving cost and accuracy of different memory systems for long-running conversational agents, showing that costs depend heavily on internal memory behavior rather than just conversation length, and that no single system is best on both cost and accuracy.
AI.motivation: As conversational agents handle longer interactions, they need memory systems to avoid resending full transcripts every turn, but there is little systematic evidence on how these memory approaches affect serving cost and answer accuracy. Practitioners lack guidance on when specialized memory systems are more efficient than simple strategies like rolling windows or full transcript resubmission.
AI.method: The authors benchmark three memory systems (Mem0, Hindsight, Mastra Observational Memory) against two baselines (fixed-size rolling window, full transcript) across two model backbones and conversations up to 400 turns. They collect cost measurements for each configuration and pair them with answer accuracy on 665 LoCoMo questions. They also build a regression model using conversation length and message size to predict serving cost and perform a break-even analysis to determine when a memory system becomes cheaper than sending the full transcript.
AI.result: The regression model that predicts cost well for the reference strategies (rolling window and full transcript) underestimates the serving cost of memory systems by 18–69%, indicating that their internal mechanisms dominate cost. Break-even points where a memory system becomes cheaper than sending the full transcript vary widely: for some systems it happens within the first tens of turns, while for others it never occurs within 400 turns. Accuracy across systems ranges from 21–54%, and both the choice of memory system and backbone significantly affect cost and performance, with no single combination dominating on both axes.
AI.conclusion: Serving cost for conversational memory cannot be reliably inferred from simple features like conversation length and message size because internal memory behaviors matter greatly. Whether a memory system is more cost-effective than resending the full transcript depends sensitively on the specific system and model backbone, and may never pay off in some settings. There is an inherent tradeoff: no evaluated system simultaneously offers the best cost and the best accuracy, so practitioners must choose based on their particular cost and performance priorities.

title: A Modular Agentic Framework for Synthetically Constrained Multi-Objective Hit-to-Lead Optimization
summary: Hit-to-lead optimization requires iterative design of hit analogs across competing potency, selectivity, physicochemical, pharmacokinetic, safety, and synthetic constraints. We present SABLE (Synthetically-accessible Agentic Bayesian Ligand Exploration), an open-source framework that employs natural-language orchestration to guide chemical structure optimization. SABLE uses an LLM to interpret user-defined goals and route tasks, while specialized tools perform reaction-templated analog enumeration, physicochemical and ADMET property prediction, structure-based affinity scoring, and Bayesian optimization. The resulting workflow is a computational twin of the analytical and prioritization stages of the design-make-test-analyze cycle, providing provenance of each numerical output. Across single, and multi-objective optimization studies, SABLE enriches candidate sets for user-defined computational objectives while evaluating only a subset of the enumerated search space. Its modular architecture allows tools and characterization backends to be replaced by editing a simple config file, without modifying operational logic. SABLE provides an extensible decision-support framework for prioritizing synthetically constrained analogs in early-stage drug discovery.

AI.tldr: SABLE is an open-source, LLM-orchestrated framework that optimizes synthetically accessible ligand analogs under multiple drug-discovery constraints using Bayesian optimization and specialized tools.
AI.motivation: Hit-to-lead optimization in drug discovery is complex, requiring simultaneous improvement of potency, selectivity, physicochemical, pharmacokinetic, safety, and synthetic feasibility. Existing workflows are often fragmented, non-transparent, and difficult to customize, making it hard to systematically and efficiently explore large analog spaces under real-world constraints. There is a need for an integrated, extensible, and provenance-aware framework that mirrors human medicinal chemistry decision-making while leveraging modern computational methods.
AI.method: The authors propose SABLE (Synthetically-accessible Agentic Bayesian Ligand Exploration), an LLM-orchestrated workflow that interprets natural-language user goals and routes subtasks to specialized computational tools. These tools perform reaction-template-based analog enumeration to ensure synthetic accessibility, compute physicochemical and ADMET properties, perform structure-based affinity scoring, and run Bayesian optimization over the accessible analog space. The system functions as a modular pipeline whose components and backends can be swapped via configuration files without changing core logic, and it tracks provenance for each numerical output.
AI.result: In single- and multi-objective optimization benchmarks, SABLE successfully enriches candidate ligand sets with respect to user-specified computational objectives (e.g., potency plus ADMET constraints) while only evaluating a subset of the full enumerated analog space. This demonstrates efficient search and prioritization under multiple constraints, mimicking key parts of the design-make-test-analyze cycle. The framework shows that natural-language-driven orchestration can coordinate diverse cheminformatics and modeling tools effectively.
AI.conclusion: SABLE offers an extensible, open-source decision-support framework for hit-to-lead optimization that integrates LLM-based orchestration, synthetically aware analog enumeration, property prediction, structure-based scoring, and Bayesian optimization. By acting as a computational twin of the analytical and prioritization phases of the DMTA cycle and by maintaining full provenance, it helps prioritize synthetically feasible analogs under complex, multi-objective criteria in early-stage drug discovery, while remaining easy to customize and extend.

title: LazyTrain: Limited-resource Allocation toward Zero-waste Yield Optimization in Large Language Model Training
summary: Training large language models on limited hardware is increasingly a scheduling problem across GPU compute, host memory, PCIe transfer, and storage bandwidth. Existing offloading systems reduce GPU residency, and MegaTrain shows that a CPU-master layer-streaming executor can train large models on a single GPU, but fixed checkpointing and placement heuristics still leave communication exposed on the critical path. We propose LazyTrain, an optimization layer over a layer-streaming executor. LazyTrain formulates checkpoint selection, activation placement, recomputation, and CPU-GPU-NVMe communication overlap as a mixed-integer scheduling problem, then executes the solved policy during training. It further couples 8-bit optimizer states with fast gradient clipping as a single Hybrid 8-bit operator: state compression reduces optimizer-state memory, while fast clipping counteracts the additional CPU-side update overhead. Across H800 experiments from Qwen2.5-3B to Qwen3.6-27B, LazyTrain improves sustained TFLOPS over matched baselines runs by approximately 1.24$\times$; RTX 3090 experiments likewise increase the maximum feasible batch size by one at each model scale. In the primary Qwen3.6-27B H800 MetaMathQA run, LazyTrain reaches 219.95 TFLOPS and 1361 tokens/s at batch size 72, peaks at 68.84\,GB of GPU memory, and obtains 95.42\% exact-match accuracy on the full evaluation split. The source code is available at https://github.com/DataArcTech/LazyTrain.

AI.tldr: LazyTrain is an optimization layer that treats large-model training with offloading as a global scheduling problem, using mixed-integer programming plus a hybrid 8-bit optimizer to improve throughput and memory efficiency on limited GPUs.
AI.motivation: Training large language models on commodity or limited GPUs is bottlenecked not just by compute but by memory capacity and bandwidth across GPU, CPU, and NVMe. Existing offloading and layer-streaming systems reduce GPU memory usage but still incur significant communication overhead and rely on fixed, heuristic checkpointing and placement strategies, leaving performance on the table. There is a need for a principled, globally optimized way to schedule activation checkpointing, placement, recomputation, and data transfers to better overlap communication with computation, while also shrinking optimizer memory without excessive CPU overhead.
AI.method: LazyTrain is built as an optimization layer on top of a CPU-master layer‑streaming executor. It formulates the joint decisions of which activations to checkpoint, where to place them (GPU, CPU, NVMe), when to recompute them, and how to overlap CPU‑GPU‑NVMe transfers with compute as a mixed‑integer scheduling problem. The solution to this scheduling problem yields an execution policy that is then enforced during training. Additionally, LazyTrain introduces a Hybrid 8‑bit operator that couples 8‑bit optimizer state compression with a fast gradient clipping mechanism, reducing optimizer memory footprint while mitigating extra CPU‑side update cost introduced by the compression.
AI.result: On NVIDIA H800 GPUs, across Qwen2.5‑3B to Qwen3.6‑27B models, LazyTrain improves sustained training TFLOPS by about 1.24× compared to matched baselines. On RTX 3090, it consistently allows using one larger batch size at each model scale, effectively expanding the feasible batch size under memory limits. In a key experiment training Qwen3.6‑27B on MetaMathQA with an H800, LazyTrain achieves 219.95 TFLOPS and 1361 tokens/s at batch size 72, with peak GPU memory usage of 68.84 GB, while reaching 95.42% exact‑match accuracy on the evaluation split.
AI.conclusion: By casting offloaded LLM training as a mixed‑integer scheduling problem and adding a Hybrid 8‑bit optimizer design, LazyTrain significantly improves throughput and memory efficiency for layer‑streaming training on limited GPUs, without sacrificing final model quality. This demonstrates that principled global scheduling plus targeted optimizer-state compression can push the capability of single- and few‑GPU setups for training large language models.

title: From Prompting to Behavioral Alignment: Personalized LLM Judges for Recommendation Evaluation
summary: Traditional offline recommendation evaluation relies heavily on complex, manually maintained feature pipelines that are difficult to scale. While Large Language Models (LLMs) offer a promising alternative by predicting user engagement directly from raw text logs, empirical analysis in this study identifies a critical failure mode termed bidirectional rationalization. In a zero-shot setting, LLMs are found to convincingly argue for both positive and negative user engagement outcomes on the exact same item with identical evidence, highlighting the unreliability of off-the-shelf LLMs in predicting user engagement. To resolve this, we develop and apply a sequential behavioral alignment framework pairing fine-tuning with preference optimization over paired correct and counterfactual rationales. Evaluated on real-world homepage interaction logs, this aligned reasoning approach achieves a 32.19\% lift in Macro-F1 score over the zero-shot baseline and matches the production feature-engineered baseline. The results demonstrate that behavioral alignment mitigates bidirectional rationalization while delivering human-interpretable reasoning traces without manual pipeline overhead.

AI.tldr: They identify and fix a key failure mode of LLMs when used for offline recommendation evaluation, enabling LLMs to match a production feature-engineered baseline using aligned, interpretable reasoning instead of manual pipelines.
AI.motivation: Offline evaluation of recommender systems typically depends on hand-crafted, complex feature pipelines that are expensive to maintain and hard to scale. LLMs could bypass this by reading raw text logs and predicting user engagement, but their reliability in this role is unclear. The authors are motivated to understand and address how and why off-the-shelf LLMs fail when used as engagement predictors.
AI.method: They first empirically show a failure mode called bidirectional rationalization: in zero-shot settings, an LLM can generate equally plausible rationales for both positive and negative engagement on the same example, showing that its reasoning is not behaviorally grounded. To address this, they design a sequential behavioral alignment framework that combines supervised fine-tuning with preference optimization on paired examples of correct rationales and counterfactual (incorrect) rationales, training the model to prefer behaviorally correct reasoning traces.
AI.result: On real homepage interaction logs, their aligned model achieves a 32.19% improvement in Macro-F1 over the zero-shot LLM baseline and reaches parity with a production system that relies on hand-engineered features and pipelines. It also produces consistent, behaviorally aligned rationales instead of contradictory ones.
AI.conclusion: Behavioral alignment via fine-tuning plus preference optimization can substantially reduce bidirectional rationalization in LLM-based engagement prediction. Properly aligned LLMs can match traditional feature-engineered baselines for offline recommendation evaluation while providing human-interpretable reasoning and avoiding the cost and rigidity of manual feature pipelines.

title: LODESTAR: Trustworthy Entropy Is Navigated, Not Merely Measured -- Reinforced Polarizer Keeps a Frozen LLM from Being Confidently Misled by the Wrong Evidence
summary: Predictive-distribution entropy makes a strong selection rule in retrieval-augmented question answering: across five QA benchmarks, keeping the candidate answer that a frozen respondent LLM produces with the lowest answer-token entropy lifts mean answer $F_1$ from 0.4769 to 0.5148 over the retriever's top-ranked passage, with no gold answers. Yet this lowest-entropy rule, which prior entropy-based selectors adopt, fails in a specific and consequential way: a misleading passage makes the respondent confidently wrong, driving its entropy down precisely where the signal looks most trustworthy. We show that the failure comes from the passage the respondent reads -- and the context that passage is read in is an input we can intervene on. We introduce LODESTAR, to our knowledge the first method to score a text intervention by the uncertainty it induces in a third-party frozen respondent, compared across one question's candidates. LODESTAR uses reinforcement learning to train, once and offline, a polarizer -- a short fixed natural-language string inserted into the respondent's prompt and never into its weights; its training labels are built offline from gold answers and two LLM judges, and inference reads neither. Evaluating every competing selector under the same frozen respondent and the same candidate pools on 5,008 questions, LODESTAR attains the highest mean $F_1$ of any inference-ready selector (0.5148 to 0.5339), the highest exact match (0.4136), and the highest GPT-4o judge score of the frozen-respondent configurations judged (0.6435); its three-seed mean wins all 70 method-by-dataset $F_1$ cells against fourteen published configurations while remaining paired-significant against every one. The gain holds both in-domain and out-of-domain, and ablating the polarizer shows it is what makes the respondent read a misleading passage less often (26.0% against 30.3%).

AI.tldr: The paper shows that using predictive-entropy alone to pick answers in retrieval-augmented QA fails on misleading passages, and proposes LODESTAR, a learned natural-language “polarizer” prompt intervention that improves answer selection performance across benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Entropy-based selection keeps the answer with lowest predictive uncertainty from a frozen LLM and empirically works well, but it fails when a retrieved passage is misleading: the model becomes confidently wrong with low entropy, precisely where entropy-based selection should be most trustworthy. There is a need for a method that can exploit the fact that the passage context is controllable input, using it to expose misleading evidence and improve selection without changing model weights or using gold answers at inference.
AI.method: They analyze the failure mode of lowest-entropy selection and attribute it to how the respondent reads misleading passages. They then introduce LODESTAR, which trains a “polarizer” – a short, fixed natural-language string inserted into the LLM’s prompt. Using offline reinforcement learning with rewards derived from gold answers and two LLM judges, they learn a polarizer that, when added to the prompt of a frozen respondent, reshapes its uncertainty over candidate answers. At inference, the system compares the entropy-induced signals across candidate answers under this fixed polarizer, without accessing gold answers or judges, and selects the answer with improved reliability.
AI.result: Across five QA benchmarks and 5,008 questions, the naive lowest-entropy rule already improves mean F1 from 0.4769 to 0.5148 versus using the retriever’s top passage. LODESTAR further improves mean F1 from 0.5148 to 0.5339, achieves the highest exact match (0.4136), and the highest GPT-4o judge score (0.6435) among all frozen-respondent selectors evaluated. In three-seed averages, it wins all 70 method-by-dataset F1 comparisons against fourteen published configurations and remains statistically significantly better than each. The performance gains hold both in-domain and out-of-domain. An ablation without the polarizer confirms that the polarizer is responsible for reducing how often the respondent selects answers from misleading passages (26.0% vs 30.3%).
AI.conclusion: Using raw predictive-entropy as an answer selector in retrieval-augmented QA is brittle in the presence of misleading passages because it can make models confidently wrong. However, this failure stems from the controllable input context, suggesting that prompt-level interventions can help. LODESTAR demonstrates that a learned, fixed natural-language polarizer, trained offline via RL to shape a frozen model’s uncertainty, can robustly improve answer selection across datasets and domains without changing model weights or requiring supervision at inference. The approach reduces harmful overconfidence on misleading evidence and sets a new state of the art among inference-ready selectors under a shared respondent and candidate pool.

title: Localizing Safety Alignment: MLP Layers and Mid-Network Blocks Encode Refusal Behavior in Large Language Models
summary: Safety alignment in large language models is often treated as a distributed property of the entire network, yet its practical brittleness suggests that refusal behavior may be concentrated in a smaller set of parameters. This work addresses where safety-aligned refusal is encoded by transplanting weights from aligned models into matched unaligned base models at multiple levels of granularity. Using two open-weight model pairs and four safety benchmarks, we conducted experiments to compare the effects of replacing attention weights, MLP weights, contiguous layer regions, and MLP blocks. Across both model families, refusal transfer is dominated by MLP weights: replacing MLP parameters recovers substantially more malicious-prompt refusal than replacing attention parameters, with gains of at least 2.7 times more across benchmarks. Within the MLP stack, refusal-relevant parameters exhibit a consistent mid-network concentration, as the block spanning layers 8-11 is selected first in all six greedy searches over model-dataset pairs. The results also show that the composition of safety-relevant components is non-additive: in five of six greedy trajectories, adding more aligned blocks can reduce refusal performance, and selective block subsets can outperform full MLP transplantation on malicious refusal, benign over-refusal, or both. Finally, greedy orders transferred to OR-Bench vary with the source benchmark used to derive them, indicating a benchmark-dependent precision-coverage trade-off. These results suggest that safety alignment in current LLMs is both localized and interaction-sensitive, offering insight into alignment brittleness and potential avenues for targeted safety interventions.

AI.tldr: The paper studies where safety-aligned refusal behavior lives inside LLMs by transplanting weights between aligned and unaligned models, finding that mid-layer MLP blocks carry most of the safety signal and interact in non-additive ways.
AI.motivation: Safety alignment of large language models is usually implemented and evaluated as a property of the full network, but in practice alignment is brittle and easily broken by prompt changes or fine-tuning. This suggests that safety behavior might be localized in specific parameters rather than uniformly distributed. Understanding where refusal behavior is encoded, and how it composes, could clarify why alignment is fragile and enable more targeted, efficient safety interventions than retraining entire models.
AI.method: The authors take pairs of open-weight models, where one is safety-aligned and the other is a closely matched unaligned base model. They then perform weight-transplant experiments: systematically replacing subsets of the base model’s parameters with those from the aligned model at multiple granularities (entire attention vs MLP modules, contiguous layer ranges, and finer MLP blocks). Using four safety benchmarks, they measure how much malicious-prompt refusal and benign over-refusal are transferred as different parameter subsets are swapped. They also run greedy searches over MLP blocks to find which layer regions most improve refusal, and test how greedy orders derived from one benchmark transfer to another (OR-Bench).
AI.result: Across both model families and all safety benchmarks, transplanting MLP weights yields much larger gains in refusal behavior than transplanting attention weights—at least 2.7x more refusal transfer. Within the MLP stack, refusal-relevant parameters cluster in mid-network layers: in all six model–dataset greedy searches, the block covering layers 8–11 is selected first as most impactful. The composition of safety-relevant parts is non-additive: in most greedy trajectories, adding additional aligned MLP blocks can actually degrade refusal performance, and some selective subsets of blocks outperform transplanting the entire MLP stack, either on malicious refusal, benign over-refusal, or both. Moreover, the specific greedy orders that work well on one benchmark do not universally transfer to OR-Bench; instead, different benchmarks yield different trade-offs between high precision (avoiding over-refusal) and high coverage (refusing more malicious inputs).
AI.conclusion: Safety alignment in current LLMs is not smoothly distributed but is instead localized primarily in mid-layer MLP parameters, and these safety components interact in complex, non-additive ways. This localization helps explain alignment brittleness: changing or fine-tuning particular regions can strongly affect refusal without global retraining, and naively adding more “aligned” components can worsen behavior. The findings point toward more surgical safety methods—such as targeted editing or transplantation of specific MLP blocks—and caution that safety components tuned for one benchmark may not generalize cleanly to others, implying an inherent precision–coverage trade-off in safety design.

title: Spark-to-Paper: End-to-End Research Paper Generation as a Composable Skill
summary: Turning a research idea into a complete paper requires more than text generation: the system must retrieve literature, design and execute experiments, revise claims according to evidence, produce publication-ready figures, and maintain consistency across a long generation process. We present Spark-to-Paper, an end-to-end research paper generation system implemented as thirteen composable skills inside an existing coding assistant, without requiring a separate agent platform or orchestration service. Spark-to-Paper separates model-based judgment from deterministic operations that can be directly executed and checked. It further separates experiment planning from reporting, so that required evidence is specified before results are observed and manuscript claims are revised according to measured outcomes. To improve reliability over long research trajectories, the system combines deterministic integrity checks with self-critique and bounds a failure mode we call the Self-Refutation Loop, in which repeated experiments continue to reject the original research objective. Spark-to-Paper also produces editable vector figures through programmatic plotting for experimental results and code-based reconstruction for generated method diagrams. Across eight controlled research topics, Spark-to-Paper achieves 99.5% citation validity and 96.4% figure editability. A controlled ablation increases fabrication detection from 14% for a single-pass draft to 92% with the full integrity and review stack, while adversarial review achieves 74% precision. The full system uses 11.9M tokens, costs $8.1 per manuscript, and requires 3.2 hours on average. These results show that end-to-end research paper generation can be implemented as a lightweight, composable workflow inside existing coding assistants while keeping experimental evidence central to how claims are accepted, revised, or abandoned.

AI.tldr: Spark-to-Paper is an end-to-end system that turns a research idea into a full paper by combining LLM-based reasoning with deterministic tools for literature retrieval, experiment execution, integrity checks, and figure generation.
AI.motivation: Existing LLMs can draft text but cannot reliably produce full, credible research papers: they hallucinate citations, fabricate results, lack robust experimental design, and struggle with long, consistent workflows. The authors aim to show that a practical, low-overhead system can be built inside a coding assistant to handle the whole pipeline from idea to complete paper while keeping evidence and integrity at the core.
AI.method: The authors implement Spark-to-Paper as thirteen composable skills integrated into a coding assistant. The system: (1) separates model judgement from deterministic, verifiable operations (e.g., code execution, plotting); (2) separates experiment planning from reporting so hypotheses and needed evidence are fixed before results; (3) introduces integrity checks, self-critique, and a mechanism to bound a failure mode called the Self-Refutation Loop, where experiments repeatedly contradict the initial idea; and (4) generates publication-ready, editable vector figures via programmatic plotting and code-based reconstruction of method diagrams. They evaluate it on eight controlled research topics and conduct ablation and adversarial review studies.
AI.result: On eight topics, Spark-to-Paper attains 99.5% valid citations and 96.4% editable figures. In ablation studies, adding the full integrity and review stack raises detection of fabricated content from 14% (single-pass draft) to 92%. Adversarial human review of generated papers achieves 74% precision in identifying issues. The system processes about 11.9M tokens per manuscript, costing around $8.1 and taking roughly 3.2 hours end-to-end.
AI.conclusion: A full research paper generation workflow can be realized as a lightweight, modular set of skills within a coding assistant, without a separate agent platform. By structurally prioritizing experimental evidence, enforcing integrity checks, and clearly separating planning from reporting, the system can generate research papers with high citation validity, editable figures, and substantially improved detection and mitigation of fabrication and self-refutation issues.

title: EnterpriseRAG: Benchmarking LLM Instruction Adherence and Robustness under Non-Ideal Enterprise Retrieval
summary: Enterprise RAG deployments face a critical reliability gap: while LLMs satisfy 80% of individual constraints, only 26.8% of responses meet all requirements simultaneously, revealing a 57-point orchestration gap. Existing benchmarks assume clean retrieval with simple queries, failing to capture production conditions where noisy documents and multi-dimensional constraints coexist. We introduce EnterpriseRAG, a benchmark of 983 expert-validated samples across six domains that systematically simulates three failure modes absent from prior work: retrieval noise, knowledge gaps, and factual conflicts, coupled with complex instructions. Evaluation of 13 state-of-the-art LLMs reveals a severe instruction adherence collapse, where high per-constraint satisfaction masks low holistic compliance. Critical findings expose deep barriers under knowledge gaps and factual conflicts, even with reasoning-enhanced inference, indicating production RAG requires explicit context-aware protocols and calibrated judgment. EnterpriseRAG provides a reproducible foundation for measuring and closing these gaps, directly informing deployment decisions for enterprise-scale RAG systems. We will release the benchmark and evaluation framework upon publication.

AI.tldr: The paper presents EnterpriseRAG, a benchmark revealing that current LLM-based RAG systems often fail to meet all enterprise constraints at once, by simulating realistic noisy retrieval and complex requirements to evaluate 13 LLMs and expose an orchestration gap in reliability.
AI.motivation: In enterprise settings, RAG systems must obey multiple simultaneous constraints (e.g., correctness, security, compliance, style), but current evaluations only test simple, clean scenarios. The authors observe that although LLMs can satisfy individual constraints much of the time, they rarely satisfy all of them together, creating an orchestration gap that is not captured by existing benchmarks. There is a need for a realistic, systematic way to assess and compare RAG systems under real-world conditions such as noisy retrieval, missing knowledge, and conflicting sources.
AI.method: The authors construct EnterpriseRAG, a benchmark of 983 expert-validated examples across six enterprise-relevant domains. For each example, they introduce realistic complexities by simulating three key failure modes: retrieval noise (irrelevant or distracting documents), knowledge gaps (missing or incomplete information), and factual conflicts (contradictory evidence), combined with complex multi-dimensional instructions and constraints. They then evaluate 13 state-of-the-art LLMs in a RAG setting against this benchmark, measuring per-constraint satisfaction and holistic compliance (all constraints satisfied simultaneously), and assessing how reasoning-enhanced inference strategies affect performance.
AI.result: The benchmark reveals a large orchestration gap: while LLMs satisfy around 80% of individual constraints, only about 26.8% of responses satisfy all constraints at once, implying a 57-point gap between per-constraint metrics and holistic reliability. The study finds a pronounced instruction adherence collapse in realistic enterprise-like conditions, with performance degrading sharply under knowledge gaps and factual conflicts, even when using reasoning-augmented inference techniques. This demonstrates that ostensibly strong models still struggle to make calibrated judgments and apply context-aware decision-making when facing noisy or conflicting retrieval contexts.
AI.conclusion: EnterpriseRAG demonstrates that existing RAG evaluations substantially overestimate reliability for enterprise deployment because they do not model realistic retrieval noise, missing knowledge, and conflicting information under complex instructions. The authors conclude that closing the orchestration gap requires explicit, context-aware protocols and better calibration mechanisms, not only stronger base models or simple reasoning enhancements. The benchmark and its evaluation framework, to be released upon publication, are intended as a standard tool for practitioners and researchers to measure, compare, and improve enterprise-scale RAG systems in conditions that more closely match real-world deployments.

title: Accuracy and Order Sensitivity Diverge Under Label-Free Strategies
summary: Multiple-choice benchmarks are widely used to evaluate large language models, but MCQ scores conflate knowledge with sensitivity to option order, which makes them unreliable measures of model knowledge. In this paper, we test whether preventing a model from seeing option labels while committing to an answer removes positional influence and, in turn, improves performance. We evaluate two different strategies for mitigating bias. The first uses a generation-then-matching approach, and the second scores options in isolation, which is positionally unbiased by construction. Neither reliably improves accuracy. A complete decomposition shows that the bottleneck is withholding options, not the matching step. The only configuration that consistently matches the baseline is the one that shows the model all options paired with an LLM matcher. However, eliminating positional influence entirely still does not reliably yield accuracy gains, while cyclic permutation often improves them. For two-stage prompting, an aggregate measure of recall imbalance and a direct per-question measure of order sensitivity both fail to show reliable debiasing.

AI.tldr: The paper examines whether removing multiple-choice option labels or scoring options independently can reduce positional bias and improve accuracy in LLM multiple-choice benchmarks, finding that these strategies do not reliably help and that option withholding is the main bottleneck.
AI.motivation: Multiple-choice benchmarks are standard for evaluating LLMs, but their scores mix true knowledge with artifacts like sensitivity to the order of answer options. This positional bias undermines the reliability of benchmark results, motivating methods that can disentangle or mitigate order effects to better measure model knowledge.
AI.method: The authors test two debiasing strategies: (1) a generation-then-matching approach where the model first generates an answer without seeing option labels and then matches it to the given choices, and (2) scoring answer options independently, without presenting them in a list, so that option position cannot affect scoring. They compare these setups against a standard baseline where the model sees all options with labels, do a full decomposition to isolate where performance changes arise (option withholding vs matching), experiment with configurations including a separate LLM matcher and cyclic permutation of options, and compute aggregate recall-imbalance and per-question order-sensitivity metrics for two-stage prompting.
AI.result: Neither of the main bias-mitigation strategies—generation-then-matching or independent option scoring—reliably improves multiple-choice accuracy over the standard baseline. Analysis shows that the key performance bottleneck comes from withholding answer options rather than from the matching step. The only configuration that consistently matches baseline accuracy is the one where the model sees all options and uses an LLM matcher. Even when positional influence is fully removed, accuracy does not reliably increase, whereas simply using cyclic permutations of option order often does. Metrics intended to capture debiasing effects, such as recall imbalance and direct per-question order sensitivity in two-stage prompting, do not show consistent reductions in order effects.
AI.conclusion: Attempts to remove positional bias by hiding option labels or scoring options independently do not consistently yield better measures of model knowledge, because the act of withholding options harms performance more than it helps. Fully eliminating positional influence is not sufficient for accuracy gains, and simple techniques like cyclic permutation can be more effective in practice. Standard MCQ evaluation remains competitive when options are visible, and current debiasing metrics for two-stage prompting do not reliably capture or correct order sensitivity, suggesting that new evaluation paradigms or metrics are needed to robustly disentangle knowledge from positional artifacts.

title: CoAdapt-GUI: Joint Workflow Context and Policy Adaptation for Unseen GUI Applications
summary: Mobile GUI agents remain brittle when deployed to applications absent from source training. We study novel-app generalization under a limited target interaction budget and without target demonstrations. We introduce CoAdapt-GUI, a test-time adaptation (TTA) framework that jointly adapts structured workflow context and policy from the agent's own target-app rollouts and rewards. The workflow context retains transferable procedures, failure modes, and verification rules while excluding app-bound source details. This separation allows reusable workflow knowledge to guide adaptation without transferring source-interface state. For policy adaptation, task-context-matched group-relative optimization updates a LoRA adapter on a frozen vision-language model. Across two unseen-app evaluations, CoAdapt-GUI reaches 45.0% on AndroidWorld-Generalization, compared with 37.5% for the reported Policy-Only TTA baseline, and raises AndroidWorld Plus performance from 38.6% to 52.9%. These results show that transfer-constrained workflow context provides substantial gains and that joint policy adaptation further improves held-out performance.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes CoAdapt-GUI, a test-time adaptation framework that improves generalization of mobile GUI agents to unseen apps using their own interaction data, achieving substantial performance gains over prior baselines.
AI.motivation: Mobile GUI agents trained on specific apps often fail to generalize to unseen applications, especially when only limited interactions and no demonstrations are available for the new app. Existing test-time adaptation methods tend to focus only on policy adaptation and may overfit to source-app interface details rather than reusable workflow knowledge. There is a need for a method that can leverage transferable procedural knowledge while adapting efficiently to new app interfaces under strict interaction budgets.
AI.method: The authors introduce CoAdapt-GUI, a test-time adaptation framework with two key components. First, it constructs and adapts a structured workflow context that captures transferable procedures, typical failure modes, and verification rules, while explicitly excluding app-specific source interface states so that the workflow knowledge can be reused across apps. Second, for policy adaptation, it employs task-context-matched group-relative optimization to fine-tune a LoRA adapter on top of a frozen vision-language model using only the agent's own rollouts and rewards on the target app. The workflow context and the policy are adapted jointly during test-time interaction with the unseen app, within a limited interaction budget and without external demonstrations.
AI.result: On two unseen-app benchmarks, CoAdapt-GUI significantly outperforms policy-only test-time adaptation baselines. It achieves 45.0% success on AndroidWorld-Generalization, compared to 37.5% for the previously reported Policy-Only TTA baseline. On AndroidWorld Plus, performance increases from 38.6% to 52.9% when using CoAdapt-GUI. These results demonstrate that leveraging a transfer-constrained workflow context yields substantial gains, and coupling it with policy adaptation provides further improvement in generalization to new apps.
AI.conclusion: The paper concludes that separating reusable workflow knowledge from app-specific interface details and using this structured workflow context for test-time adaptation is highly beneficial for mobile GUI agents in unseen apps. Jointly adapting both workflow context and a lightweight policy component (via LoRA on a frozen VLM) using only interaction data and rewards enables more robust and sample-efficient generalization than policy-only TTA approaches. The empirical improvements on AndroidWorld benchmarks validate the effectiveness of the proposed CoAdapt-GUI framework for constrained, demonstration-free adaptation to new mobile applications.

title: Benchmarking Trustworthiness of SLMs: Pre-trained vs. Compressed
summary: Small Language Models (SLMs) have emerged as a more efficient alternative to traditional Large Language Models (LLMs), offering promising potential in resource-constrained scenarios. Existing approaches to building SLMs typically follow two paths: training compact models from scratch, or compressing larger pre-trained models using methods such as pruning, quantization, or distillation. As language models become increasingly integrated into real-world applications, ensuring their trustworthiness has become a critical concern. However, how to build trustworthy SLMs remains an underexplored question. In this work, we present a comprehensive evaluation of SLM trustworthiness across multiple dimensions, including fairness, robustness, privacy, and ethics. We first examine the effects of pruning and quantization, and find that quantization is significantly more effective in preserving trustworthiness compared to pruning. More importantly, we demonstrate that compressing a reliable large model via quantization can produce SLMs with superior trustworthiness and adaptability compared to using small models trained from scratch. Furthermore, knowledge distillation from trustworthy teacher models can further enhance the reliability of SLMs. We hope our findings provide practical guidance and a foundation for future research into the development and deployment of trustworthy small language models.

AI.tldr: The paper evaluates how to build trustworthy small language models (SLMs) and finds that quantizing reliable large models, especially with distillation, yields more trustworthy SLMs than training small models from scratch or using pruning.
AI.motivation: As SLMs gain popularity for deployment in resource-constrained settings, it is unclear how different construction strategies (training from scratch vs. compressing LLMs) affect critical trustworthiness properties such as fairness, robustness, privacy, and ethics. The authors aim to fill this gap and provide guidance on building trustworthy SLMs.
AI.method: They conduct a comprehensive empirical evaluation of SLMs built via different compression techniques—primarily pruning and quantization—and compare them against small models trained from scratch. Trustworthiness is measured along several dimensions: fairness, robustness, privacy, and ethical behavior. They also study the effect of knowledge distillation from trustworthy large teacher models into SLMs.
AI.result: Quantization preserves trustworthiness properties substantially better than pruning. SLMs obtained by quantizing a reliable large model are more trustworthy and adaptable than similarly sized models trained from scratch. Additionally, applying knowledge distillation from trustworthy teacher models further improves the reliability and trustworthiness of the resulting SLMs.
AI.conclusion: To obtain trustworthy SLMs, the most effective strategy is to start from a reliable large model and compress it using quantization, optionally enhanced with knowledge distillation, rather than relying on heavy pruning or training small models from scratch. These findings offer practical guidelines and a research foundation for developing and deploying trustworthy SLMs in real-world applications.

title: Learning from Online User Feedback for Shopping Agents
summary: Large language model-based shopping agents are increasingly deployed in real-world e-commerce platforms, generating massive amounts of user interaction logs that provide valuable supervision for improving these agents. However, existing approaches primarily rely on offline training signals, such as user-item interactions or synthetic preference data, while largely overlooking the rich supervision contained in users' natural conversational feedback. Moreover, the available online feedback is heterogeneous, sparse, and noisy, making it difficult to transform into reliable learning signals automatically. To address these challenges, we propose LOFA, a framework that enables shopping agents to learn directly from real online interaction logs without human annotation. LOFA combines reinforcement learning over verifiable purchase outcomes with feedback-aware on-policy distillation, which identifies users'in-dialogue directives and converts them into dense token-level supervision. These complementary objectives capture both collaborative behavioral patterns and user-specific preferences. Extensive experiments on real-world e-commerce logs demonstrate that LOFA consistently improves recommendation quality, response helpfulness, and user-satisfaction alignment over strong baselines, highlighting the effectiveness of learning shopping agents from real online user feedback.

AI.tldr: LOFA is a training framework that lets LLM-based shopping agents learn directly from noisy real-world e-commerce chat logs, using both purchase-based reinforcement learning and conversational feedback distillation, to better align with user preferences and improve recommendations and responses.
AI.motivation: Current LLM shopping agents are trained mostly from offline data like user–item interactions or synthetic preferences, ignoring rich natural-language feedback in real conversations. Existing online feedback is heterogeneous, sparse, and noisy, so it is hard to automatically convert it into reliable training signals. There is a need for a method that can exploit real user interaction logs in a scalable, annotation-free way while handling noise and sparsity.
AI.method: The paper proposes LOFA, a framework that learns from real e-commerce interaction logs without human labeling. LOFA has two main components: (1) reinforcement learning that optimizes policies based on verifiable purchase outcomes as rewards, and (2) feedback-aware on-policy distillation, which parses user dialogue to identify explicit directives, corrections, or preferences and turns them into token-level supervision for the model. These two learning signals are combined to capture both general collaborative behavior patterns and fine-grained, user-specific preferences.
AI.result: On real-world e-commerce logs, LOFA-trained agents outperform strong baselines on multiple metrics: they provide higher-quality recommendations, more helpful responses, and better alignment with user satisfaction indicators. The experiments demonstrate consistent gains across settings, suggesting that leveraging real conversational feedback and purchase outcomes yields more effective shopping agents.
AI.conclusion: Learning directly from real online user feedback, including both purchase outcomes and in-dialogue conversational signals, is an effective way to improve LLM-based shopping agents. LOFA shows that combining reinforcement learning with feedback-aware distillation can transform noisy, heterogeneous interaction logs into useful supervision, leading to better recommendation performance and user-aligned behavior without requiring manual annotation.

title: Asymptotic Risk Calibration for Selective Question Answering
summary: Large language models (LLMs) may generate fluent but incorrect answers, making uncertainty quantification important for reliable question answering. However, heuristic uncertainty scores cannot perfectly distinguish correct predictions from incorrect ones, and directly applying a fixed uncertainty threshold provides no statistical control over the error rate among accepted answers. To address this limitation, we propose A-CRC-QA, a post-hoc calibration framework for uncertainty-aware selective question answering. The proposed method reformulates selection-conditioned error control as a linear expectation constraint and applies a monotonized empirical-risk calibration procedure inspired by conformal risk control. Since the resulting instance-wise loss is generally non-monotone with respect to the acceptance threshold, our framework targets asymptotic rather than finite-sample risk control. A-CRC-QA is model-agnostic, requires no additional training, and can be combined with different uncertainty estimators. Experiments on CoQA and MedMCQA demonstrate its applicability to both open-ended and closed-ended question answering, achieving a favorable trade-off between accepted-answer reliability and answer retention compared with uncalibrated and confidence-bound-based baselines.

AI.tldr: They propose A-CRC-QA, a post-hoc calibration framework that uses conformal-style risk control ideas to calibrate LLM uncertainty scores for selective QA, improving the trade-off between reliability and coverage.
AI.motivation: LLMs often answer confidently but incorrectly. Existing uncertainty scores are imperfect and using a fixed uncertainty threshold cannot statistically control the error rate among accepted answers. There is a need for a principled way to ensure that the subset of answers the system chooses to output has a controlled error rate.
AI.method: They formulate selection-conditioned error control as a linear expectation constraint and adapt a monotonized empirical-risk calibration procedure inspired by conformal risk control. The framework is post-hoc, model-agnostic, and works with any uncertainty estimator. It focuses on asymptotic risk control because the per-instance loss is not monotone in the acceptance threshold.
AI.result: On CoQA and MedMCQA, A-CRC-QA works for both open-ended and multiple-choice QA and achieves a better trade-off between accepted-answer reliability (lower error among answered questions) and answer retention (fraction of questions answered) than uncalibrated methods and confidence-bound baselines.
AI.conclusion: A-CRC-QA provides a practical, training-free, model-agnostic way to calibrate uncertainty for selective LLM question answering, offering asymptotic risk control and empirically improving reliability–coverage trade-offs over standard thresholding or confidence-based approaches.

title: Foresight Without Seeing: Latent Futures for World Action Models
summary: World Action Models (WAMs) couple future visual prediction with robot action generation, enabling policies to model how the physical world evolves during interaction. Existing WAMs differ in how predictive dynamics are exposed to the action pathway. Explicit-future WAMs provide direct access to predicted scene evolution, but incur substantial inference costs from iterative video denoising. In contrast, direct-policy WAMs efficiently predict actions from the current observation but lack an explicit inference-time interface for exposing predictive dynamics to the Action DiT. To bridge this gap, we propose ForeWAM, a dynamics-conditioned direct-policy WAM that provides predictive context for action generation without decoding future videos. At its core, Future-KV performs a single Video DiT prefill over the current visual latent and stochastic future slots, and reuses the resulting layer-wise key-value states throughout action denoising. We further introduce dynamics registers supervised by a frozen latent action teacher, encouraging the implicit future states to capture interaction-induced transitions such as object motion, contact changes, and task progress. Ground-truth future observations and the teacher are used only during training; deployment requires neither and performs no future video generation. Without embodied robot data pretraining, the standard and accelerated variants of ForeWAM achieve average success rates of 96.7% and 96.9% on LIBERO, respectively. The standard variant further achieves 61.6% success on LIBERO-Plus. These results demonstrate that direct-policy WAMs can retain efficient action prediction while exposing predictive dynamics to the action pathway without explicitly generating future observations.

AI.tldr: ForeWAM is a world action model that lets a robot policy use predicted dynamics without actually generating future video, keeping inference efficient while improving performance.
AI.motivation: World action models either explicitly generate future video (good dynamics access but slow and costly) or directly output actions from current observations (fast but with no explicit access to predicted dynamics during inference). There is a need to combine the efficiency of direct policies with the benefits of conditioning on predicted world evolution, so that robot policies can leverage future-aware context without paying the high cost of video denoising at test time.
AI.method: The authors introduce ForeWAM, a dynamics‑conditioned direct‑policy world action model. They design Future‑KV, which runs a single Video DiT prefill step over current visual latents and stochastic future slots, then reuses the resulting layer‑wise key–value (KV) states throughout the action denoising process. They also add dynamics registers, trained under supervision from a frozen latent action teacher, to force the implicit future states to encode interaction‑relevant changes such as object motion, contact events, and task progress. During training, ground‑truth future observations and the teacher supervise these components, but at inference, only current observations are used and no future videos are generated.
AI.result: On the LIBERO benchmark, ForeWAM without any embodied robot data pretraining attains average success rates of 96.7% for the standard model and 96.9% for the accelerated variant. On the more challenging LIBERO‑Plus benchmark, the standard model achieves 61.6% success. These metrics compare favorably to existing approaches while preserving inference efficiency.
AI.conclusion: ForeWAM shows that direct‑policy world action models can remain computationally efficient yet still benefit from rich predictive dynamics by conditioning the action pathway on learned future‑aware representations, without explicitly decoding future visual observations. This bridges the gap between explicit-future and direct-policy WAMs and yields strong performance on challenging robot manipulation benchmarks.

title: Poly-Dialectal Neural Machine Translation System for Bangla Regional Dialects
summary: Regional dialectal variation poses a fundamental challenge to natural language processing (NLP) in Bangla, where over 240 million speakers communicate across diverse regional variants that diverge significantly from Standard Colloquial Bangla (SCB) in phonology, morphology, and lexicon. Contemporary neural machine trans- lation (NMT) architectures and large language models (LLMs) predominantly as- sume a homogeneous language distribution, resulting in severe performance degra- dation when translating low-resource regional dialects. In this work, we present a unified Poly-Dialectal Neural Machine Translation System capable of multi-directional translation across 12 Bangla regional dialects without routing through an inter- mediary standard pivot. We compile the largest multi-dialect parallel corpus for Bangla to date, comprising 51,531 non-null parallel sentence pairs across 12 di- alects, incorporating 2,500 expert-verified, bidirectional parallel sentence pairs for five previously unaddressed dialects. Evaluating sequence-to-sequence architec- tures under Weight-Decomposed Low-Rank Adaptation (DoRA), our fine-tuned BanglaT5 model achieves state-of-the-art translation performance (29.26 BLEU, 57.26 chrF++), outperforming NLLB-200 (615M) and mBART-50 (611M) while preserving morphological coherence. Furthermore, we conduct a systematic cross- dialectal transfer analysis and dataset scaling study, establishing empirical thresh- olds for low-resource dialect adaptation. Finally, we deploy the optimized INT8- quantized model as an open-access web application to promote digital inclusion for marginalized dialect communities. The complete dataset is publicly available at Mendeley Data (https://data.mendeley.com/datasets/v9cf66fk2t/2).

AI.tldr: They build and evaluate a unified machine translation system that directly translates between 12 Bangla regional dialects and Standard Colloquial Bangla using a new multi-dialect corpus and a fine-tuned BanglaT5 model with DoRA, achieving state-of-the-art results and releasing models and data publicly.
AI.motivation: Bangla has over 240 million speakers across many regional dialects that differ substantially from Standard Colloquial Bangla, but most NMT and LLM systems assume a single homogeneous language variety. This causes large performance drops on low-resource dialects and excludes marginalized dialect communities from high-quality translation and digital tools. The authors want to address this gap by supporting multiple dialects in a unified way instead of forcing translation through a standard pivot dialect.
AI.method: They compile the largest Bangla multi-dialect parallel corpus so far, with 51,531 non-null sentence pairs across 12 dialects, including 2,500 expert-verified bidirectional pairs for five previously unaddressed dialects. They train and evaluate sequence-to-sequence NMT architectures, focusing on fine-tuning a BanglaT5 model using Weight-Decomposed Low-Rank Adaptation (DoRA) for efficient parameter adaptation. They perform multi-directional translation across dialects without using a standard pivot, conduct cross-dialect transfer experiments and dataset scaling analyses to study how well knowledge transfers between dialects and how much data is needed for effective low-resource adaptation. They also apply INT8 quantization for efficient deployment and build a public web application.
AI.result: The fine-tuned BanglaT5 model with DoRA achieves state-of-the-art performance for Bangla dialect translation, with scores of 29.26 BLEU and 57.26 chrF++, outperforming strong multilingual baselines NLLB-200 (615M parameters) and mBART-50 (611M parameters) while better preserving morphological coherence. Their analyses identify empirical data thresholds for successful adaptation in low-resource dialects and demonstrate beneficial cross-dialect transfer. The corpus reaches 51,531 parallel sentence pairs, including new expert-verified data for five dialects previously not covered in MT research.
AI.conclusion: A single unified NMT system can effectively handle multi-directional translation among many diverse Bangla dialects without relying on a standard pivot, provided an appropriate multi-dialect corpus and efficient adaptation methods like DoRA are used. Their BanglaT5-based system sets a new state of the art for Bangla dialect MT, offers practical, compressed deployment via INT8 quantization, and is released as an open web tool, supporting digital inclusion for under-served dialect communities. The publicly available dataset and analyses on cross-dialect transfer and data scaling give a foundation for future research on low-resource dialectal NLP.

title: MBA: Multimodal Benchmark and Agents for Real-World Business Ideation
summary: Agentic systems powered by large language models (LLMs) have opened new opportunities for business ideation. Yet existing approaches remain confined to a text-only paradigm, despite the inherently multimodal nature of real-world contexts. We thus introduce MBA-Bench, the first multimodal benchmark for training and evaluating business ideation agents, comprising 30K samples across six domains, each domain characterized by distinct visual cues not fully conveyed by text alone. Concretely, we automatically caption images and employ GPT-4o to generate five reference ideas for each of three business questions through retrieval query generation, market evidence retrieval, and evidence-augmented synthesis. Following prior work, we evaluate agents across six business-oriented criteria using MLLM-as-a-Judge. To consider settings where criteria are hidden or disclosed, we present MBA-b and MBA-k for blind and known, respectively. We train both with two novel reward objectives---creativity and feasibility---while MBA-k further optimizes the six disclosed criteria for eight in total. Both are trained via LoRA-based supervised fine-tuning followed by group relative policy optimization with these setting-specific rewards. For extensive experiments on MBA-Bench, we set up two baselines accommodating either captions only or multimodal inputs, with the latter nearing closed-source performance on several metrics. MBA-b and MBA-k outperform caption baselines by 63.9% and 77.1%, and multimodal baselines by 25.6% and 35.8%, respectively.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces MBA-Bench, a large multimodal benchmark and corresponding agentic systems (MBA-b and MBA-k) for evaluating and training business ideation agents, showing strong gains over caption-only and multimodal baselines.
AI.motivation: Existing agentic systems with large language models support business ideation but are limited to text-only inputs, which fails to capture the inherently multimodal nature (especially visual cues) of many real-world business contexts. There is also a lack of standardized, large-scale benchmarks and training setups tailored specifically to multimodal business ideation and its evaluation along meaningful business criteria.
AI.method: The authors construct MBA-Bench, a 30K-sample multimodal benchmark spanning six visually distinctive domains. For each image, they auto-generate captions and then use GPT-4o to create five reference business ideas for three business questions via a pipeline of retrieval query generation, external market evidence retrieval, and evidence-augmented synthesis. They evaluate agents with an MLLM-as-a-Judge framework on six business criteria and define two settings: MBA-b (criteria hidden) and MBA-k (criteria known). They then build two agent variants, each trained via LoRA-based supervised fine-tuning followed by group relative policy optimization. MBA-b uses two reward signals (creativity and feasibility), while MBA-k optimizes all eight rewards (creativity, feasibility, plus the six disclosed business criteria). Baselines include caption-only and fully multimodal models for comparison.
AI.result: On MBA-Bench, the multimodal baseline approaches closed-source model performance on several metrics, validating the benchmark and training setup. The proposed MBA-b and MBA-k agents significantly outperform caption-only baselines by 63.9% and 77.1%, and multimodal baselines by 25.6% and 35.8%, respectively, across the business evaluation metrics. This demonstrates that reward-optimized, benchmark-aligned training yields much better business ideation quality than naive multimodal or caption-based approaches.
AI.conclusion: MBA-Bench provides a large-scale, multimodal, and business-focused benchmark that enables systematic training and evaluation of business ideation agents. The MBA-b and MBA-k agents, trained with targeted reward objectives and RL-style optimization, deliver substantially better performance than strong baselines, highlighting the value of multimodal inputs and explicit, criterion-aligned reward design for business ideation systems.

title: Preference Tree Optimization: Enhancing Goal-Oriented Dialogue with Look-Ahead Simulations
comment: 13 pages, 4 figures. Accepted at an ICLR 2025 workshop
summary: Developing dialogue systems capable of engaging in multi-turn, goal-oriented conversations remains a significant challenge, especially in specialized domains with limited data. This research proposes a novel framework called Preference Tree Optimization (PTO), designed to iteratively improve agent models in such dialogue systems, by generating preference data using a method called Preference Tree with Look-Ahead. Focusing on Motivational Interviewing (MI) -- a counseling technique aimed at facilitating behavioral change -- we leverage virtual patients and an oracle evaluator to simulate conversations and generate rich preference datasets. By combining this method with Direct Preference Optimization (DPO), we aim to enhance the agent's decision-making capabilities over iterative training cycles. The proposed framework addresses data scarcity and advances the development of more nuanced and effective dialogue systems in goal-oriented domains. Experimental evaluations demonstrate that the PTO framework enhances dialogue agents' performance in goal-oriented conversations within the domain of Motivational Interviewing (MI). Models trained with PTO consistently outperformed the baseline in key metrics such as session satisfaction and working alliance. Additionally, incorporating look-ahead simulations led to improved long-term planning and more effective conversational strategies, with deeper look-ahead configurations yielding the most stable and high-scoring results.

AI.tldr: Proposes Preference Tree Optimization (PTO) to improve multi-turn, goal-oriented dialogue agents in low-data specialized domains using look-ahead preference trees and DPO.
AI.motivation: Multi-turn, goal-oriented dialogue in specialized, data-scarce domains is hard; existing systems struggle with long-term planning, nuanced strategies, and limited supervision signals.
AI.method: Introduce Preference Tree Optimization, which uses virtual patients and an oracle evaluator to simulate Motivational Interviewing (MI) dialogues. It builds preference trees with look-ahead to generate rich preference data, then applies Direct Preference Optimization over iterative training cycles to refine the agent’s policy and planning.
AI.result: In MI dialogue tasks, agents trained with PTO outperform baselines on session satisfaction and working alliance. Deeper look-ahead configurations improve long-term planning and yield more stable, higher-scoring conversational strategies.
AI.conclusion: PTO is an effective framework for improving goal-oriented dialogue agents in specialized, low-resource domains, particularly by leveraging simulated interactions, look-ahead preference trees, and DPO to enhance long-term planning and conversational quality.

title: Making AI-Generated Feedback Matter: From Provision to Student Enactment
summary: Feedback processes strongly influence student learning, yet their educational value depends on addressing two distinct challenges: providing high-quality, timely, and individualised feedback at scale, and supporting students to interpret, evaluate, and act on that feedback productively. Generative AI offers a credible means of addressing the provision challenge, but students' uptake of AI-generated feedback remains limited. We conducted a large-scale quasi-experimental sequential cohort study comparing three AI-mediated feedback workflows across 13,037 students and 51,296 student-authored resources. In Directed Feedback (n = 3,723), students received AI-generated feedback comments without structured support. In Self-Directed Feedback (n = 3,951), students could initiate optional AI-supported dialogue. In Enacted Feedback (n = 5,363), students were prompted to select feedback suggestions, evaluate their relevance, and engage in targeted AI-supported dialogue anchored to those selections. Enacted Feedback was associated with significantly higher uptake of AI-generated feedback, with an estimated probability of 26.2%, compared with 14.1% for Directed Feedback and 0.1% for Self-Directed Feedback. It was also associated with significantly higher self-assessment confidence and submitted-work quality than both comparison conditions. These findings suggest that the educational value of AI-generated feedback depends not only on the quality of feedback comments, but also on workflows that actively structure students' enactment of feedback literacy processes. The results have implications for the design of AI feedback systems that position learners as active participants in judgement, dialogue, and improvement rather than passive recipients of comments. Overall findings show that AI access alone is insufficient; purposeful workflow design is central to productive feedback use.

AI.tldr: The paper evaluates different AI-mediated feedback workflows in higher education and finds that structured, enacted feedback workflows significantly increase students' uptake of AI feedback, their confidence, and the quality of their submitted work compared with unstructured or purely self-initiated AI feedback access.
AI.motivation: Although feedback is critical for learning, two persistent challenges remain: (1) delivering high-quality, timely, individualised feedback at scale, and (2) ensuring that students can effectively interpret and use that feedback. Generative AI can help with scalable feedback provision, but current systems show low student uptake and limited impact. The authors aim to understand how different ways of integrating AI feedback into learning workflows affect students' engagement with, and benefit from, AI-generated feedback.
AI.method: The authors conducted a large-scale quasi-experimental sequential cohort study involving 13,037 students and 51,296 student-authored resources. They compared three AI-mediated feedback workflows: (1) Directed Feedback, where students passively receive AI-generated feedback comments; (2) Self-Directed Feedback, where students can optionally initiate AI-supported feedback dialogues; and (3) Enacted Feedback, where students are prompted to actively select feedback suggestions, evaluate their relevance, and engage in focused AI-supported dialogue anchored to those selections. They then measured feedback uptake, self-assessment confidence, and the quality of submitted work across the three conditions.
AI.result: The Enacted Feedback workflow led to substantially higher uptake of AI-generated feedback (26.2% estimated probability) than Directed Feedback (14.1%) and Self-Directed Feedback (0.1%). Enacted Feedback was also associated with significantly higher self-assessment confidence and higher quality of students' submitted work compared with both other workflows.
AI.conclusion: The study concludes that the impact of AI-generated feedback on learning depends not only on the quality of the feedback itself but also on the design of feedback workflows that scaffold students' feedback literacy. Workflows that require learners to actively judge, select, and discuss feedback (enacted feedback) are more effective than merely providing AI comments or optional access to AI dialogue. Therefore, AI feedback systems should be designed to position learners as active agents in judgement, dialogue, and improvement, highlighting that mere access to AI tools is insufficient without purposeful workflow design.

title: Structuring the Space of Perspectives
comment: Under review for TACL (editor decision: b)
summary: The same event can be reported from different perspectives depending on the experiences, background, and beliefs of the writer or speaker. A variety of NLP areas engage with perspectives, spanning from text analysis to algorithm optimization. A wide range of operative concepts (such as stances, sentiment, frames, and arguments) has been used to capture perspectives in texts, however the precise relationships among those concepts remain unclear. Arguably, a deeper theoretical understanding of these concepts would empower more effective research on perspectives.
