In this paper, we address this gap by reviewing the space of perspectives in NLP and defining a set of properties that help distinguishing perspective-related concepts. Our analysis leads us to posit a hierarchy which organizes these concepts linearly along a single axis. Finally, we show how this principled conceptual hierarchy can help researchers navigate the field and select operationalizations of perspective that align with their specific research objectives.

AI.tldr: The paper surveys how different NLP subfields model “perspective” in text and proposes a unifying hierarchy of perspective-related concepts.
AI.motivation: Many NLP tasks deal with how people express viewpoints (e.g., stance, sentiment, framing, argumentation), but these notions are used inconsistently and their interrelations are poorly understood. This conceptual fragmentation makes it hard to compare work across tasks and to choose the right operationalization of “perspective” for a given research goal. The authors aim to provide a coherent theoretical foundation to structure this space.
AI.method: The authors conduct a conceptual and methodological review of NLP work that models perspectives, collecting and systematizing operative concepts such as stance, sentiment, frames, and arguments. They then define a set of discriminative properties (dimensions) that characterize how these concepts relate to perspectives in text. Using these properties, they analyze existing perspective-related notions and derive a linear hierarchy that places them along a single organizing axis.
AI.result: They identify key properties that distinguish different perspective-related concepts and use these to build a principled, linear hierarchy that orders concepts like sentiment, stance, framing, and argumentation within a unified space. The hierarchy clarifies overlaps and differences between concepts and reveals how they relate in terms of abstraction and proximity to underlying perspectives.
AI.conclusion: The paper concludes that perspective-related phenomena in NLP can be systematically organized using a small set of properties, leading to a linear conceptual hierarchy. This hierarchy offers a theoretical scaffold that helps researchers choose and define perspective operationalizations that best fit their aims, and facilitates clearer comparisons across subfields and tasks that deal with viewpoints in text.

title: CLAIM: Leading Open-domain Active Clarification of Large Language Models with Uncertainty Measurement
summary: In open-domain human-computer interaction scenarios, large language models (LLMs) frequently encounter user queries that are ambiguous or incomplete. In such cases, directly producing an answer often leads to overgeneralized, erroneous, or low-information responses. In contrast, asking clarifying questions can substantially improve interaction quality. However, existing approaches still rely heavily on manually annotated data or preference alignment to address two fundamental challenges: when clarification is necessary, and which aspect of the query should be clarified. This reliance incurs high annotation costs and limits generalization. To address these challenges, we propose CLAIM, an uncertainty-driven framework for active clarification learning in open-domain settings. CLAIM eliminates the need for explicit human preference annotations by quantifying query uncertainty through the entropy induced by answer disagreements across multiple models. This uncertainty signal is then used to construct high-quality synthetic data, enabling the training of a unified clarification decision model through a combination of supervised learning and reinforcement learning. Specifically, we propose an entropy-driven synthetic data generation pipeline that integrates entropy-based uncertainty estimation with semantic clustering and reasoning-based judgments, enabling reliable automatic annotation of clarification requirements. To train CLAIM, we formulate the clarification process as a structured decision generation problem and adopt a training paradigm that combines supervised fine-tuning (SFT) with group-relative policy optimization (GRPO). Experimental results demonstrate that CLAIM can learn stable and generalizable clarification strategies without relying on manually labeled data, offering a low-cost and robust solution for proactive understanding in real-world open-domain interactions with LLMs.

AI.tldr: CLAIM is an uncertainty-driven framework that automatically decides when and how to ask clarifying questions in open-domain LLM interactions, using entropy-based disagreement across models and synthetic data instead of manual annotations.
AI.motivation: In open-domain dialogue, LLMs often receive ambiguous or underspecified queries. Directly answering such queries leads to vague, incorrect, or unhelpful responses. Clarifying questions can improve interaction, but existing methods depend on costly human annotations or preference alignment to determine when clarification is needed and what to clarify. This limits scalability and generalization, motivating a method that can learn clarification behavior without manual labels.
AI.method: The authors propose CLAIM, which quantifies uncertainty in user queries via entropy computed from disagreements among multiple model answers. This entropy-based uncertainty is used in an automatic synthetic data generation pipeline that combines: (1) entropy-based uncertainty estimation, (2) semantic clustering of queries, and (3) reasoning-based judgments to decide whether clarification is needed and what aspect to clarify. These automatically labeled data are then used to train a unified clarification decision model. The clarification process is formulated as a structured decision generation task, and training uses supervised fine-tuning (SFT) followed by group-relative policy optimization (GRPO), a reinforcement learning approach, to refine clarification strategies.
AI.result: Experiments show that CLAIM learns stable and generalizable strategies for when to ask clarification questions and what to clarify, without relying on manually labeled preference data. The framework yields improved clarification behavior and interaction quality in open-domain LLM settings, while reducing annotation costs.
AI.conclusion: CLAIM provides a low-cost, robust solution for proactive clarification in open-domain LLM interactions by leveraging entropy-based uncertainty and synthetic data instead of manual annotations. The framework successfully addresses the key challenges of deciding when clarification is necessary and which aspects of a query to clarify, demonstrating good generalization and stability across scenarios.

title: QV-PIC: Query-Aware Visual Position-Independent Caching for Efficient RAG Serving
summary: Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) repeatedly prefills identical text chunks across queries, incurring redundant computations. Position-Independent Caching (PIC) mitigates it by reusing precomputed Key-Value (KV) across positions, but its efficiency is constrained by the large volume of text tokens. Rendering text chunks as images can compress the text into fewer visual tokens, but the rendered-image PIC suffers more severe quality degradation than the text PIC. This representation-specific gap primarily arises from contextual mismatches across independently compiled caches and the loss of fine-grained textual evidence during visual compression. Existing PIC repair methods mainly address the former through selective recomputation, but they incur online computation and cannot recover lost textual details. We propose QV-PIC, a query-aware dual-resolution PIC reuse framework guided by model-native templates. Offline, QV-PIC compiles visual caches under the model's native chat-template prefix, improving PIC quality without online recomputation. Online, it preserves global context with low resolution and restores fine-grained textual evidence within a high-resolution budget by cumulative query relevance scores, retaining the efficiency benefit of visual compression. Across six tasks, QV-PIC improves average F1 by 21.6 points over vanilla rendered-image PIC, closes the gap to vanilla text PIC, and surpasses optimized text PIC by 2.58 F1 while reducing TTFT by 17.2\%. Relative to full prefill, it cuts TTFT by 83.8%.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes QV-PIC, a query-aware dual-resolution position-independent caching framework that uses visual token compression plus smart cache construction and retrieval to speed up RAG while recovering much of the quality lost in prior rendered-image PIC methods.
AI.motivation: RAG systems repeatedly prefill the same text chunks, wasting computation. Position-Independent Caching (PIC) can reuse KV caches but becomes inefficient when many text tokens are involved. Rendering text as images compresses tokens but degrades model quality more severely than text-based PIC, due to contextual mismatch across caches and loss of fine-grained text details. Existing PIC repair methods rely on online recomputation and cannot restore lost details. The paper aims to maintain or improve RAG performance while significantly reducing prefill cost by fixing these shortcomings of visual PIC.
AI.method: The authors introduce QV-PIC, a query-aware dual-resolution PIC reuse framework designed for rendered images. Offline, they build visual caches using the model’s native chat-template prefix so that the cached contexts better match actual inference conditions, removing the need for online recomputation. Online, they use a two-level resolution strategy: low-resolution visual tokens preserve global document context for efficiency, while high-resolution budgets are allocated selectively based on cumulative query relevance scores to reconstruct fine-grained textual evidence only where it matters. This approach keeps the compression benefits of visual tokens while mitigating both contextual mismatch and detail loss.
AI.result: On six evaluation tasks, QV-PIC achieves an average F1 improvement of 21.6 points over standard rendered-image PIC. It nearly closes the performance gap to vanilla text PIC and even outperforms optimized text PIC by 2.58 F1, while reducing time-to-first-token (TTFT) by 17.2%. Compared to full prefill without caching, QV-PIC cuts TTFT by 83.8%, demonstrating substantial efficiency gains with competitive or superior quality.
AI.conclusion: QV-PIC shows that carefully constructed, query-aware visual caches can make rendered-image PIC viable for RAG: it recovers much of the quality lost in naive visual compression while preserving large speedups. By compiling caches under the model’s native chat template and using dual-resolution, relevance-guided reuse at inference, QV-PIC both narrows the gap with text-based PIC and offers better latency–quality trade-offs than full prefill or prior PIC repair methods.

title: XBridge: Entity-Grounded Latent Bridge for Heterogeneous LLM Communication
summary: Heterogeneous multi-agent LLM systems, where agents are powered by different model families, can outperform homogeneous configurations by reducing redundant reasoning patterns. Yet existing communication protocols either operate through text, discarding the sender's internal representations, or require architectural homogeneity for latent-level transfer. We identify the entity grounding problem in cross-architecture communication: cross-attention bridges that transfer continuous representations across different LLM families suffer from rare-token compression collapse, where entity identity is lost in the continuous bottleneck (bridge-only F1 ~30%). We propose XBRIDGE, a decode-free communication protocol that addresses this through two mechanisms. Lexical Anchor Mapping (LAM) maps the sender's original context tokens to the receiver's vocabulary, providing discrete entity anchors. A Latent Enrichment Bridge (LEB) lets the receiver query the sender's hidden states for contextual enrichment. The entity anchors ground the bridge's contextual signals to specific entities through the receiver's own self-attention. Across three model families (Llama, Qwen, and Mistral), seven benchmarks, and both communication directions, XBRIDGE outperforms text-based communication on all seven tasks for each model pair while achieving 11x lower latency, and in a same-architecture setting it also exceeds a KV-sharing baseline on six of seven tasks. LEB requires only 264M trainable parameters (3.8% of the receiver), is trained on a small balanced sample set, and adds negligible inference overhead.

AI.tldr: XBRIDGE is a decode-free communication protocol enabling effective latent-level collaboration between heterogeneous LLM agents by grounding shared continuous representations with discrete lexical anchors, improving performance and latency across models and tasks.
AI.motivation: Heterogeneous multi-agent LLM systems can perform better than homogeneous ones by diversifying reasoning, but current inter-agent communication is limited: text-only transfer discards rich internal representations, while latent-level sharing typically assumes identical architectures. Cross-architecture latent bridges further suffer from an entity grounding problem where rare or specific entities are lost (rare-token compression collapse), drastically hurting performance. The paper aims to enable efficient and accurate cross-model communication without requiring architectural homogeneity or expensive decoding.
AI.method: The authors propose XBRIDGE, a decode-free protocol for cross-architecture communication between LLM agents. It has two key components: (1) Lexical Anchor Mapping (LAM), which aligns tokens from the sender’s context to tokens in the receiver’s vocabulary, generating discrete entity anchors that preserve identity across architectures; and (2) a Latent Enrichment Bridge (LEB), a lightweight cross-attention style module that lets the receiver query the sender’s hidden states to obtain contextual enrichment. The receiver then uses its own self-attention to integrate the latent enrichment conditioned on the lexical anchors. LEB is parameter-efficient (~264M parameters, 3.8% of the receiver) and trained on a small balanced dataset to enable robust transfer between model families without requiring joint training of the full models.
AI.result: On seven benchmarks spanning different tasks and using three LLM families (Llama, Qwen, Mistral) in both communication directions, XBRIDGE consistently outperforms text-based agent communication for every model pair, while also providing an 11x latency reduction versus decode-and-encode protocols. In same-architecture settings, XBRIDGE surpasses a strong KV-cache sharing baseline on six of seven tasks, indicating it is competitive even when architectures match. Bridge-only approaches without lexical anchors suffer from low F1 (~30%), highlighting the severity of entity grounding issues without the proposed mechanisms. LEB adds minimal inference overhead despite being trained as a separate module with only 264M parameters.
AI.conclusion: The paper concludes that effective cross-architecture multi-agent LLM collaboration requires solving an entity grounding problem that arises when transferring continuous representations alone. XBRIDGE addresses this by combining discrete lexical anchors with a lightweight latent enrichment bridge, allowing heterogeneous LLMs to communicate at the representation level without decoding. This approach improves both accuracy and efficiency compared to text-based communication and even beats KV-sharing in many same-architecture scenarios, suggesting a general, scalable strategy for building high-performance heterogeneous LLM systems.

title: SAG: SQL-Retrieval Augmented Generation with Query-Time Dynamic Hyperedges
summary: While retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) has proven effective at giving LLMs access to external knowledge, mainstream dense-retrieval implementations remain inherently limited in handling structured constraints and multi-hop reasoning. Graph-based methods address this by constructing knowledge graphs offline, but they often fragment semantics, incur high maintenance, and complicate incremental updates. We propose SAG (SQL-Retrieval Augmented Generation), a structured retrieval architecture that organizes documents into an event-entity index without building a global knowledge graph. SAG represents each chunk as a semantically complete event paired with its entities, forming a latent hyperedge that preserves n-ary relations without decomposing them into triples. At query time, SAG treats shared entities as join keys to connect related chunks. This dynamically yields a query-scoped neighborhood of events, and yet every piece of evidence remains the original chunk throughout. Experiments on HotpotQA, 2WikiMultiHopQA, and MuSiQue show that SAG achieves the best retrieval and end-to-end QA performance on every benchmark, with gains that widen as reasoning-chain complexity increases. On MuSiQue, where multi-hop evidence chaining is most demanding, SAG reaches 80.36% Recall@5, outperforming the strongest baseline by 11.52 points. This work paves the way for knowledge infrastructure that enables LLM agents to retrieve and reason over continually growing organizational knowledge.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces SAG, a SQL-style retrieval-augmented generation framework that indexes text as event-entity hyperedges instead of a global knowledge graph, enabling better multi-hop, constraint-aware reasoning and achieving state-of-the-art results on multi-hop QA benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Existing RAG systems with dense retrieval struggle with structured constraints and multi-hop reasoning, while graph-based methods require costly, brittle knowledge graph construction and maintenance. The authors want a retrieval framework that captures rich event-level structure and n-ary relations, supports dynamic multi-hop reasoning at query time, and scales to continually updated organizational knowledge without building or maintaining a global KG.
AI.method: They propose SAG (SQL-Retrieval Augmented Generation), which organizes documents into an event-entity index. Each chunk is reformulated as a semantically complete event plus its participating entities, treated as a latent hyperedge that preserves n-ary relations. Instead of pre-building a global knowledge graph, SAG uses shared entities as join keys at query time to connect related chunks, dynamically constructing a query-scoped neighborhood of events. This neighborhood serves as structured, multi-hop evidence for downstream LLM-based QA. They evaluate SAG against strong RAG and graph-based baselines on multi-hop QA datasets.
AI.result: On three multi-hop QA benchmarks—HotpotQA, 2WikiMultiHopQA, and MuSiQue—SAG consistently achieves the best retrieval and end-to-end QA performance. The performance gap widens as the required reasoning-chain length increases. On the most demanding dataset, MuSiQue, SAG attains 80.36% Recall@5, surpassing the strongest baseline by 11.52 percentage points, demonstrating substantially improved multi-hop evidence retrieval.
AI.conclusion: SAG’s event-entity indexing and on-the-fly entity-join mechanism provide a practical alternative to dense retrieval and static knowledge graphs for multi-hop reasoning. By preserving original chunks as evidence and avoiding explicit KG construction, SAG offers better retrieval quality, scales more easily to evolving knowledge, and forms a promising foundation for LLM agents that must continually retrieve and reason over complex organizational information.

title: AgenticTwin: An Agentic LLM Framework Integrated with Digital Twin for Anomaly Detection
summary: Digital twins are increasingly used to monitor and simulate the behavior of cyber-physical systems. Even with skilled operators, interpreting anomalies detected within digital twin pipelines is challenging, as the sheer complexity and volume of raw sensor data make thorough analysis difficult. Recent advances in large language models (LLMs) offer promising capabilities for reasoning and explanation, yet their integration into digital twin-driven anomaly analysis remains underexplored. In this work, we propose AgenticTwin, an agentic framework that integrates LLM-driven reasoning with a digital twin-based anomaly detection pipeline. The framework grounds LLM-generated explanations in outputs from a digital twin-driven anomaly classifier and enables human operators to ask relevant natural-language questions about the system. Beyond the framework itself, we introduce a benchmark-oriented evaluation pipeline constructed over synthetic anomalies injected into a real-world weather sensor dataset, enabling controlled generation of operator queries over anomaly events. We further evaluate the feasibility of deploying lightweight, open-source LLMs for practical cyber-physical environments. Experimental results demonstrate that structured agent collaboration and knowledge-grounded reasoning improve diagnosis quality, contextual retrieval, and mitigation quality across diverse possible anomaly scenarios.

AI.tldr: The paper presents AgenticTwin, an LLM-powered agentic framework that explains and helps diagnose anomalies detected by digital twins in cyber-physical systems, evaluated via a synthetic-anomaly benchmark on real weather data.
AI.motivation: Digital twins generate huge volumes of complex sensor data, making it hard for human operators—even skilled ones—to interpret anomalies flagged by automated pipelines. While LLMs are good at reasoning and explanation, there is little work on systematically integrating them with digital twin anomaly detection in a way that is grounded in system data and usable by operators.
AI.method: The authors design AgenticTwin, an agent-based architecture that combines a digital twin-based anomaly classifier with LLM-driven reasoning agents. The system grounds LLM explanations in classifier outputs and supports natural-language question answering for operators. They also build a benchmark-style evaluation pipeline using controlled synthetic anomalies injected into a real-world weather sensor dataset, which allows generation of standardized operator queries around anomaly events. They investigate deployment with lightweight, open-source LLMs suited to cyber-physical settings.
AI.result: Experiments on the benchmark show that the proposed agentic, knowledge-grounded setup yields better anomaly diagnosis quality, more relevant contextual information retrieval, and improved mitigation suggestions across a variety of anomaly types compared with baselines or less structured approaches.
AI.conclusion: Integrating structured, collaborating LLM agents with digital twin anomaly detection pipelines can make anomaly analysis more interpretable and actionable for operators. The AgenticTwin framework, together with its synthetic-anomaly benchmark, demonstrates the practicality and benefits of using lightweight, open LLMs for grounded reasoning in cyber-physical digital twin environments.

title: A corpus-specific clinical RAG system matches or outperforms newer frontier LLMs on HealthBench
summary: General-purpose large language models (LLMs) have recently been reported to match or exceed specialized clinical AI tools on medical benchmarks, but such comparisons draw on a narrow set of systems and on benchmarks developed largely in high-income settings. We evaluate VITA, a retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) system purpose-built for contextual knowledge retrieval in India and other low- and middle-income (LMIC) settings. VITA retrieves from a curated corpus of disease-specific guidelines, India-specific antimicrobial resistance data, national formulary constraints, and resource-limited care protocols; its architecture and corpus are proprietary, but the benchmark, the physician-written rubrics, and our full response and scoring outputs are public for independent verification. On 4,023 English-language HealthBench questions (80.5% of the benchmark), scored with a GPT-4.1 judge, VITA ranked first with 51.9% of possible rubric points, ahead of GPT-5.4 (46.1%), o4-mini (44.3%), Gemini 3.1 Pro (42.6%), and Claude Sonnet 4.6 (37.3%), and scored highest on 45.4% of questions. To test robustness to newer models and judge lineage, a 500-question subset was re-run against current-generation models (GPT-5.5, Claude Opus 4.8, Gemini 3.5 Pro, Grok 4.3) and graded by a neutral open-weight judge (DeepSeek-V4-Pro) sharing no lineage with any system tested. Here the gap narrowed to parity: VITA and GPT-5.5 were statistically indistinguishable on mean per-question score, while VITA led on points-weighted score and won the most questions. VITA's advantages in accuracy and completeness persisted under the neutral judge; its communication scores were lower. These results indicate that a purpose-built clinical RAG system remains competitive with frontier LLMs on an open benchmark, consistent with corpus specificity as a design variable that improves grounding at some cost to communication polish.

AI.tldr: The paper evaluates VITA, a specialized clinical retrieval-augmented generation system tailored to India/LMICs, showing it matches or outperforms frontier general-purpose LLMs on a large open medical benchmark due to corpus specificity, though with slightly weaker communication polish.
AI.motivation: Most medical AI benchmarks and model comparisons focus on general-purpose LLMs and datasets from high-income countries, which may not reflect the needs and constraints of India and other LMICs. There is a need to test whether a purpose-built, locally grounded RAG system can outperform or at least remain competitive with state-of-the-art general LLMs, especially when using region-specific clinical guidelines, resistance patterns, formularies, and resource-limited protocols.
AI.method: The authors build VITA, a proprietary clinical RAG system backed by a curated corpus including disease guidelines, India-specific antimicrobial resistance data, national formulary constraints, and resource-limited care protocols. They evaluate it on HealthBench, using 4,023 English questions scored via a GPT-4.1 judge and compare it against several frontier models (GPT-5.4, o4-mini, Gemini 3.1 Pro, Claude Sonnet 4.6). They then perform a robustness study on a 500-question subset against newer models (GPT-5.5, Claude Opus 4.8, Gemini 3.5 Pro, Grok 4.3), graded by an independent open-weight model (DeepSeek-V4-Pro) with no lineage ties to the tested systems. Metrics include proportion of rubric points obtained, per-question scores, points-weighted scores, win rates, and sub-scores for accuracy, completeness, and communication.
AI.result: On the main 4,023-question evaluation, VITA obtained 51.9% of total rubric points, outperforming GPT-5.4 (46.1%), o4-mini (44.3%), Gemini 3.1 Pro (42.6%), and Claude Sonnet 4.6 (37.3%), and achieving the highest score on 45.4% of questions. In the 500-question robustness subset graded by DeepSeek-V4-Pro, VITA and GPT-5.5 had statistically indistinguishable mean per-question scores, but VITA led on points-weighted score and won the largest fraction of questions. Across evaluations, VITA showed higher accuracy and completeness than competitors, but tended to receive lower scores for communication quality.
AI.conclusion: A focused clinical RAG system built around region-specific and resource-aware medical knowledge can compete with or surpass cutting-edge general-purpose LLMs on an open medical benchmark. Corpus specificity and contextual grounding appear to materially improve clinical accuracy and completeness, although they may trade off some communication polish. The work supports the value of purpose-built, locally tailored clinical AI systems for LMIC contexts and provides an open benchmark and scoring outputs for independent verification, even though the model and corpus themselves remain proprietary.

title: FrontierFinance: A Challenging Benchmark for Measuring Frontier Intelligence of Finance Agents
summary: AI agents are increasingly deployed for professional investment research, yet no benchmark captures the complexity of the full investor workflow. Existing benchmarks mainly target financial data extraction, a narrow slice that current models have largely saturated, while reference-based metrics and generic LLM-as-a-judge scoring fall short on the open-ended, long-form answers that real analyst queries demand. We introduce FrontierFinance, a fully open benchmark of 220 expert-crafted queries and 11,543 source-attributed rubrics spanning six crucial use cases across the full investor workflow. FrontierFinance is both broader and harder than existing public finance benchmarks. Evaluating frontier models and agent systems under a common harness restricted to publicly available data, we find that the tool harness, not the model alone, strongly shapes quality and efficiency; that Samaya's in-house system leads at 56.0%, ahead of the strongest frontier model (Claude Fable 5, 49.2%) at roughly 2.2x lower cost; and that the best open-weight model (Kimi K3, 46.4%) nearly matches the best proprietary model at 4.5x lower cost. Screening & Discovery and Sector, Industry & Macro remain the hardest use cases across all systems, where even the best systems reach only 33% and 39%. We make the dataset and grading code publicly available.

AI.tldr: FrontierFinance is an open benchmark that evaluates AI agents on the full professional investment research workflow using expert-crafted queries and detailed rubrics, showing that tool integration and system design matter as much as the base model, and that strong open-weight models can rival proprietary ones at lower cost.
AI.motivation: Current financial AI benchmarks focus narrowly on data extraction and use reference-based or generic LLM-judge metrics that do not capture the open-ended, long-form, and workflow-level nature of real investment research. There is a need for a benchmark that reflects the true complexity of professional investor workflows and can meaningfully differentiate modern frontier models and agentic systems.
AI.method: The authors build FrontierFinance, an open benchmark consisting of 220 expert-designed investment research queries with 11,543 fine-grained, source-attributed rubric items, spanning six key use cases across the full investor workflow. They evaluate multiple frontier language models and full agent systems under a standardized tool harness that is limited to publicly available data, and compare their performance, efficiency, and cost on these tasks.
AI.result: FrontierFinance is more comprehensive and challenging than existing public finance benchmarks. Results show that the design of the tool harness and agent system has a major impact on both quality and efficiency, beyond the base model alone. Samaya's in-house system performs best at 56.0% score, outperforming the strongest standalone frontier model (Claude Fable 5 at 49.2%) while costing about 2.2 times less, and the best open-weight model (Kimi K3 at 46.4%) nearly matches the top proprietary model at about 4.5 times lower cost. Screening & Discovery and Sector, Industry & Macro use cases are consistently the hardest, with top systems scoring only 33% and 39%, respectively.
AI.conclusion: FrontierFinance provides a challenging, realistic, and fully open benchmark for assessing AI agents in professional investment research across the full workflow. The findings underscore that well-designed tool harnesses and agent systems can outperform stronger raw models at lower cost, and that open-weight models can come close to proprietary model performance. The benchmark, along with its dataset and grading code, is released to facilitate further research and progress in financial AI agents.

title: Massive Activations in Hybrid Linear Attention Large Language Models: Pre-Attention Spikes and Inter-Spike Plateaus
summary: We present the first systematic study of Massive activations (MAs) in layer-interleaved HLA LLMs and uncover two architecture-aligned morphologies: MAs consistently spike immediately before full attention layers, forming pre-attention spikes (PAS), and can persist through intervening linear attention layers, giving rise to inter-spike plateaus (ISP). As full attention becomes denser, successive PAS become increasingly connected through ISP, ultimately recovering the stable MA morphology of full attention LLMs. We establish the recurrence of this organization across five linear attention architectures, six hybridization configurations, five data domains, and representative open-source hybrid models spanning 1.2B to 397B total parameters. Controlled pretraining of GDN-based hybrids at scales up to 1.3B shows that both morphologies emerge early and respond asymmetrically to output gating: full attention output gating strongly attenuates their absolute magnitudes without eliminating their layerwise organization, whereas removing GDN gates yields comparatively modest amplification. Mechanistically, our systematic-outlier analysis supports a shared lifecycle account governed by the timing of MA cancellation. PAS follows a localized write-sink-cancel process, while the extended persistence of ISP is consistent with delayed cancellation. At the full attention limit, this account recovers the stable MA morphology characteristic of full attention LLMs. Our code is available at https://github.com/StartluxLabs/Massive-Activations-HLA.

AI.tldr: This paper systematically studies Massive Activations (MAs) in layer-interleaved hybrid linear-attention (HLA) LLMs, discovering consistent activation morphologies aligned with architecture and explaining them via an MA lifecycle governed by cancellation timing.
AI.motivation: Massive activations are a key phenomenon in full-attention LLMs, but how they behave in emerging hybrid / linear-attention models is poorly understood. As industry moves toward scalable, memory-efficient attention variants, it is important to know whether MA-related behaviors, risks (e.g., instability), and interpretability structures carry over and how they change with architecture. The authors aim to fill this gap with the first systematic characterization of MAs in HLA LLMs.
AI.method: The authors empirically analyze activation distributions and temporal patterns in a wide range of HLA architectures and configurations. They examine where and how MAs arise relative to attention layers, compare different densities of full attention, and track the evolution of MA patterns during controlled pretraining of GDN-based hybrid models up to 1.3B parameters. They apply systematic-outlier analysis to trace the lifecycle of MA tokens and study the effect of output gating manipulations (gating/removing full attention and GDN gates) on the magnitude and organization of MAs across depths and architectures.
AI.result: They discover two robust, architecture-aligned MA morphologies: (1) pre-attention spikes (PAS), where MAs consistently surge immediately before full attention layers; and (2) inter-spike plateaus (ISP), where elevated activations persist across sequences of linear-attention layers between full attention blocks. As attention density increases, ISPs connect successive PAS to resemble the stable MA morphology known from pure full attention LLMs. These patterns recur across five linear-attention designs, six hybridization schemes, five data domains, and open-source hybrids from 1.2B to 397B parameters. Pretraining experiments show both PAS and ISP emerge early. Gating full attention outputs sharply reduces MA magnitudes but preserves their layerwise structure, while removing GDN gates only modestly amplifies MAs.
AI.conclusion: Massive activations in hybrid linear-attention LLMs are not random anomalies but follow a consistent, architecture-governed organization. The authors propose a shared lifecycle explanation: PAS result from a localized write–sink–cancel process, whereas ISP reflects delayed cancellation of MAs across intervening linear-attention layers. In the limit of dense full attention, this lifecycle reproduces the stable MA morphology seen in standard full-attention LLMs. This work suggests that MA behavior transfers in a principled way from full-attention to hybrid models, informing both interpretability and design choices for scalable attention architectures.

title: HUGIN: Enhancing Vision-Language Planning for Autonomous Logistics Sorting
summary: Autonomous logistics sorting systems (ALSS) are an important industrial application of embodied AI, which requires joint planning over spatially disjoint camera views. We formulate this setting as Joint Multi-Scene Understanding (JMSU). With open-world visual understanding and task-planning capabilities, vision-language models (VLMs) are promising candidates for JMSU. However, directly applying existing VLMs to JMSU is non-trivial due to scarce cross-scene supervision and attention dispersion caused by long visual context in JMSU. To address these challenges, we propose HUGIN, a training framework with two complementary components. Endogenous Data Augmentation recombines verified atomic facts under operating constraints, while Global Context Ranking aligns the instruction representation more strongly with the complete visual context than with a partial visual context. To support ongoing research, we construct a high-quality industrial sorting dataset and benchmark named SortingBench from four layouts of autonomous logistics sorting systems. Across five open VLMs, HUGIN consistently outperforms matched baselines; for example, the accuracy on SortingBench of Qwen3-VL-8B increases from 63.6% to 78.8%. Additional experiments verify the effectiveness of each component and JMSU's spillover benefits in embodied tasks. Deployment tests involving more than 15,000 packages support the practical viability of VLM-based planning for autonomous logistics sorting.

AI.tldr: They introduce HUGIN, a training framework that makes vision-language models better at planning across multiple camera views in autonomous logistics sorting systems, achieving strong gains on their new SortingBench dataset and working in real-world deployment.
AI.motivation: Autonomous logistics sorting systems need to understand and jointly reason over multiple, spatially separated camera views to plan how to sort packages. Existing vision-language models struggle in this Joint Multi-Scene Understanding (JMSU) setting because there is little labeled data that ties multiple scenes together and long visual inputs cause attention to be spread too thin, hurting performance. The authors want a way to adapt open-world VLMs so they can handle these practical industrial sorting tasks effectively and reliably.
AI.method: They formalize the problem as Joint Multi-Scene Understanding (JMSU) and propose HUGIN, a training framework for VLMs with two key components: (1) Endogenous Data Augmentation, which generates additional training signals by recombining internally verified atomic facts about scenes while respecting real-world operating constraints; and (2) Global Context Ranking, which trains the model so that its instruction representation aligns more strongly with the full, global visual context than with partial views, thereby encouraging joint reasoning across all camera inputs. They also build SortingBench, a curated dataset and benchmark of four different autonomous logistics sorting layouts, and fine-tune five open-source VLMs within this framework.
AI.result: On the SortingBench benchmark, HUGIN consistently improves performance of five open VLMs compared to comparable baselines. For instance, Qwen3-VL-8B’s accuracy on SortingBench rises from 63.6% to 78.8% when trained with HUGIN. Ablation studies show that each component (Endogenous Data Augmentation and Global Context Ranking) contributes to the performance gains. They additionally demonstrate that improving JMSU transfers positively to other embodied tasks and scenarios, indicating broader benefits beyond the core sorting benchmark.
AI.conclusion: The paper concludes that vision-language models, when trained with their HUGIN framework, can successfully handle Joint Multi-Scene Understanding required by autonomous logistics sorting systems. The combination of structured internal data augmentation and global context-aware ranking alleviates issues of scarce multi-scene supervision and attention dilution in long visual contexts. Their SortingBench dataset and extensive experiments, including a real-world deployment involving over 15,000 packages, indicate that VLM-based planning is viable for industrial autonomous logistics sorting and that JMSU is a useful abstraction for studying embodied multi-scene reasoning.

title: Information Abundance Paradox: Long-Context Training Undermines Parametric Knowledge
summary: Large language models are increasingly trained and deployed with long contexts that span documents, code repositories, and interaction histories. This scaling reflects the implicit assumption that training on longer contexts will only help the model by exposing it to richer evidence. We challenge this view by studying how the context window shapes a model's mode of learning, shifting it between parametric internalization and contextualization. We propose the Information Abundance Paradox, which hypothesizes that abundant relevant information in the training context can reduce the incentive to encode that information parametrically, thereby increasing reliance on context. In pretraining with long documents, increasing the context window improves language modeling, natural language understanding, and closed-book MCQA only up to an intermediate optimum, after which performance consistently declines. In supervised fine-tuning, more task-relevant train-time context improves performance with supporting context, but reduces robustness when context is absent or misleading at test time. Our analysis suggests that this behavior arises when longer context provides a lower complexity solution. Mechanistically, training with informative context shifts gradient pressure from feed-forward networks, often linked to parametric knowledge, toward attention modules, and causal interventions show that this shift increases reliance on context during inference. Overall, these findings support the Information Abundance Paradox and suggest that scaling toward near-infinite context is not simply a matter of supplying more data, even when high-quality long-context data is abundant.

AI.tldr: The paper shows that making context windows very long can hurt how well language models learn and remember knowledge, because they start relying too much on the provided context instead of encoding information in their parameters.
AI.motivation: As LLMs get larger context windows, it is usually assumed that more visible information during training and inference can only help. However, it is unclear whether very long, information-rich contexts change *how* models store and use knowledge—specifically, whether they reduce the incentive to internalize knowledge in parameters and instead push models to rely on context. Understanding this trade-off is crucial for designing long-context training strategies and for avoiding unintended degradations in robustness and parametric knowledge.
AI.method: The paper formulates the Information Abundance Paradox and empirically tests it in two settings: (1) pretraining with long documents and (2) supervised fine-tuning with task-relevant context. The authors vary the context window length and the amount of information in context, then evaluate language modeling, NLU, and closed-book MCQA performance, as well as robustness when test-time context is absent or misleading. They analyze model behavior via training dynamics, complexity arguments, gradient distribution across components (feed-forward vs attention), and causal interventions on these components to see how reliance on context vs parametric knowledge changes.
AI.result: They find that increasing context window length helps up to an intermediate optimum, after which performance on language modeling, NLU, and closed-book MCQA declines. In supervised fine-tuning, adding more task-relevant context improves performance when supporting context is present, but reduces robustness when context is removed or misleading at test time. Mechanistic analysis shows that longer, more informative contexts shift gradient pressure away from feed-forward networks towards attention modules, consistent with the model learning lower-complexity, context-dependent solutions and relying less on parametric knowledge during inference.
AI.conclusion: The experiments support the Information Abundance Paradox: abundant relevant information in training context can disincentivize parametric encoding and increase dependence on context. Consequently, simply scaling context windows and feeding more long-context data is not uniformly beneficial and can undermine parametric knowledge and robustness. Effective long-context training will require balancing contextualization with parametric internalization rather than assuming that more context is always better.

title: Making Your LLMs More Objective: Stabilizing LLM Safety Behavior Across Traits with Trait-Invariant Safety Tuning
summary: Aligned large language models (LLMs) are expected to exhibit safety behavior based on the content of the user request: they should refuse unsafe requests and comply with safe ones. However, we show that the same request can elicit substantially different safety decisions under different traits assigned in the system prompt, a failure mode we call trait-induced safety variation. To measure this failure, we introduce refusal-based metrics: Trait-Induced Deviation measures dataset-level deviation from the no-trait baseline, while Trait-Induced Flip Rate measures whether the same request receives different safety decisions across traits. We then provide a representation-level analysis of the mechanism behind trait-induced safety shifts and find that traits perturb the model's safety representations within a low-dimensional subspace. To achieve trait-invariant safety, where safety behavior remains stable across traits, we introduce Trait-Invariant Safety Tuning (TIST), a simple yet effective self-distillation framework that aligns an LLM's trait-conditioned behavior with its no-trait behavior. Guided by our analysis, we further propose Trait-Subspace Neutralization (TraSN), an instantiation of TIST, which enforces invariance only within the identified trait subspace. Experiments show that TraSN improves trait-invariant safety and strengthens harmful-request safety while preserving general capability. Our results highlight traits as an important factor in LLM safety and robust model behavior.

AI.tldr: The paper finds that large language models’ safety responses can change simply based on assigned traits in the system prompt, and proposes methods to make safety behavior stable across traits without hurting overall capability.
AI.motivation: Aligned LLMs are supposed to base their safety decisions only on the content of user requests, but in practice, adding different persona-like traits in the system prompt can cause the model to accept or refuse the same request inconsistently. This undermines reliability and safety evaluation, so the authors aim to quantify and reduce this trait-induced variability.
AI.method: 1) Define two refusal-based metrics: Trait-Induced Deviation to measure dataset-level deviation from a no-trait baseline, and Trait-Induced Flip Rate to measure how often the same request gets different safe/unsafe decisions across traits. 2) Perform a representation-level analysis showing that trait prompts perturb internal safety-related representations mainly in a low-dimensional subspace. 3) Propose Trait-Invariant Safety Tuning (TIST), a self-distillation framework that trains the model so that its trait-conditioned outputs match its no-trait outputs. 4) Introduce Trait-Subspace Neutralization (TraSN), a specific TIST method that only enforces this invariance within the identified low-dimensional “trait subspace.”
AI.result: Empirically, the authors show that LLMs exhibit significant trait-induced variation in safety decisions under different trait prompts. Their TraSN method reduces this variation (improves trait-invariant safety), enhances refusal behavior on harmful requests, and maintains general task performance, outperforming baselines that do not use subspace-based neutralization.
AI.conclusion: Trait prompts are a previously underappreciated source of instability in LLM safety behavior. By analyzing how traits influence internal safety representations and constraining these effects within a low-dimensional subspace, it is possible to make safety responses more consistent across traits while preserving overall capability. Trait-invariant safety should be a design goal for robust aligned LLMs.

title: One Frozen Simulator Is Not Enough: Simulator Collapse in Multi-Agent RL
summary: Multi-agent reinforcement learning for human-AI interaction typically relies on a single large language model to simulate user behavior. We show that this approach systematically fails to generalize, and trace the failure to simulator collapse: because the simulator LLM is mode-collapsed, an LLM policy trained against it overfits to narrow strategies that exploit the simulator's dominant mode, and such a policy transfers poorly to unseen simulators and real users. We formalize this collapse theoretically and propose two complementary solutions, one at inference time and one at training time. The inference-time solution, Verbalized Sampling, broadens the simulator's behavior by sampling from a verbalized response distribution, reducing mode collapse. The training-time solution, Co-Training, jointly optimizes the policy against a population of trainable simulators, preventing it from overfitting to any single simulator's mode. We validate both solutions on three multi-turn benchmarks: Persuasion for Good, $τ^2$-bench, and CooperBench. Verbalized Sampling improves held-out success by up to 9% over single-simulator RL, and Co-Training pushes gains further to 14%; the human study shows similar gain on real users. Both solutions preserve the policy diversity that collapses under single-simulator RL. To support further work in this direction, we release SCOPE, an open-source framework for Population Co-Training multi-agent RL. More broadly, our results suggest that the diversity of the training environment, not only the policy, is critical to the generalization of multi-turn RL to real-world deployment.

AI.tldr: The paper identifies and addresses a generalization failure in multi-agent RL for human-AI interaction caused by using a single LLM simulator, and proposes two methods plus a framework to improve robustness and diversity.
AI.motivation: Multi-agent RL systems for human-AI interaction commonly train policies against a single LLM-based user simulator. However, policies trained this way often perform poorly when deployed to real users or different simulators. The authors aim to understand why this generalization gap occurs and how to fix it, in order to make RL-trained conversational agents more robust and reliable in real-world settings.
AI.method: First, the authors analyze and formalize a phenomenon they call ‘simulator collapse,’ where the LLM user simulator is effectively mode-collapsed, causing the RL policy to overfit to a narrow behavior pattern. They then propose two remedies: (1) Verbalized Sampling (inference-time), which samples user behavior from an explicitly verbalized response distribution to broaden the simulator’s behavior; and (2) Co-Training (training-time), which jointly optimizes the policy against a population of trainable simulators, increasing environmental diversity and discouraging overfitting to any single simulator mode. They implement these methods in SCOPE, an open-source framework for population co-training in multi-agent RL, and evaluate them on three multi-turn benchmarks (Persuasion for Good, τ^2-bench, and CooperBench).
AI.result: On the three benchmarks, Verbalized Sampling yields up to a 9% improvement in held-out success over standard single-simulator RL, while Co-Training further increases gains to 14%. A human user study shows comparable improvements on real users. Additionally, both proposed methods maintain higher policy diversity compared to single-simulator RL, where diversity tends to collapse.
AI.conclusion: Using a single LLM simulator in multi-agent RL for human-AI interaction induces simulator collapse and harms generalization. Increasing the diversity of the training environment—via Verbalized Sampling and population-based Co-Training—substantially improves transfer to new simulators and real users while preserving policy diversity. The SCOPE framework facilitates further research in this direction. Overall, the work underscores that the diversity and structure of the training environment are as important as the policy architecture itself for successful real-world multi-turn RL deployment.

title: Proportional Analogies on Probability Distributions via Bayesian Updating
summary: Analogies are quaternary relations of the form "A is to B as C is to D". Among the various formalizations of analogical reasoning, proportional analogies provide an important axiomatic framework by characterizing valid analogies through a set of postulates. While proportional analogies have been extensively studied over Boolean, symbolic, and real-valued domains, their extension to probability distributions remains largely unexplored. In this paper, we introduce a notion of proportional analogy for probability distributions based on Bayesian updating. Our approach builds upon the idea that two distributions are related whenever one can be transformed into the other through Bayesian updating induced by a suitable set of observations. We investigate this framework for several standard members of the exponential family and discuss how it naturally extends to arbitrary probability distributions through Gaussian mixture approximations.

AI.tldr: Paper defines proportional analogies between probability distributions using Bayesian updating.
AI.motivation: Extend the well-studied framework of proportional analogies (A:B::C:D) from Boolean, symbolic, and real-valued settings to the largely unexplored domain of probability distributions.
AI.method: Define an analogy relation between distributions where one can be obtained from another via Bayesian updating with suitable observations; instantiate and study this construction for common exponential-family distributions and extend to general distributions via Gaussian mixture approximations.
AI.result: A formal notion of proportional analogy over probability distributions is proposed and analyzed for standard exponential-family members, with a demonstrated path to handle arbitrary distributions using Gaussian mixtures.
AI.conclusion: Bayesian updating provides a natural and principled mechanism to define proportional analogies between probability distributions, and the framework is broadly applicable via exponential-family models and Gaussian mixture approximations.

title: A Cascaded Unsupervised-Supervised NLP Pipeline for Detecting Accusatory Language in Public Procurement
summary: Public procurement involves the allocation of substantial financial resources; therefore, continuous oversight through audits, controls, and monitoring mechanisms is essential. However, stakeholder comments and publicly available government data are often underutilized, despite their potential to reveal procedural irregularities. To address this gap, this paper analyzes metadata from Ecuador's Sistema Oficial de Contratación Pública (SOCE, Official Public Procurement System), with particular emphasis on participant comments generated during the pre-contractual phase. We propose a hybrid modeling framework that integrates unsupervised clustering and supervised classification within a natural language processing (NLP) pipeline to uncover latent patterns and detect potentially irregular procurement processes. Semantic embeddings are generated using Word2Vec, LLaMA, and RoBERTa, followed by Gaussian Mixture Models (GMMs) for unsupervised clustering. A supervised classification stage is then applied to identify accusatory or whistleblowing-style comments. Experimental results show that the combination of domain-trained Word2Vec embeddings, GMM-based clustering, and a Random Forest classifier achieves high precision and recall, even under severe class imbalance. These findings demonstrate that lightweight, domain-adapted NLP architectures can effectively support risk identification and enhance transparency in public procurement systems without requiring large-scale computational infrastructure.

AI.tldr: The paper develops an NLP-based hybrid framework to detect potential irregularities in public procurement using stakeholder comments and procurement metadata from Ecuador’s SOCE platform.
AI.motivation: Public procurement uses large amounts of public funds and requires strong oversight. Traditional audits underuse rich, unstructured information like stakeholder comments and open data that could highlight irregularities or risks. There is a need for scalable, cost‑effective tools that can mine this data to flag suspicious processes early, especially in resource‑constrained settings.
AI.method: The authors analyze metadata and pre‑contractual phase comments from Ecuador’s SOCE system. They build a hybrid NLP pipeline that combines unsupervised and supervised learning. First, they generate semantic text embeddings using domain‑trained Word2Vec and large language model–based embeddings (LLaMA, RoBERTa). Then they apply Gaussian Mixture Models (GMMs) for unsupervised clustering to discover latent structure in the comments. Finally, they perform supervised classification (with models like Random Forest) to detect accusatory or whistleblowing‑style comments, addressing severe class imbalance in the data.
AI.result: The best performance is obtained using domain‑specific Word2Vec embeddings, GMM clustering, and a Random Forest classifier. This configuration yields high precision and recall in identifying accusatory or whistleblowing comments despite strong class imbalance, outperforming other tested combinations involving LLaMA and RoBERTa embeddings.
AI.conclusion: Lightweight, domain‑adapted NLP architectures can effectively extract risk signals from public procurement comments and metadata without requiring heavy computational resources. The proposed framework can support early risk identification and enhance transparency in procurement systems, particularly in contexts where large‑scale AI infrastructure is not feasible.

title: Harness-IF: Evaluating Instruction Following Across Instruction Surfaces in Coding Agents
summary: When a coding agent obeys a rule, it may simply have been going to do that anyway. Existing instruction-following benchmarks cannot tell the difference: they concentrate rules in the user turn, while coding-agent benchmarks emphasize final task success. We introduce Harness-IF, which scores operational rules one at a time from execution evidence: 60 realistic multi-turn coding items drawn from a 642-rule library, 256 rules receiving verdicts, placed on the five configurable surfaces a deployed agent reads. To separate compliance from coincidence we introduce Against-Prior Accuracy (AP-Acc), which scores only rules labeled as opposing unprompted defaults, observed by re-running tasks with the rule withheld across nine probe builds and curated otherwise. Across 12 frontier models, accuracy spans 72.1-85.9% and AP-Acc 66.1-78.6%; every model is worse on against-prior rules, by 3.6 to 7.4 points (mean 5.81), and the direction survives a common-support analysis with item-clustered intervals. Aggregate scores therefore overstate compliance by a model-specific margin: prior control leaves the top build unchanged and exchanges three adjacent rank pairs. A counterbalanced conflict pilot on nine separate builds adds a second result: pooled precedence does not follow prompt depth, with system prompts, project files, and user instructions ahead of tool and skill descriptions.

AI.tldr: The paper presents Harness-IF, a benchmark to separate true instruction-following from coincidental behavior in coding agents, introducing Against-Prior Accuracy to measure compliance on rules that go against a model’s default behavior.
AI.motivation: Existing instruction-following and coding benchmarks cannot distinguish whether a model follows a rule because of the instruction itself or because it would have done that by default. This leads to inflated views of agents’ true controllability and instruction adherence.
AI.method: The authors design Harness-IF, a benchmark of 60 realistic multi-turn coding tasks linked to a library of 642 operational rules, of which 256 receive scored verdicts. Rules are placed on five prompt “surfaces” (e.g., system prompts, project files). To isolate genuine compliance, they introduce Against-Prior Accuracy (AP-Acc) by identifying rules that contradict the model’s unprompted default behavior via rerunning tasks without the rule across nine probe builds and manual curation. They evaluate 12 frontier models on both standard accuracy and AP-Acc, and also run a counterbalanced conflict experiment to probe precedence between different instruction surfaces.
AI.result: Across 12 frontier models, overall rule-following accuracy ranges from 72.1–85.9%, while AP-Acc is lower at 66.1–78.6% for all models. Each model performs worse on against-prior rules by 3.6–7.4 percentage points on average (mean 5.81). A common-support analysis with item-clustered intervals confirms that this gap is robust. Adjusting for prior-driven behavior changes overall rankings only modestly but shows that aggregate scores systematically overstate true controllability. The conflict pilot finds that models prioritize instructions from system prompts, project files, and user instructions over tool and skill descriptions, and that this precedence does not simply track prompt depth.
AI.conclusion: Harness-IF reveals that existing benchmarks overestimate instruction-following in coding agents by failing to separate true compliance from default behavior. Against-Prior Accuracy provides a more realistic measure of controllability, and the observed precedence ordering of instruction sources suggests that model behavior is sensitive to where rules are placed, not just how “deep” in the prompt they appear.

title: Structural Silence: When AI Infrastructure Fails Speakers of Underrepresented Languages
comment: An associated poster version of this work was presented at the 69th Annual Conference of the International Linguistic Association (ILA 2026), New York, NY, April 30-May 2, 2026
summary:
Artificial intelligence tools for education and language support are increasingly framed as scalable responses to access gaps in under-resourced communities. Yet the infrastructure underlying these tools, including training corpora, tokenization schemes, evaluation benchmarks, and deployment architectures, can systematically disadvantage speakers of underrepresented languages before a model is trained.
  This paper examines these structural barriers through Bengali, one of the world's most widely spoken languages, focusing on AI-assisted education in low-connectivity environments. We identify four interlocking failures: a severe web presence gap, with Bengali accounting for less than 0.5% of global web content despite representing nearly 4% of the global population; a 67:1 training-token deficit between English and Bengali in major multilingual corpora; a tokenization penalty associated with Bengali's alphasyllabary script that compounds the data deficit through higher token fertility; and connectivity exclusion, with individual internet penetration at 36.5% in rural areas compared with 71.4% in urban areas.
  These failures reflect longstanding resource-allocation decisions, institutional priorities, and design defaults that did not center underrepresented languages in mainstream AI development. We argue that dataset scarcity should be understood as a structural barrier rather than an isolated technical limitation, and that offline-first design should be treated as an equity-oriented infrastructure strategy. We conclude with directions for linguistics and AI research aimed at reducing these structural inequalities.

AI.tldr: The paper argues that current AI infrastructures (data, tokenization, benchmarks, connectivity assumptions) structurally disadvantage Bengali and similar underrepresented languages, undermining AI-assisted education, and proposes treating data scarcity and offline-first design as core equity and infrastructure issues.
AI.motivation: Although AI tools are promoted as scalable solutions to educational access gaps in under-resourced communities, their underlying infrastructure is primarily built around dominant languages like English. This leads to systemic disadvantages for widely spoken but under-resourced languages such as Bengali, especially in low-connectivity settings. The paper is motivated by the need to unpack and quantify these hidden structural barriers so that equity-focused AI for education can be meaningfully developed for such communities.
AI.method: The authors use Bengali as a case study to interrogate the AI infrastructure stack relevant to education: (1) they quantify Bengali’s representation on the web relative to its share of the global population; (2) they compare the volume of Bengali versus English training tokens in major multilingual corpora to demonstrate a training-token deficit; (3) they analyze tokenization behavior for Bengali’s alphasyllabary script to show a tokenization penalty (higher token fertility) that further amplifies the data gap; and (4) they examine connectivity statistics, contrasting rural and urban internet penetration to reveal connectivity exclusion in deployment contexts. This yields a conceptual framework of four interlocking failures rather than a single technical shortfall.
AI.result: The study finds: (1) a large web presence gap, where Bengali makes up less than 0.5% of global web content despite nearly 4% of the global population; (2) a severe 67:1 deficit in training tokens between English and Bengali in major multilingual datasets; (3) a tokenization penalty rooted in Bengali’s script, which results in more tokens per unit of text and effectively deepens the data scarcity; and (4) connectivity exclusion, with rural internet penetration at 36.5% versus 71.4% in urban areas, limiting practical access to AI tools in the very communities they are meant to serve.
AI.conclusion: The authors conclude that these four failures—web content underrepresentation, training-token deficits, tokenization penalties, and connectivity exclusion—are manifestations of structural, historically rooted decisions in AI data collection, modeling, and deployment, not merely incidental technical issues. They argue that dataset scarcity should be framed as a structural barrier tied to institutional and infrastructural priorities. As a remedy, they propose treating offline-first design as a central equity strategy in AI for education and call for targeted research in linguistics and AI to systematically address these structural inequalities for Bengali and other underrepresented languages.

title: HyperANFIS: Enhancing Rule Representation and Interpretability in Adaptive Neuro-Fuzzy Systems via Hyperbolic Geometry
summary: The adaptive neuro-fuzzy inference system (ANFIS) is an interpretable reasoning framework capable of generating explicit IF-THEN fuzzy rules, making it suitable for tasks requiring transparent reasoning. However, existing ANFIS models generally construct rule antecedents and perform inference in Euclidean space, limiting their representational capacity and predictive performance. To address this issue, we propose Hyperbolic ANFIS (HyperANFIS), a hyperbolic extension of ANFIS. HyperANFIS preserves the fuzzy semantics and core architecture of conventional ANFIS while performing rule-prototype learning, rule activation, and consequent aggregation in hyperbolic space. It also retains the ability to generate interpretable IF-THEN rules. By exploiting the representational properties of hyperbolic geometry, HyperANFIS strengthens the fuzzy inference process, thereby improving predictive accuracy, inter-rule collaboration, and the credibility of its interpretable rules. Experimental results show that HyperANFIS consistently outperforms the standard ANFIS baseline and various ANFIS variants across all datasets, while also generating higher-quality fuzzy rules.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes HyperANFIS, a hyperbolic-geometry extension of the traditional Adaptive Neuro-Fuzzy Inference System (ANFIS), to improve predictive accuracy and rule quality while maintaining interpretability.
AI.motivation: Traditional ANFIS operates in Euclidean space, which limits its capacity to model complex, hierarchically structured or tree-like data, reducing both representational power and predictive performance.
AI.method: Extend ANFIS to hyperbolic space by redefining key components—rule-prototype learning, rule activation, and consequent aggregation—under hyperbolic geometry while preserving fuzzy semantics and the core ANFIS architecture, so that explicit IF-THEN fuzzy rules remain interpretable.
AI.result: Across multiple datasets, HyperANFIS consistently surpasses standard ANFIS and various ANFIS variants in predictive performance and produces fuzzy rules that are judged to be of higher quality and more credible.
AI.conclusion: Using hyperbolic geometry within the ANFIS framework enhances the fuzzy inference process, leading to better predictive accuracy, improved collaboration among rules, and more trustworthy, interpretable IF-THEN rules compared with Euclidean-based ANFIS models.

title: The Sleeping Agent: What Gist-Based Context Compression Loses and Why
comment: 7 pages, 5 tables, appendices. Code and results at https://github.com/kyrkewood/sleeping-agent
summary: Gist-based context compression---summarising older conversation history into compact representations---is a common approach in long-horizon language model agents, yet its effect on different types of memory retrieval is poorly understood. We use Salience-Weighted Consolidation (SWC), a biologically-inspired compression framework motivated by sleep-based memory consolidation, as a diagnostic probe to study when gist compression helps and when it hurts. SWC scores conversation history by salience, partitions it into priority tiers, and applies structured gist abstraction to mid-priority content. Evaluating four conditions on all ten LoCoMo conversations---1,935 matched text-only questions in total, 1,501 used in the primary aggregate after excluding Category 5 (adversarial) questions---at temperature 0, we find a consistent task-type interaction: gist compression substantially outperforms truncation on multi-hop reasoning and single-hop factual questions, but temporal questions remain substantially harder under compression, with compressed conditions scoring well below the full-context reference on the conversations where both are evaluated. We trace this failure to a specific mechanism: the gist abstraction prompt preserves relational and event structure while discarding dates and times. A preservation analysis across all ten conversations confirms the mechanism: an approximately 20-fold increase in temporal expression preservation (3.05% to 62.39%) with a one-sentence prompt modification, while named entity and event preservation rates barely change (x1.02 and x1.11), demonstrating that the fix is a precision instrument. The prompt modification recovers +0.314 [0.254, 0.375] judge accuracy on category-2 (temporal) questions in the matched set. Code and results: https://github.com/kyrkewood/sleeping-agent.

AI.tldr: The paper studies how gist-based context compression in language model agents affects different types of memory retrieval, using a biologically inspired framework called Salience-Weighted Consolidation (SWC). It finds that while gist compression helps multi-hop and factual QA versus simple truncation, it harms temporal reasoning because dates/times are discarded, and shows that a small prompt tweak can precisely fix this temporal failure without hurting other information types.
AI.motivation: Long-horizon language model agents often need to handle very long conversation histories that exceed context windows. A common workaround is gist-based compression, where older history is summarized into a compact form. However, it is unclear when such compression actually helps retrieval and reasoning and when it damages performance, especially across different task types (multi-hop, factual, temporal, adversarial, etc.). The authors are motivated to systematically diagnose the effects of gist compression, drawing inspiration from sleep-based memory consolidation in humans, and to understand specific failure modes and how to mitigate them.
AI.method: The authors use Salience-Weighted Consolidation (SWC), a biologically inspired compression framework, as a diagnostic tool. SWC assigns salience scores to pieces of conversation history, partitions the history into priority tiers, and then applies structured gist abstraction to mid-priority content while presumably keeping high-priority content more verbatim. They evaluate language model performance under four different context conditions across all ten LoCoMo benchmark conversations, yielding 1,935 matched text-only questions (1,501 in the primary analysis after excluding adversarial category-5 questions). At temperature 0, they compare truncation, full context, and SWC-based compressed contexts on question answering performance for different categories, with particular focus on temporal (category-2) questions. They also conduct a preservation analysis measuring how well different information types (temporal expressions, named entities, events) survive the compression, and then modify the gist abstraction prompt to better preserve temporal expressions and re-evaluate.
AI.result: The experiments show a task-type interaction with gist compression. Compared to simple truncation, SWC-style gist compression substantially improves performance on multi-hop reasoning and single-hop factual questions. However, temporal questions (category-2) perform much worse under compression than with full, uncompressed context on the same conversations. The authors identify the key mechanism: the gist abstraction prompt preserves relational and event structure but systematically discards dates and times, which are crucial for temporal reasoning. In the preservation analysis, they demonstrate that a minimal one-sentence modification to the abstraction prompt produces an approximately 20-fold increase in temporal expression preservation, from 3.05% to 62.39%, while barely affecting named entity and event preservation (multipliers of about 1.02 and 1.11). This prompt change leads to a substantial gain of +0.314 in judged accuracy on temporal (category-2) questions, with a confidence interval [0.254, 0.375], on the matched question set.
AI.conclusion: The paper concludes that gist-based context compression is not uniformly beneficial: it helps for multi-hop and factual retrieval but can severely harm temporal reasoning if temporal information is not explicitly preserved. Salience-Weighted Consolidation provides a useful diagnostic framework to reveal such differentiated effects across task types. A small, targeted prompt modification that instructs the compression process to retain temporal expressions can largely fix the temporal failure mode without degrading preservation of other information, demonstrating that gist compression can be tuned as a precise, task-aware instrument rather than a blunt summarization tool. This has implications for designing long-horizon language model agents that rely on compressed memory.

title: Agent Skills Can Be Harmful: An Empirical Study of Skill-Induced Failures in LLM Agents
summary: Agent skills are the de facto mechanism for extending LLM agents with reusable guidance. A skill can shape the agent's task execution, including planning, tool use, problem-solving, and validation. Prior work reported mixed results of agent skills: some skills improve task success rates, while others have no effect, increase token use and execution time, and even reduce success rates. This paper presents a comprehensive analysis of skill-induced agent failures by attributing task failures and cost regressions to specific loaded skills. We introduce a differential analysis framework that attributes a failure or regression to a skill by comparing a target skill-guided run against a no-skill or semantically matched skill reference run that solves the same task, or solves it more cheaply. We instantiate this framework on SkillsBench and SWE-Skills-Bench, yielding 307 skill-induced failures, including 125 functional failures and 182 efficiency regressions. We also build SkillTriage, a taxonomy-guided attribution tool that normalizes paired cases, extracts differential evidence, and produces triage reports. Our major findings include: (1) Skill induced functional failures are rarely caused by obviously irrelevant skills; instead, seemingly relevant skills often make the agent incorrectly implement or omit task-required implementation elements. (2) Skill-induced efficiency regressions are not explained by prompt length alone. (3) The largest sources within Excessive Procedure are excessive verification and heavy implementation pipelines, contributing 67 and 30 cases, respectively. This shows that skills often turn validation checklists and construction recipes into mandatory work. Based on our findings, we propose research topics and tooling improvements for safer and more cost-aware skill reuse.

AI.tldr: The paper analyzes when and how reusable agent skills in LLM agents hurt performance, building a differential-analysis framework and taxonomy to attribute failures and cost regressions to specific skills, and extracting design lessons for safer, more efficient skill reuse.
AI.motivation: LLM agents are often extended with reusable skills that are intended to guide behavior (planning, tool use, validation, etc.), but empirical results show mixed or even negative impact: some skills lower success rates or increase cost and latency. There is little systematic understanding of why seemingly useful skills sometimes cause functional failures or efficiency regressions. The paper aims to provide a principled way to attribute such failures to specific skills and to characterize common failure modes, so that skills can be designed, selected, and reused more safely and cost-effectively.
AI.method: The authors propose a differential analysis framework that compares an agent run using a particular skill (the target) with a reference run that solves the same task either without that skill or with a semantically matched alternative skill. By contrasting these paired runs, they attribute functional failures and efficiency regressions to specific skills. They instantiate this framework on two benchmarks, SkillsBench and SWE-Skills-Bench, and systematically collect cases where skill use leads to failure or higher cost.
