They then introduce SkillTriage, a taxonomy-guided tool that normalizes the paired traces, extracts differential evidence, and categorizes each case into a structured taxonomy of failure and regression types, supporting semi-automated triage reports.
AI.result: Applied to SkillsBench and SWE-Skills-Bench, the framework identifies 307 skill-induced failures: 125 functional failures (where tasks that could be solved without the skill now fail) and 182 efficiency regressions (where tasks become more expensive in tokens/time). The analysis shows that these issues are often caused by skills that appear relevant, not obviously irrelevant ones. Efficiency regressions cannot be explained by prompt length alone; instead, skills frequently induce excessive verification steps and heavy implementation pipelines—labeled under “Excessive Procedure”—with 67 and 30 cases, respectively. The study thus quantifies how and where skills degrade performance and cost efficiency.
AI.conclusion: The paper concludes that reusable skills for LLM agents are double-edged: even seemingly relevant skills can cause agents to omit or misimplement required elements and to perform unnecessary, costly work. Failures are rarely due to trivial irrelevance and cannot be diagnosed by prompt length alone. A differential, taxonomy-guided attribution approach like SkillTriage is effective for identifying and characterizing skill-induced problems. The authors advocate for new research and tooling to make skill reuse safer and more cost-aware, for example by detecting excessive procedure, decoupling optional checklists from mandatory execution, and more carefully evaluating skills’ impact before deployment.

title: Policy-as-logic for robust reasoning over rules
summary: In many practical applications of generative AI systems, from tax rules to airline baggage allowance, responses to natural language queries must respect written policies or rules. We present a hybrid symbolic approach that expresses policies in formal logic and at inference time exploits the representation power of language models for fact extraction to ground predicates, and an answer set solver for reasoning such that responses are interpretable, auditable, and as we show, accurate and robust under input perturbations. Specifically, we show this separation of extraction and reasoning steps outperforms policy-as-prompt and policy-as-code methods in most cases with ~10x reduction in token usage. The results point to the value of structured reasoning and symbolic solvers in conjunction with generative models to make robust decisions involving objective criteria.

AI.tldr: A hybrid system uses LLMs for fact extraction and symbolic logic solvers for policy reasoning, yielding interpretable, robust, and efficient policy-compliant answers.
AI.motivation: Generative AI must often follow precise written policies (e.g., tax rules, baggage allowance), but direct prompting or ad‑hoc code tends to be brittle, opaque, and token‑hungry. There is a need for methods that strictly respect policies, remain interpretable/auditable, and are robust to input variations.
AI.method: Encode policies as formal logic. At inference time, (1) use a language model to extract relevant facts from the natural language query and map them to logical predicates; (2) feed these grounded predicates into an answer set solver that performs the reasoning and produces compliant decisions/answers. Compare this hybrid approach against policy-as-prompt and policy-as-code baselines, measuring accuracy, robustness, and token usage.
AI.result: The hybrid symbolic–neural method generally outperforms policy-as-prompt and policy-as-code approaches on policy-compliance tasks and is more robust to input perturbations, while reducing token usage by about 10×. Outputs are also interpretable and auditable due to the explicit logical reasoning.
AI.conclusion: Separating language-based fact extraction from symbolic reasoning is an effective strategy for policy-compliant decision making. Combining LLMs with structured reasoning and answer set solvers yields more accurate, robust, efficient, and transparent behavior than purely prompt-based or purely code-based policy implementations.

title: OEIS Open: How many conjectures can language models turn into theorems?
summary: We construct OEIS Open, a benchmark based on 492 open mathematical conjectures from the OEIS, formalized in Lean by Tsoukalas et al. Whereas these conjectures had previously been attempted only with a bespoke agent, our open-source evaluation code runs any generic language model (LM) against them, and is secure against LM cheating attempts. We find that LMs equipped with a minimal set of tools resolve 147 of these conjectures with a budget of \$50 per attempt, scoring 30% on OEIS Open. OEIS Open Lite is a random subset of 100 conjectures for cheaper evaluation. When evaluated with a budget of \$200 per attempt, the best current LM scores 44% on OEIS Open Lite. Giving LMs access to the mathematics literature via 476,000 papers from arXiv did not increase performance on OEIS Open Lite, and nor did using more sophisticated agent loops. The conjectures covered in this work are of uncertain mathematical significance, and most have likely received little previous attention. Nevertheless, our results show that LMs can resolve open research conjectures autonomously and at modest cost.

AI.tldr: They build OEIS Open, a formal Lean benchmark of 492 open OEIS conjectures, and show current language-model agents can autonomously resolve a non-trivial fraction of them at modest cost.
AI.motivation: Prior work formalized many OEIS conjectures in Lean but evaluated only a bespoke agent, with no open, LM-agnostic, cheating-resistant benchmark for "automated theorem proving on genuinely open problems." The authors want a standardized way to test whether modern LMs plus tools can actually solve unsolved, formalized math conjectures, not just textbook problems, and to do so reproducibly and securely.
AI.method: They take 492 conjectures from OEIS that were already formalized in Lean, package them into OEIS Open, and build open-source evaluation code that can run arbitrary LMs equipped with a minimal toolset (Lean, search, etc.) under a fixed dollar-budget per attempt and with safeguards against cheating (e.g., accessing ground-truth solutions). They also define OEIS Open Lite, a random subset of 100 conjectures for cheaper runs. They run a variety of LM agents, with and without access to a large arXiv math corpus and with different agent-loop complexities, and measure the fraction of conjectures formally resolved within the budget limits.
AI.result: With a roughly $50-per-problem budget and simple tools, the best LM agents can formally resolve 147 of 492 conjectures (30%) on OEIS Open. On OEIS Open Lite, with a higher budget of about $200 per conjecture, the top LM reaches 44% solved. Neither giving access to 476k arXiv math papers nor more sophisticated agent loops led to further performance gains on OEIS Open Lite.
AI.conclusion: The benchmark demonstrates that contemporary LMs, using straightforward tool integrations and within modest cost limits, are already capable of autonomously resolving a significant portion of genuinely open, formalized mathematical conjectures. However, additional external literature and more complex agent designs do not yet translate into improved performance, and the mathematical importance of the solved conjectures is uncertain. Still, OEIS Open provides a reproducible, cheating-resistant standard for future evaluation and highlights the emerging potential of LMs as tools for open mathematical research.

title: ExRole: From Team Trajectories to Executable Roles in Multi-Agent Language Models
summary: Roles provide an interpretable interface for organizing language-model agents, yet most multi-agent systems treat them as hand-written prompt labels disconnected from learned behavior and parameter updates. We argue that a useful role should instead be an executable control variable: it should summarize behavior predictive of future utility, guide subsequent interaction, and identify the trainable capacity responsible for that behavior. We introduce ExRole, a trajectory-to-role framework that learns future-aware role prototypes from prefix-local team traces, resolves them into readable instructions and token-aligned role markers, and optionally routes shared LoRA rank slots with turn-aligned credit. Across MuSiQue and 2WikiMultiHopQA, ExRole improves over single-agent search by 15.0/14.4 and 13.5/16.1 EM/F1 points, respectively. Against the strongest non-ExRole controls, the corresponding gains remain 11.5/11.6 and 7.7/9.7 points. Across both benchmarks, the controlled results consistently favor trajectory-induced role conditioning over role-free, manual, random, and shuffled alternatives. Role-Agent-Turn interventions further show that the induced roles capture transferable behavioral specialization beyond fixed agent identities or turn positions.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes ExRole, a framework that turns abstract “roles” in multi-agent language-model systems into executable, learned control variables that improve multi-hop QA performance.
AI.motivation: Existing multi-agent language-model systems typically use roles as static, hand-written prompt labels that do not tightly connect to the actual learned behavior or model parameters. This limits interpretability, control, and the ability to leverage roles for better coordination and learning. The authors aim to make roles operational: roles should summarize behavior that predicts future utility, guide how agents interact next, and localize which parts of the model are responsible, thereby enabling more effective and interpretable multi-agent LLM systems.
AI.method: They introduce ExRole, a trajectory-to-role learning framework. From team interaction traces, ExRole infers future-aware role prototypes using only prefix-local information. These prototypes are then turned into (1) human-readable role instructions and (2) token-aligned role markers that condition the model during inference. Additionally, ExRole can route shared LoRA (Low-Rank Adaptation) rank slots based on dialogue turns, assigning credit and specialization to particular roles. The framework is evaluated in multi-agent settings on MuSiQue and 2WikiMultiHopQA benchmarks, comparing against single-agent search and several non-ExRole role baselines (manual, random, shuffled, or role-free).
AI.result: On MuSiQue and 2WikiMultiHopQA, ExRole substantially boosts exact match (EM) and F1 scores over a strong single-agent search baseline: +15.0/14.4 EM/F1 on MuSiQue, and +13.5/16.1 EM/F1 on 2WikiMultiHopQA. Relative to the strongest non-ExRole multi-agent controls, ExRole still yields large gains: +11.5/11.6 EM/F1 on MuSiQue and +7.7/9.7 EM/F1 on 2WikiMultiHopQA. Experiments show that systems conditioned on trajectory-induced roles consistently outperform role-free, manual, random, and shuffled-role variants. Role-Agent-Turn intervention studies indicate that the learned roles encode transferable behavioral specialization that is not reducible to fixed agent IDs or turn positions.
AI.conclusion: Turning roles into learned, executable control variables via ExRole leads to more effective and specialized multi-agent LLM behavior than using static or ad-hoc role labels. By inducing roles from interaction trajectories and tying them to both instructions and parameter routing, the framework improves multi-hop QA performance and reveals interpretable, transferable specializations. The work suggests that future multi-agent LLM systems should learn roles directly from behavior traces rather than relying on manually assigned or loosely defined roles.

title: Retry, Switch, or Abstain? Learning Strategy-Aware Tool-Use Policies via Controlled Error Injection
summary: Tool-using LLM agents are commonly trained and evaluated in environments where tool calls succeed reliably, yet deployed tools can fail transiently, persistently, or silently. Robust recovery therefore requires more than repeated retries: an agent may need to retry the same path, switch to an alternative, or recognize that no viable path remains. We present BENCH2ROBUST, a framework that converts failure-free tool-use benchmarks into controlled stochastic environments with scenario-controlled solvability, where episodes explicitly require retrying, switching, or stopping after available paths are exhausted. We use BENCH2ROBUST to study two complementary interventions: structured runtime recovery context through Bayesian Tool Memory (BTM), and curriculum-controlled reinforcement learning. Across 7 models from 4 families and two multi-turn benchmark families, tool failures produce a near-universal robustness gap. On held-out Retail tasks, BTM improves robustness by up to 16.8 percentage points without retraining, while RL learns complementary recovery behavior that remains beneficial without inference-time BTM. Combining the two reaches 40.8-45.5% under injection while preserving failure-free performance. These results suggest that robust tool use benefits from combining environment-specific recovery knowledge with learned recovery behavior.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces BENCH2ROBUST, a framework to evaluate and improve the robustness of tool-using LLM agents under realistic tool failures, and shows that combining a Bayesian Tool Memory with RL-based training significantly improves recovery from failures while preserving normal performance.
AI.motivation: Most tool-using LLM agents are developed and tested assuming tools almost always work, but in real deployments tools can fail intermittently, permanently, or in subtle ways. Simple retry logic is inadequate: agents must decide when to retry, switch tools, or give up. Existing benchmarks thus overestimate robustness and do not systematically test recovery strategies. A new framework is needed to stress-test and improve agents’ behavior under diverse, controllable failure patterns.
AI.method: 1) Propose BENCH2ROBUST, which transforms existing failure-free tool-use benchmarks into stochastic environments with configurable tool failure processes and known solvability, generating scenarios that require retrying, switching tools, or terminating. 2) Introduce Bayesian Tool Memory (BTM), a structured context mechanism that tracks and summarizes past tool outcomes to inform future calls without retraining. 3) Apply curriculum-controlled reinforcement learning so agents can learn recovery strategies in increasingly challenging failure environments. 4) Evaluate 7 LLMs from 4 model families on two multi-turn benchmark families, measuring robustness gaps and the effect of BTM, RL, and their combination, including held-out Retail tasks and injected-failure settings.
AI.result: They find a consistent robustness gap across all 7 evaluated models: performance drops substantially when tool failures are injected, even though tasks remain solvable. On held-out Retail tasks, Bayesian Tool Memory alone improves robustness by up to 16.8 percentage points without any model retraining. RL training learns additional, complementary recovery behavior that continues to help even when BTM is not used at inference. When BTM and RL are combined, task success under injected failures reaches about 40.8–45.5%, while performance on failure-free benchmarks is preserved.
AI.conclusion: Tool-using LLM agents are significantly less robust to realistic tool failures than standard benchmarks suggest. Robust behavior requires more than naive retries and benefits from both explicit, environment-specific state tracking (BTM) and learned recovery policies (RL). The BENCH2ROBUST framework provides a systematic way to create and evaluate such failure scenarios, and the experiments indicate that combining structured memory of tool reliability with learned strategies substantially improves recovery without hurting performance when tools behave ideally.

title: Claim-Level Reliability Assessment for Efficient Test-Time Reasoning
summary: We propose claim-level falsification as a principle for test-time scaling and instantiate it through Claim-Level Reliability Assessment (CLR), a training-free framework that reallocates test-time compute from additional solution sampling to targeted verification. Since whole-trace evaluation often obscures decisive errors due to signal dilution from routine tokens, CLR condenses each reasoning trace into a compact set of decision-critical claims, thereby isolating its logical anchors. Furthermore, recognizing the inherent difficulty of generating entirely correct solutions under fixed model capabilities, CLR shifts the focus to semantic falsification. This approach exploits a fundamental asymmetry between solution construction and claim refutation. Constructing a valid solution requires a flawless reasoning path, whereas refuting an incorrect claim requires identifying only a single decisive flaw. This targeted search for negative evidence systematically compresses the survival space of high-confidence incorrect traces, effectively suppressing erroneous consensus via nonlinear reliability scoring. Across four LLMs and four reasoning benchmarks under matched budgets, CLR generally improves upon pass@1 and self-consistency. On GPT-OSS-20B/CMIMC25, for instance, CLR exceeds pass@1 by 27.15 percentage-points and raises self-consistency accuracy from 77.50\% to 82.19\% with 37.0\% fewer tokens.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces Claim-Level Reliability Assessment (CLR), a training-free test-time framework that reallocates compute from generating many full solutions to selectively verifying key claims within each reasoning trace, substantially improving reliability and accuracy under fixed budgets.
AI.motivation: Reasoning-focused LLM benchmarks often rely on generating multiple complete solution traces (e.g., self-consistency) and scoring them holistically. This whole-trace evaluation dilutes error signals because most tokens are routine and non-decisive, making it difficult to detect critical logical mistakes. Moreover, achieving fully correct solutions is inherently hard for models with fixed capabilities, limiting gains from pure sampling. The authors are motivated to find a more computationally efficient and logically targeted way to improve test-time reliability by identifying and falsifying crucial reasoning errors at the claim level instead of relying on more sampling or coarse sequence-level checks.
AI.method: The authors propose claim-level falsification as a principle for test-time scaling and instantiate it in a training-free framework called Claim-Level Reliability Assessment (CLR). CLR first parses each reasoning trace into a compact set of decision-critical claims that act as the logical anchors of the solution. Instead of sampling more full reasoning traces, CLR uses the remaining compute to perform semantic verification: it attempts to falsify each critical claim by searching for decisive counterevidence or logical flaws. The core idea exploits an asymmetry between solution construction and refutation: building a correct solution requires all steps to be sound, whereas refuting an incorrect claim only requires finding one clear error. CLR then aggregates the falsification outcomes into a nonlinear reliability score that downweights or eliminates traces whose key claims are successfully challenged, thereby reducing the survival of high-confidence but incorrect solutions.
AI.result: Across four large language models and four reasoning benchmarks, CLR consistently improves performance over standard test-time methods such as pass@1 and self-consistency under matched compute budgets. In a representative example on GPT-OSS-20B evaluated on the CMIMC25 benchmark, CLR boosts accuracy by 27.15 percentage points over pass@1. Relative to self-consistency, CLR increases accuracy from 77.50% to 82.19% while using 37.0% fewer tokens, demonstrating both increased reliability and better compute efficiency.
AI.conclusion: The paper concludes that reallocating test-time compute from more solution sampling to targeted claim-level verification substantially enhances the reliability of LLM reasoning without additional training. By focusing on semantic falsification of decision-critical claims, CLR effectively suppresses erroneous consensus and improves accuracy and efficiency compared to existing decoding and self-consistency approaches. This establishes claim-level falsification as a promising principle for scalable, training-free test-time reliability improvements in reasoning LLMs.

title: CTBench: Evaluating Troubleshooting Capabilities of AI Agents in Realistic Telecom Network Operations
summary: Agents are increasingly considered for automating network operations and maintenance, where engineers must diagnose network faults, optimize configurations to enhance services, and reduce operational costs while acting under strict constraints. However, existing evaluations fail to accurately model real network characteristics or assess agents under partially observable telecom environments with diverse vendors, devices, protocols, and interfaces. In this paper, we introduce CTBench, a public benchmark for assessing whether an agent behaves like a competent telecom troubleshooting engineer. CTBench focuses on root cause analysis and path restoration. Each task is constructed by experts and annotated with rich task metadata, including golden evidence steps. CTBench uses expert-grounded metrics that evaluate both final answers and the diagnostic evidence. Experiments with representative harness-model combinations show that state-of-the-art agents perform very well at identifying endpoints in path-restoration tasks but, more generally, underperform in root cause analysis. In particular, agents struggle with interface state, link-layer, service-management, and other operational faults. Most importantly, even when agents produce plausible or correct final answers, they often fail to provide the evidence-grounded diagnoses required in operational practice. Our results further show that path restoration is generally more resource expensive, yet larger resource usage does not necessarily translate into better diagnosis.

AI.tldr: CTBench is a benchmark to evaluate whether AI agents can troubleshoot telecom networks like human engineers, especially for root cause analysis and path restoration.
AI.motivation: As telecom networks grow complex and heterogeneous, operators want to use AI agents to automate troubleshooting and maintenance. Current evaluations are unrealistic: they do not capture partial observability, multi-vendor environments, or the need for step-by-step diagnostic reasoning. There is a need for a benchmark that faithfully reflects real troubleshooting workflows and measures not just final answers but also the evidence and reasoning process.
AI.method: The authors design CTBench, a public benchmark built from expert-crafted telecom troubleshooting tasks. Tasks focus on root cause analysis and path restoration and include detailed metadata, such as golden diagnostic steps and evidence. They define expert-grounded metrics that score both the correctness of the final answer and the alignment of the agent’s reasoning with the expert evidence. They then evaluate multiple representative agent setups (model + harness) on the benchmark.
AI.result: Evaluated agents can reliably identify endpoints in path-restoration tasks, but they generally perform poorly on root cause analysis. They particularly struggle with diagnosing issues related to interface state, link-layer problems, service-management faults, and other operational issues. Agents frequently produce answers that look plausible, or are even correct, but their supporting diagnostic steps do not match the expert evidence. Path restoration tasks also consume more computational resources, but greater resource usage does not systematically improve diagnostic quality.
AI.conclusion: CTBench exposes important weaknesses of current AI agents in realistic telecom troubleshooting: they are far from matching expert engineers in evidence-grounded root cause analysis, and more resources alone do not fix this. The benchmark provides a standardized way to measure both outcome and reasoning quality, highlighting key gaps that future troubleshooting agents must address to be viable in operational telecom environments.

title: Mechanist: AI as a Scientific Instrument for Discovering the Mechanisms of Intelligence
summary: AI models have achieved remarkable success across diverse domains, yet the mechanisms underlying their capabilities and the risks they may pose remain poorly understood. As AI development becomes faster and increasingly automated, mechanistic exploration remains largely manual, widening the gap between what models can do and our ability to understand and control them. To bridge this gap, we introduce Mechanist, an agentic system that uses AI as a scientific instrument for the autonomous discovery of mechanisms underlying AI intelligence. To support autonomous mechanistic discovery, we construct an interpretability-focused knowledge graph of approximately 13,000 papers and integrate it with a multidisciplinary database of 43 million papers spanning 26 fields. We further curate a library of 32 foundational methods for mechanism analysis, causal intervention, and validation. Compared with Claude Code and existing AI-scientist systems, Mechanist generates more valuable mechanism hypotheses and executes experiments more reliably. Mechanist also demonstrates a progression from discovering model behaviors to explaining and controlling AI models. Specifically, Mechanist first uncovers a counterintuitive safety risk in scientific laboratories, showing that unsafe traits can transfer across modalities through apparently safe training data. Mechanist then develops a mechanism theory of belief, revealing how models represent world knowledge, form beliefs, infer the beliefs of others, and how these mechanisms emerge during pretraining. Finally, Mechanist translates these mechanistic insights into practical interventions that improve model performance across diverse scenarios and steer scientific foundation models toward generating DNA sequences with specified properties.

AI.tldr: Mechanist is an agentic AI system that autonomously discovers and tests mechanistic explanations of how AI models work, using a large interpretability knowledge graph, method library, and experimental tools.
AI.motivation: AI systems are rapidly increasing in capability, but the internal mechanisms behind their behavior and risks are poorly understood. Existing mechanistic interpretability work is highly manual and cannot keep up with the pace and automation of model development, creating a growing gap between what models can do and our ability to understand and control them. The paper aims to automate mechanistic discovery itself, turning AI into a scientific instrument that can systematically generate, test, and refine mechanistic hypotheses about AI models.
AI.method: The authors build Mechanist, an agentic system that orchestrates language models and tools for mechanistic interpretability. They (1) construct an interpretability-centric knowledge graph of ~13k papers and link it to a broader 43M-paper, 26-field database; (2) curate a library of 32 core methods for mechanism analysis, causal intervention, and validation; and (3) design an AI-scientist workflow that autonomously searches the literature, proposes mechanism hypotheses, designs and runs experiments on models, and iteratively refines theories. They benchmark Mechanist against Claude Code and other AI-scientist systems on hypothesis quality and experimental reliability.
AI.result: Mechanist outperforms Claude Code and existing AI-scientist baselines, producing more useful mechanistic hypotheses and executing experiments more reliably. It successfully progresses from identifying behaviors to explaining and controlling models. Concretely, it (a) discovers a lab safety risk where unsafe traits transfer across modalities via apparently benign training data; (b) develops a mechanistic theory of belief formation and representation in models, including how models encode world knowledge and reason about others’ beliefs through pretraining; and (c) uses these mechanistic insights to implement interventions that enhance model performance and to steer scientific foundation models to generate DNA sequences with targeted properties.
AI.conclusion: Automated mechanistic discovery is feasible and valuable: an agentic system like Mechanist can treat AI models as experimental subjects, autonomously generate and test mechanistic theories, and translate these insights into practical control interventions. This helps narrow the gap between rapidly advancing AI capabilities and our understanding and governance of those systems, and suggests a path toward scalable, semi-automated mechanistic interpretability and safer, more controllable AI models.

title: Graph-Structured Rubrics: Compiling Rubrics into Typed Evaluation Graphs for LLM Judges
summary: Rubric-based evaluators commonly treat rubrics as prompt context or flat criteria: they specify what to judge but leave criterion composition implicit, even when natural-language rules state it. We introduce Graph-Structured Rubrics (GSR), which compiles a rubric into a response-independent typed evaluation graph before observing responses. Criterion nodes elicit judgments; transformation, reduction, and gating operators compose them through named ports; and a task-specific output mapping, termed Readout, converts the unique sink into a score or preference. Compilation rejects malformed or type-incompatible graphs. Pointwise evaluation judges rubric dimensions separately before graph aggregation; pairwise evaluation reuses the graph with one judgment for each candidate under every criterion. Under GPT-OSS-120B, GSR improves exact score agreement by 0.62--6.75 percentage points over Prometheus-style scoring on four pointwise datasets and achieves the numerically highest end-to-end pairwise accuracy on two preference benchmarks under native tie and abstention policies.

AI.tldr: They propose Graph-Structured Rubrics (GSR), a formal, typed graph representation of rubrics that yields more accurate, consistent LLM-based evaluation than standard rubric-as-prompt approaches, for both scoring and pairwise preference tasks.
AI.motivation: Existing LLM rubric-based evaluators typically just paste rubrics into prompts or treat criteria as a flat list. This leaves the composition and dependencies between criteria implicit, even when the rubric text includes specific rules for combining judgments (weights, gates, transformations). As a result, evaluations can be inconsistent, hard to validate, and difficult to reuse across pointwise (scoring) and pairwise (preference) settings. There is a need for a more explicit, structured, and machine-checkable representation of rubrics that can be compiled, validated, and executed predictably before seeing responses.
AI.method: They define Graph-Structured Rubrics (GSR), where a rubric is compiled into a typed evaluation graph independent of any particular response. Nodes in the graph are of several types: criterion nodes that ask the model for atomic judgments; transformation nodes that convert or normalize these judgments; reduction nodes that aggregate multiple judgments; and gating nodes that control which criteria apply based on earlier judgments. Ports and types for each node enforce compatibility, and a compilation process statically rejects malformed or type-incompatible graphs. A task-specific Readout function maps the unique sink node of the graph to a final scalar score or pairwise preference. They support pointwise evaluation by first computing each rubric dimension separately and then aggregating via the graph, and pairwise evaluation by reusing the same graph while eliciting one judgment per candidate for each criterion.
AI.result: Using the GPT-OSS-120B model, GSR outperforms a Prometheus-style baseline that treats rubrics as flat prompts. On four pointwise scoring datasets, GSR improves exact score agreement with ground truth by 0.62 to 6.75 percentage points. On two pairwise preference benchmarks, with native handling of ties and abstentions, GSR attains the numerically highest end-to-end accuracy among compared methods.
AI.conclusion: Making rubric structure explicit as a typed evaluation graph improves the reliability and accuracy of LLM-based evaluators. GSR provides a compile-time check for rubric validity, a unified framework for both pointwise and pairwise evaluation, and empirically better alignment with reference scores and preferences than conventional prompt-based rubric usage. This suggests that future evaluation systems should treat rubrics as executable, structured programs rather than unstructured text prompts.

title: GUIDE: Governed Unified Intelligence for Document-to-Artifact Generation in Enterprise Settings
summary: Enterprise guideline documents are heterogeneous and multimodal, combining narrative text, complex tables, and embedded images. Existing LLM and VLM systems face hallucinated content, table structure degradation, and lack governed workflows extending beyond extraction to validation and artifact generation. This leaves enterprises to perform this manually, consuming 2-3 days per document. To address this, we introduce GUIDE, a governed multi-agent framework built on a shared versioned rule store with schema-validated inter-agent contracts and end-to-end provenance tracking. Six specialized agents handle parsing, VLM-driven extraction, consistency checking, evaluation, human-in-the-loop (HITL) escalation, and persona-tailored artifact synthesis. Evaluated on 120 real-world enterprise guideline documents, GUIDE achieves 96% document success, extracts 3,896 rules with 71.4% auto-approved, produces 812 deployment-ready artifacts, and reduces turnaround to 40-125 minutes per document.

AI.tldr: GUIDE is a governed multi-agent framework that automates understanding and operationalizing complex enterprise guideline documents, greatly reducing manual processing time while preserving structure and provenance.
AI.motivation: Enterprise guideline documents are complex, heterogeneous, and multimodal (text, tables, images). Current LLM and VLM solutions struggle with hallucinations, loss of table structure, and lack of end-to-end, governed workflows that go beyond raw extraction to include validation and generation of usable deployment artifacts. As a result, enterprises spend 2–3 days per document doing this work manually. The motivation is to create a robust, governed, and efficient system that can reliably parse, extract, validate, and operationalize guideline content at scale while keeping humans in the loop where needed.
AI.method: The paper proposes GUIDE, a governed multi-agent framework. It is built around a shared, versioned rule store and uses schema-validated contracts for communication between agents plus end-to-end provenance tracking. GUIDE defines six specialized agents: (1) a parsing agent that ingests heterogeneous guideline documents, (2) a VLM-powered extraction agent to pull rules from multimodal content, (3) a consistency-checking agent to detect conflicts and gaps, (4) an evaluation agent to score quality and readiness, (5) a human-in-the-loop escalation agent for uncertain or low-confidence cases, and (6) an artifact synthesis agent that creates persona-tailored, deployment-ready artifacts. Inter-agent interactions are governed and auditable via the rule store and provenance mechanisms.
AI.result: On a test set of 120 real-world enterprise guideline documents, GUIDE successfully processes 96% of documents end-to-end. It extracts 3,896 rules, of which 71.4% are auto-approved without requiring human intervention, and generates 812 deployment-ready artifacts. Compared to manual workflows that take 2–3 days per document, GUIDE reduces the turnaround time to approximately 40–125 minutes per document.
AI.conclusion: GUIDE demonstrates that a governed, multi-agent LLM/VLM framework with shared rule stores, schema-validated contracts, and full provenance can reliably operationalize complex multimodal guideline documents in enterprises. It substantially reduces manual effort and processing time while maintaining governance and enabling human oversight through targeted HITL escalation. This suggests that such governed multi-agent architectures are a practical way to integrate generative models into enterprise workflows for high-stakes, document-driven domains.

title: Who Thinks Best Depends on How Long You Let Them: Budget-Dependent Rankings in LLM Evaluation
summary: Standard evaluation of large language models assumes stable model rankings across inference conditions. We challenge this assumption by varying the token generation budget, i.e., the maximum tokens a model may produce, across seven levels (64--4,096), evaluating four models on three reasoning benchmarks (56,476 inferences). We report four findings: (i) 3--19% of items exhibit non-monotone behavior (accuracy decreasing with more budget), even after controlling for truncation, and this phenomenon is model-specific (cross-model overlap: 6--14%). (ii) Model rankings reverse across budgets on all benchmarks ($p {<} 0.01$, McNemar). (iii) Oracle analysis reveals model complementarity up to $+27.8$pp, most pronounced at constrained budgets. (iv) A budget-aware router captures 14.1% of the oracle gap cross-domain; budget features help within-domain ($+1.6$ to $+5.7$pp) but are domain-specific and hurt transfer ($-1.2$pp). These results argue for budget-conditioned evaluation protocols.

AI.tldr: The paper studies how changing the maximum number of tokens (generation budget) affects LLM accuracy, rankings, and routing, finding that performance and rankings are unstable across budgets and advocating budget-aware evaluation.
AI.motivation: Most LLM benchmarks assume that model performance rankings are stable regardless of decoding parameters like maximum generation length. However, in practical applications, systems often operate under different token budgets (for cost, latency, or UI reasons). The authors aim to test whether model accuracy and relative rankings are actually stable when the token generation budget changes, and to investigate how this interacts with model complementarity and routing strategies.
AI.method: They systematically vary the maximum generation length (token budget) across seven levels from 64 to 4,096 tokens. Four LLMs are evaluated on three reasoning benchmarks, yielding 56,476 total inferences. They analyze non-monotonic accuracy behavior as budgets increase, check for ranking reversals using McNemar tests, perform an oracle analysis to quantify best-possible gains from choosing the best model per item and budget, and train a budget-aware router to predict which model to use given an input and budget. They also assess within-domain vs cross-domain transfer of the router, examining whether budget features generalize.
AI.result: (i) Between 3% and 19% of evaluated items show non-monotonic behavior where accuracy actually drops when more tokens are allowed, even when controlling for truncation; this effect is model-specific with only 6–14% overlap across models. (ii) Relative model rankings change with budget and even reverse on all benchmarks, with reversals statistically significant (p<0.01 by McNemar’s test). (iii) An oracle that always selects the best model-bucket combination per item reveals strong complementarity between models, with potential gains up to +27.8 percentage points, especially under tight budgets. (iv) A learned budget-aware routing system recovers 14.1% of this oracle advantage across domains; incorporating budget features boosts within-domain routing performance by +1.6 to +5.7 percentage points, but these budget-dependent patterns do not transfer well to new domains and can slightly harm cross-domain performance (-1.2pp).
AI.conclusion: Model performance and rankings are not stable across different token generation budgets, and more budget does not always mean better accuracy. There is significant model complementarity that depends on the budget, and routing systems can partially exploit this but are sensitive to domain and budget conditions. The authors argue that evaluation protocols for LLMs should explicitly condition on token budgets rather than assuming a single, budget-agnostic ranking, especially for reasoning tasks and real-world deployment scenarios with varying cost or latency constraints.

title: How to Spend Your Oracle Budget: Practical Guidance for Protein Structure Prediction Models
comment: Proceedings of the ICML 2026 Workshop on Structured Probabilistic Inference & Generative Modeling (SPIGM)
summary: Foundation models for protein structure prediction remain unreliable on certain targets. External oracles can flag and correct these failures, but biological oracles are expensive, making oracle budget a critical constraint. Existing guidance methods, such as FK-steering, DPO, and Best K-of-N sampling, differ in how they spend this budget, yet no systematic comparison exists to guide method selection. To bridge this gap, we benchmark these methods alongside the recently proposed Optimisation Over Outputs (O3), which applies off-the-shelf optimisers within a generative model's latent subspace. We extend the usage of O3 to protein structure prediction models. Overall, our work provides the first practical reference for oracle budget-aware guidance. Our evaluation on two protein targets, calmodulin (1CLL) and E. coli aspartate transcarbamoylase (9EEH), reveals that no single method consistently dominates across all budgets and oracles. Specifically, O3 proves most effective at low oracle budgets, while FK-steering and DPO demonstrate improved performance as the budget increases. We distil these findings into actionable recommendations for practitioners operating under real-world oracle-budget constraints.

AI.tldr: They benchmark and compare several oracle-guided methods for improving protein structure prediction under limited oracle budgets, extending O3 to this domain.
AI.motivation: Protein structure foundation models can be unreliable on some targets, and biological oracles that can correct them are expensive, so it is important to know how to best use a limited oracle budget when guiding these models.
AI.method: They systematically benchmark multiple oracle-guidance strategies—FK-steering, DPO, Best K-of-N sampling, and the O3 optimisation-over-outputs framework—applied within the latent space of protein structure generative models, evaluating performance across different oracle budgets and oracle types on two protein targets (1CLL and 9EEH).
AI.result: No single method is universally best across all oracle budgets and oracle types: O3 performs best at low oracle budgets, whereas FK-steering and DPO become more effective as the oracle budget increases.
AI.conclusion: The paper offers the first practical, comparative reference for oracle budget-aware guidance in protein structure prediction, showing that method choice should depend on available oracle budget and providing concrete recommendations for practitioners under realistic resource constraints.

title: An Agentic Workflow for Legacy HPC Modernization: Converting the Two-Electron-Integral Core of GAMESS
summary:
Modernizing legacy Fortran is a problem of volume: the transformations are individually routine, but the codebases can be enormous, and across much of computational science the work simply goes undone. We propose an agentic workflow that takes this work on at production scale, and we set out to measure how far such delegation can reach. In this work, three prompt-specialized agent roles operate under a version-controlled specification that the agents themselves authored and revised, while humans hold a small number of gates. The arrangement is kept safe by an exact verification oracle inherited from the domain, and the boundary of safe delegation lies exactly where that oracle stops seeing.
  We apply the proposed workflow in a case study, converting the two-electron-integral routines of GAMESS (General Atomic and Molecular Electronic Structure System), a mature quantum-chemistry package with a 48-year development history, from fixed-form Fortran 77 to free-form Fortran 2008. The scope of this work was twelve source files, 56,448 lines, and 225 subroutines for computing electron repulsion integrals. The agents ran as three Claude Code roles in isolated worktrees, and the work spanned four Claude model generations. Because the GAMESS group ships a standard test suite whose printed energies its user community treats as canonical, we could adopt bit-for-bit reproduction of those energies as the merge criterion, where a deviation in the twelfth decimal place counts as a failure rather than drift. All twelve source files pass a 51-test validation battery comprising the 49 standard GAMESS tests and two additional calculations, and across 612 test runs the number of chemistry-relevant differences is zero, and every file also passes the Jenkins tests that are used for continuous integration.

AI.tldr: The paper presents an AI-agent workflow that safely modernizes large legacy Fortran codebases, demonstrated by converting key GAMESS quantum-chemistry routines from Fortran 77 to Fortran 2008 with bit-for-bit identical scientific results.
AI.motivation: Legacy Fortran code underpins much of computational science, but it is difficult to modernize at scale due to huge code volumes and largely manual, tedious transformations. As a result, critical scientific software remains outdated, harder to maintain, extend, and integrate with modern tooling. The authors want to see how much of this modernization work can be reliably delegated to AI agents while preserving scientific correctness.
AI.method: They design an agentic workflow with three specialized AI agent roles (prompt-tailored Claude Code instances) working in isolated version-controlled worktrees. The agents themselves author and iteratively revise a modernization specification, while humans only intervene at a few gated decision points. Safety is ensured using an exact verification oracle from the application domain: the standard GAMESS test suite that checks bit-for-bit identity of computed energies. Any deviation, even in the twelfth decimal place, is treated as failure. The workflow is applied to modernize GAMESS two-electron-integral routines from fixed-form Fortran 77 to free-form Fortran 2008 across multiple model generations.
AI.result: Twelve GAMESS source files, including 56,448 lines and 225 subroutines for electron repulsion integrals, are converted from Fortran 77 to Fortran 2008. Using the standard GAMESS test suite (49 tests) plus two additional calculations, all twelve files pass a 51-test validation battery with 612 total test runs. There are zero chemistry-relevant differences in outputs, and all files also pass the Jenkins CI tests, indicating complete functional equivalence after modernization.
AI.conclusion: An AI-driven, agentic workflow can modernize large, complex legacy Fortran codebases while preserving strict scientific correctness, as validated by exact domain-specific oracles. With minimal human gating and strong automated verification, such systems can operate at production scale, and the safe delegation boundary is precisely defined by the reach of the verification oracle. This demonstrates a viable path for large-scale modernization of legacy scientific software.

title: VAKRA: Evaluating Multi-Hop Reasoning Across APIs and Retrieval Under Tool-Use Policies
summary: Agents deployed in enterprise settings must reason across structured APIs and document collections, yet existing benchmarks evaluate these capabilities in isolation. We introduce VAKRA (e\textbf{V}aluating \textbf{A}PI and \textbf{K}nowledge \textbf{R}etrieval \textbf{A}gents), a benchmark of over $8{,}000$ executable APIs across $62$ domains with tasks spanning three settings of increasing difficulty: diverse API interaction styles, multi-hop reasoning over structured APIs, and multi-source reasoning with natural-language tool-use policy constraints. Correctness is verified by re-executing predicted tool calls against live APIs, accommodating multiple valid paths. Using a fixed ReAct harness to isolate model capabilities from agent architecture, we evaluate frontier and open-weight models and find that even the best model achieves only 70.4\% on single-hop endpoint-style tasks and drops to 50--51\% on compositional APIs; performance degrades by over 50\% as reasoning depth increases, and policy-constrained questions expose severe failures (as low as 2.4\% on unanswerable queries). Trace analysis shows failures concentrate at language-mediated reasoning - entity disambiguation, cross-source grounding, rather than tool invocation mechanics. Code is available https://github.com/IBM/VAKRA. Dataset is available https://huggingface.co/datasets/ibm-research/VAKRA

AI.tldr: VAKRA is a benchmark to evaluate enterprise agents’ ability to combine structured API calls and document retrieval, revealing large gaps in current models’ reasoning under realistic tool-use conditions.
AI.motivation: Real-world enterprise agents must handle both structured APIs and unstructured document collections together, but existing benchmarks typically test API use and knowledge retrieval separately, failing to capture the combined, multi-step, policy-constrained reasoning these agents actually need.
AI.method: The authors build VAKRA, a benchmark with 8,000+ executable APIs across 62 domains and design tasks in three settings: (1) diverse single-hop API interaction styles, (2) multi-hop reasoning over compositional/structured APIs, and (3) multi-source reasoning that also obeys natural-language tool-use policy constraints. They verify correctness by re-executing predicted tool calls against live APIs and allow multiple valid solution paths. Using a fixed ReAct-style agent harness, they evaluate both frontier and open-weight models to isolate model capability from agent architecture.
AI.result: Even strong models only reach about 70.4% accuracy on simpler single-hop endpoint-style tasks and about 50–51% on compositional APIs. As required reasoning depth increases, performance drops by more than 50%, and on policy-constrained questions—especially unanswerable ones—accuracy can fall as low as 2.4%. Error trace analysis shows that failures cluster around language-mediated reasoning steps like entity disambiguation and cross-source grounding rather than basic tool invocation mechanics.
AI.conclusion: Current LLM-based agents struggle significantly when required to perform deep, multi-hop, and policy-constrained reasoning that combines structured APIs and document retrieval, even though they can execute individual tool calls. VAKRA exposes these limitations and offers a realistic, executable benchmark for measuring and improving enterprise agents’ capabilities in such settings.

title: Constructing Dynamic Master Logic Models as Knowledge Graphs for Complex System Diagnostics Using Retrieval-Augmented Large Language Models
summary: Dynamic Master Logic (DML) provides a hierarchical framework for representing system behavior by linking functional objectives to underlying structural elements. However, DML construction typically relies on expert interpretation of technical documentation, limiting scalability for complex systems. This study presents a framework for automated construction of DML models from system descriptions and their representation as Knowledge Graphs (KG-DML), using Retrieval-Augmented Generation and Large Language Models as enabling tools. Building on prior work with small-scale systems, the framework extends automated KG-DML construction and evaluation to substantially larger and more complex systems. Model construction proceeds across the DML hierarchy using targeted retrieval while preserving functional dependencies and explicit logical relationships. The resulting KG-DML supports diagnostic reasoning, safety assessment, upward failure propagation, and downward dependency tracing. A multi-level validation methodology evaluates layer-specific precision and recall, logical gate consistency, and overall structural integrity. Application to the Low-Pressure Coolant Injection system of a decommissioned Boiling Water Reactor demonstrates consistent reconstruction across repeated runs. The results show that automated KG-DML construction can transform technical documentation into executable functional models for diagnostic and reliability analysis.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes an automated method to build Dynamic Master Logic (DML) models as knowledge graphs from system documentation using LLMs and retrieval, and validates it on a complex nuclear plant subsystem.
AI.motivation: Traditional DML models, which link system functions to structure hierarchically, are powerful for diagnostics and safety analysis but are manually constructed from technical documents by experts, making them time-consuming, subjective, and hard to scale to large, complex systems. There is a need to automate DML construction to handle more complex systems and to systematically exploit existing documentation.
AI.method: The authors design a framework that converts system descriptions into Dynamic Master Logic knowledge graphs (KG-DML) using Retrieval-Augmented Generation with Large Language Models. The method incrementally builds the DML hierarchy layer by layer, using targeted retrieval of relevant documentation for each part of the model while enforcing preservation of functional dependencies and explicit logical gate relationships. They introduce a multi-level validation methodology that checks precision and recall at each hierarchical layer, consistency of logic gates, and global structural integrity, and evaluate repeatability across multiple model-generation runs.
AI.result: Applied to the Low-Pressure Coolant Injection system of a decommissioned Boiling Water Reactor—a substantially larger and more complex system than in previous work—the framework consistently reconstructs KG-DML models across repeated executions. The generated models maintain functional dependencies and logical structures sufficiently well to support diagnostic reasoning, safety assessment, and both upward failure propagation and downward dependency tracing.
AI.conclusion: Automated construction of KG-DML models from technical documentation using RAG and LLMs is feasible and robust enough to handle complex engineering systems. The approach can reliably transform unstructured system descriptions into executable functional models suitable for diagnostic and reliability analyses, suggesting it can significantly reduce expert effort and improve scalability of DML-based safety and diagnostic modeling.
